The Herodians were exactly that party: courtiers and supporters of Herod Antipas, worldly, political, invested in the arrangement with Rome that kept them comfortable. A Pharisee would not eat at a Herodian's table. On religion, politics, money and nationhood they agreed on nothing whatsoever.

And they are in a room together within minutes of the healing, and they agree at once.

Nothing on earth makes allies like a shared hatred of the light. Men who cannot agree on a single positive thing will find they can cooperate beautifully on a negative one. Pilate and Herod, Luke notes drily, became friends with each other that same day — the day they both had a hand in condemning Jesus (Luke 23:12). It is one of the ugliest reliable facts about human nature, and it is on display in Galilee before the Gospel is a fifth of the way through.

How to destroy him. Not how to discredit him, out-argue him, or have him disciplined. The word is destroy, and Mark is not softening it.

Now set the whole verse against the day it happened on. It is still the Sabbath. Jesus has been accused of violating the day by restoring a man's hand with a sentence; his accusers spend the remainder of the same holy day organising a killing. They would not have carried a bed. They will carry a cross to the authorities.

That is what a hardened heart looks like from the inside: entirely convinced it is defending God, with murder in the diary. Nobody in that consultation thought of himself as wicked. They thought of themselves as serious.

And here is the sober word for anyone who takes doctrine seriously, as we should. Correct theology is not a preservative. These were the orthodox party. They believed in the resurrection, the authority of Scripture, the coming Messiah, the moral law — and they left a service in which God had visibly acted and went straight into a meeting about how to kill him. The safeguard was never the doctrine on its own. It was whether the doctrine was still attached to love for God and pity for people, and in these men it had come away.

One more thing, and Mark means you to feel it. Chapter 3 of sixteen, and the death of Jesus is already decided. Everything from here is a man walking, with his eyes open, toward a verdict that has already been reached — and he heals somebody in nearly every chapter on the way.

verseByVerse.quote: Jesus withdrew with his disciples to the sea, and a great crowd followed, from Galilee and Judea and Jerusalem and Idumea and from beyond the Jordan and from around Tyre and Sidon. When the great crowd heard all that he was doing, they came to him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus withdrew. He does not escalate. He does not go looking for the men who have just decided to kill him, and he does not stay in the synagogue to make a point. He leaves the building and goes down to the lake, and the ministry gets bigger.

That is worth marking. The opposition of the leaders did not thin the crowd; it thickened it. What was intended to shut him down pushed him out of a room that held eighty people and onto a shoreline that could hold thousands.

And a great crowd followed. Then Mark does something he rarely bothers with: he lists the addresses. Six regions in two verses, and the list is not padding — it is a map, and it is worth reading with a finger on it.

Galilee is home, the northern province. Judea and Jerusalem are the religious heartland eighty and ninety miles south, which means people have walked for the better part of a week. Idumea is the old country of Edom, down beyond the southern desert — the descendants of Esau, forcibly converted a century earlier, still regarded as barely Jewish; Herod's own people. Beyond the Jordan is the east bank, Gentile-mixed. And Tyre and Sidon are not in Israel at all: they are Phoenician port cities on the coast to the north-west, pagan cities, the cities of Jezebel's father.

Now look at the shape of that list. It runs from the centre outward in every direction — north, south, east, west, Jew, half-Jew, Gentile. Mark is not just reporting attendance figures. He is showing you a crowd assembling that looks, in miniature, like the church that is coming: everyone from everywhere, drawn to one man, most of them nowhere near understanding him yet.

And it is a rehearsal of a promise older than any of them. To Abraham: in you all the families of the earth shall be blessed (Gen. 12:3). To the Servant: it is too light a thing that you should be my servant... I will make you as a light for the nations, that my salvation may reach to the end of the earth (Isa. 49:6). By the end of this Gospel a Roman soldier will look at a dead man on a cross and say the true thing that none of the crowd said (15:39), and by Acts the same list will have kept going until it reaches Rome.

When the great crowd heard all that he was doing, they came to him. Be honest about why they came. Not for the teaching — Mark says they had heard what he was doing. This is a crowd assembled by reports of power, and within a few chapters most of it will be gone, because the day comes when he says something hard and many of his disciples turned back and no longer walked with him (John 6:66).

Which is a fair question to put to yourself, since crowds are still gathered by what God might do. What brought you? And more to the point, what is keeping you? Some of the people who walked a hundred miles to that shoreline were there because of what they had heard he could give. Some were there because of who he was. The shoreline looked identical either way, and only one of the two survives a hard winter.

verseByVerse.quote: And he told his disciples to have a boat ready for him because of the crowd, lest they crush him, for he had healed many, so that all who had diseases pressed around him to touch him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Here is a detail nobody expects in a Gospel: Jesus arranges an escape route.

Have a boat ready for him. A small fishing boat, kept just offshore, a few yards out. Not to sail anywhere — as a platform, and as a way out. Mark tells us plainly why: lest they crush him. The verb is the one you would use of a mob pressing a man against a wall.

Understand what was actually happening on that beach. This is not an audience. It is a crowd of desperate, sick, frightened people who have heard that touching this man works, and every one of them wants to get a hand on him. Mark says they were pressing around him — the word means falling upon him. There were children in that crowd. People got hurt in crowds like that.

And Jesus, who could have stilled them with a sentence, quietly asks his friends to get a boat.

Sit with that, because it is more pastoral than it looks. The Son of God, in a real human body, with a real human back and real human exhaustion, took an ordinary practical precaution. He did not despise the means. He did not stand there and let himself be trampled in order to prove something about faith.

There is a lesson here that tired Christians badly need and rarely give themselves permission to hear. Jesus did not meet every need that presented itself, and he did not stay available every hour that people wanted him. He withdrew (v. 7). He slept in boats (4:38). He got up before dawn and went where they could not find him (1:35). He let a crowd stand on a beach while he pushed out a few yards into the water.

If you are the person everyone comes to — in a family, a church, a job — take the boat. Being finite is not a character flaw; it is how you were made, and the Lord himself worked within it. The needs around you are genuinely infinite and you are genuinely not, and pretending otherwise is not devotion. It is a slow way of becoming useless to everybody.

For he had healed many. Mark gives the reason for the crush almost as an aside, and it is worth stopping on. Many. Not a handful of documented cases. So many that the beach became dangerous.

All who had diseases pressed around him to touch him. Mark's word here is a strong one — literally scourges, the word for a whip. Their diseases are not described as inconveniences but as things that flog them. That is how illness feels from the inside, and Mark does not tidy it up.

And notice that he heals them. This is a crowd with no theology, no invitation, no understanding of who he is; they are simply people in pain who have heard he helps, mobbing him so hard he needs an exit. He does not lecture them about their motives first. He heals them.

Which is a mercy to remember when you come to him yourself with mixed motives and a bad attitude, wanting relief far more than you want him. He has never yet turned away a person for coming to him badly. Come as the crowd came, and let him sort out your motives once you are near enough for him to reach.

verseByVerse.quote: And whenever the unclean spirits saw him, they fell down before him and cried out, "You are the Son of God." And he strictly ordered them not to make him known.
verseByVerse.commentary:
In that whole heaving crowd — hundreds of people from six regions, apostles included — the only voices saying anything theologically exact belong to the demons.

They fell down before him. Mark's word is the ordinary word for prostration, the posture of worship. They are not doing it willingly; they are doing it because in his presence they cannot do anything else. It is a small, involuntary rehearsal of a day that is coming: at the name of Jesus every knee should bow, in heaven and on earth and under the earth (Phil. 2:10). Every knee. Including these. The only question any creature gets to decide is whether it bows now in love or later in ruin.

You are the Son of God. That is not an approximation. It is the exact phrase from the voice at the Jordan (1:11), and it is more than the disciples have managed to say, and more than the crowd has understood, and more than the scribes will allow.

And it does the demons no good at all.

Take hold of that, because it dismantles something a lot of people are resting on. A creed can be word-perfect and worthless. James puts it with no cushioning: you believe that God is one; you do well. Even the demons believe — and shudder (Jas. 2:19). These spirits have better Christology than most of the crowd. They fall down, which is more than the Pharisees did. They confess his identity out loud, which is more than Peter has yet done. And they remain exactly what they are.

So here is the test, and it is uncomfortable in a church where doctrine is valued, as it should be. Could you tick every box on a statement of faith and still be, in your own heart, at a distance from the Person the statements are about? The difference between the demons' confession and a Christian's is not accuracy. It is that one says you are the Son of God and means keep away from me, and the other says the same words and means have me. Mark will end this very chapter by telling you which one you are: not by what you can recite, but by whether you do the will of God (v. 35).

And he strictly ordered them not to make him known. The verb is forceful — he rebuked them into silence.

Why refuse testimony that is true? Partly timing. If Mark 1 showed the reason in a single synagogue, here it is a mass movement: in Galilee in that decade, Son of God shouted over a crowd of thousands from six regions would have been heard as a call to arms — a king to drive out Rome. Jesus will not be crowned before he is crucified, because a title taken on those terms would have to be unlearned at the cross. He lets the words stand at last when a Roman officer says them at the foot of it (15:39), where nobody can mistake what kind of King he is.

And partly the messenger. The truth about the Son of God is not going to be carried on the tongue of the father of lies. He will not have his name announced by his enemies. That commission belongs to a fisherman, a tax collector, a Zealot — and to you.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 13–35 — The Twelve, the Accusation, and the True Family
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The mountain (vv. 13–19). Jesus goes up, calls whom he wants, and constitutes twelve men — a number nobody in Israel could hear innocently. The stated purpose comes in two halves in a deliberate order: that they might be with him, and that he might send them out. The list ends on a name that ruins it.

The two accusations (vv. 20–22). Back at the house the pressure is such that they cannot even eat, and two verdicts arrive from opposite directions. His family says he is out of his mind and comes to take him home. A delegation from Jerusalem says he is possessed and works by the prince of demons. Both agree something is badly wrong with him; they differ only on whether he is mad or evil.

The answer (vv. 23–27). Jesus takes the charge apart with cold logic and then turns it round: the reason demons are leaving is that a stronger man has broken into the house, tied up the owner, and is carrying out his property.

The warning and the family (vv. 28–35). The widest promise of forgiveness in the Gospel, with one terrible exception attached — and then his mother and brothers arrive outside, and he looks round at the people sitting on the floor and calls them his family.
verseByVerse.theology:
The strong man of v. 27 is the hinge of the chapter and of the Gospel. Jesus concedes the scribes' premise that there is a real kingdom of darkness with a real ruler and a securely held house. What he denies is which side of the door he is on. He is not an agent of the owner. He is the burglar.

And the order in the picture is exact: the binding comes first, the plundering after. You cannot carry off a strong man's goods while he is loose. Every exorcism in Mark, every healing, every sinner set free, is loot being carried out of a house whose owner has already been tied up. This is why the New Testament can speak of Christians as people delivered from the domain of darkness and transferred to the kingdom of his beloved Son (Col. 1:13) — transferred is a word for moving property.

Then ask when the binding happened, and the answer is the surprise at the centre of the faith. He bound the strong man by being bound himself. He disarmed the rulers and authorities and put them to open shame, triumphing over them in him — in the cross (Col. 2:15). The strong man was tied up by a stronger man who let himself be tied up first, so that through death he might destroy the one who has the power of death (Heb. 2:14).
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: twelve men appointed so that they might be with him — and only then be sent out. Three years of watching him pray, eat, weep, touch lepers, sleep in boats, before a single one of them preached a sermon.

Now: the order is still not negotiable, and it is still the thing we reverse. It is entirely possible to be extremely busy for God and scarcely ever with him — to run a rota, lead a group, defend the faith online, and go months without an unhurried hour in his company. The activity is not the problem; the sequence is. Ministry that does not flow out of being with Jesus becomes performance, and performance eventually becomes exhaustion or pride, and often both.

The plainest way to test it is the calendar. Look at last week honestly. How much of it was doing things for him, and how much was being with him? If the first number is large and the second is near zero, you have inverted verse 14, and no amount of usefulness will make up for it — because the sending was never meant to be the source of the strength.

And there is comfort in the same verse for the person who cannot do much at all: the first calling on every disciple is one that illness, age and obscurity cannot take away.

verseByVerse.quote: And he went up on the mountain and called to him those whom he desired, and they came to him. And he appointed twelve (whom he also named apostles) so that they might be with him and he might send them out to preach and have authority to cast out demons.
verseByVerse.commentary:
He went up on the mountain. Mark does not name it, and the vagueness is a signal — in the Bible, going up a mountain to constitute a people is not a neutral piece of travel. Moses went up and came down with a nation ordered around twelve tribes. Luke adds that Jesus spent the whole night there in prayer before he chose (Luke 6:12).

Called to him those whom he desired. Sit on that phrase, because it decides who is in charge of this. Not those who volunteered. Not those who qualified. Those whom he wanted. The initiative is entirely his, and it always is: You did not choose me, but I chose you (John 15:16).

If you belong to Christ today, that is the reason. Not that you were searching harder than your neighbour or that something in you recommended itself. He wanted you. There is nothing behind that but his own good pleasure, which is exactly why nothing can get behind it and undo it.

And they came to him. Four words that are easy to skip and are half the doctrine. He calls, and they come. His wanting is what produces their coming; the call is not an offer left on the table but a summons that creates the answer, the way the same voice once said let there be light and there was light.

He appointed twelve. Nobody in Israel could hear that number innocently. Twelve sons of Jacob, twelve tribes, twelve stones on the high priest's breastplate, twelve pillars at the foot of Sinai. Ten of those tribes had been lost for seven hundred years, and the prophets had promised they would be gathered again. Jesus does not preach a sermon about restoring Israel. He appoints twelve men, and every Jew watching understands that a claim has just been made without a word of argument. This is Israel, beginning again, around him.

So that they might be with him. Here is the first purpose, and it is not what a modern reader expects. Not so that they might be trained, or deployed, or made useful. So that they might be with him. Their first job description is his company.

Take the measure of that. These men are about to spend three years mostly watching. Watching him pray before dawn, watching him handle a hostile room, watching what he does when he is tired and interrupted, watching him touch a leper, watching him eat with the wrong people. Almost none of it will feel like ministry. All of it is the training.

And he might send them out to preach and have authority to cast out demons. Then the second purpose, and the two are in an order that never reverses. Sent men are with-him men first. You cannot go out with his authority if you have not been in his company, and the moment a church or a Christian swaps those round, the work starts to hollow out from the inside.

That is the diagnosis for a very common kind of Christian tiredness. Not too much work. Too much work fed from too little Christ — a rota, a group, an argument to win online, and months without an unhurried hour with him. Verse 14 is the cure and it is very simple: go back and be with him. Everything else is downstream, and always was.

And there is a mercy in it for anyone who can no longer do much of anything — the elderly, the ill, the housebound, the one whose usefulness has been taken away. The first calling on every disciple is one that no illness can revoke. You are called to be with him, and you can do that from a bed.

verseByVerse.quote: He appointed the twelve: Simon (to whom he gave the name Peter); James the son of Zebedee and John the brother of James (to whom he gave the name Boanerges, that is, Sons of Thunder); Andrew, and Philip, and Bartholomew, and Matthew, and Thomas, and James the son of Alphaeus, and Thaddaeus, and Simon the Zealot,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Mark writes out the names, and it is worth reading them slowly, because a list is easy to skim and this one is an argument.

Simon, to whom he gave the name Peter. Not a nickname; a verdict spoken in advance. Peter means rock, and at the moment it was given, Simon was anything but — impulsive, loud, and less than three years from swearing in a courtyard that he had never met the man. Jesus names him for what grace will make him, not for what he is. That is how he speaks to his people: he calls things that are not as though they were.

James and John, Boanerges, Sons of Thunder. A name with a smile in it and an edge under the smile. Thunder is loud, sudden, and does no work; and Mark will show you exactly why they earned it. These are the brothers who ask to call down fire on a village that will not receive him (Luke 9:54), and who come privately to request the two best seats in the kingdom (10:35–40). Jesus knew their temperament on the day he chose them, gave it a name, and appointed them anyway. He is not recruiting finished men.

Andrew. Peter's brother, who was there first (John 1:40–42) and who spends his whole New Testament career bringing people to Jesus and disappearing — his brother, a boy with some bread and fish, some Greeks who asked to see him. He is second in the family and second in the lists, and he never once shows any sign of minding. If your service is small and nobody attaches your name to it, Andrew is your man.

Philip, Bartholomew, Thomas, James the son of Alphaeus, Thaddaeus. Of these, most say almost nothing in the New Testament, and three say nothing at all. There is no recorded sermon of Thaddaeus. We have not one line from James the son of Alphaeus. They were with him for three years and are known to history as a name in a list — and their names are in the foundations of the city of God (Rev. 21:14). If it troubles you that your life will leave no trace anyone can point to, look hard at the middle of this list.

Matthew. The tax collector of chapter 2, the collaborator, the man whose repentance his own religion had judged impossible.

Simon the Zealot. And now do the arithmetic that Mark expects you to do. The Zealots were the nationalist resistance — men committed to driving Rome out of Israel by violence, and to whom a Jew who collected Rome's money was a traitor deserving a knife. In any other year of the world's history, Simon the Zealot's ambition would have been to kill a man like Matthew.

They are on the same list. They walked the same roads for three years, ate from the same bag, and slept in the same fields. Nothing in the politics of the day could have reconciled them; nothing did, except the man in the middle. That is the church, from the very first day it had members — people with nothing in common but Christ, which turns out to be more than everything they had against each other. If the church you attend contains people you would never otherwise have chosen, it is working.

verseByVerse.quote: and Judas Iscariot, who betrayed him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And Judas Iscariot, who betrayed him.

Mark has been listing names in a plain, unhurried way, and then the sentence ends and the floor gives way. Every list of the Twelve in the New Testament ends here, and every one of them attaches the same clause. Nobody could say the name afterwards without saying what he did.

Iscariot most likely means the man of Kerioth, a town in southern Judea — which would make him the only one of the Twelve who was not a Galilean. The perpetual outsider in the group, if so; the one with the different accent.

And he was appointed on the mountain with the rest. He was called by name. He was one of those whom he desired (v. 13). He was there to be with him for three years — at the feeding of the five thousand, at the transfiguration's aftermath, at every private explanation of every parable. He was sent out with the others to preach and given authority to cast out demons (6:7, 13), and there is no hint anywhere that his mission failed or that the others suspected him. When Jesus said at the last supper that one of them would betray him, nobody turned and looked at Judas. They each asked whether it was themselves (14:19).

Which raises the two questions this verse always raises, and both deserve a straight answer.

Did Jesus know? Yes. John says so without qualification: Jesus knew from the beginning who those were who did not believe, and who it was who would betray him (John 6:64). The appointment of Judas is not an error later regretted. Nor does it make Judas a puppet. Mark holds the two together without embarrassment at the end: the Son of Man goes as it is written of him, but woe to that man by whom the Son of Man is betrayed (14:21). It was written; and he did it, and he is answerable for it. Both.

And there is a strange comfort in it if you have ever been betrayed by someone close. Your Lord chose his traitor with his eyes open, kept him at his own table, washed his feet, and called him friend in the garden. He was not caught out. Nothing that has been done to you has caught him out either.

Then can I fall away like Judas? This is the question that keeps sensitive people awake, so let it be answered plainly. Judas was never a believer who lost his salvation; he was a man who was near Christ without ever being in Christ, and John names the mechanism — he had been helping himself to the money bag for a long time (John 12:6). The rot was private, ordinary and financial, and it ran for years under an unblemished public record. He did not fall in one night. He arrived at that night.

So no, you cannot be snatched out of the Father's hand (John 10:28–29). But do not use that as a reason to skip the examination; use it as the reason you can bear to make it. The honest test is not whether you have ever sinned badly — Peter denied him with oaths that same week and was restored on a beach. The test is what you do afterwards. Judas felt remorse, threw the money into the temple, and went out to a rope. Peter wept, and came back. Remorse looks at itself and despairs; repentance turns to Christ and lives.

If you fear you are a Judas, that fear is not the mark of a Judas. Judas sat through the warning at the supper and reached for the bread. Go to Christ with the thing you are afraid of. That is the one move Judas never made, and it was always available to him.

verseByVerse.quote: Then he went home, and the crowd gathered again, so that they could not even eat. And when his family heard it, they went out to seize him, for they were saying, "He is out of his mind."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then he went home. Back to the house in Capernaum, presumably Peter's, and immediately the whole thing starts again — the crowd gathered again, so that they could not even eat.

Mark keeps giving us these small physical details and they are not decoration. Not that they could not rest, or could not talk: they could not eat. The Son of God missed meals because of the volume of human need at the door. Whatever else was true of that household, it was chaotic, exhausting and loud, and it had been for weeks.

And when his family heard it. Word travels twenty-five miles up the road to Nazareth: the crowds, the missed meals, the confrontation with the authorities, the reports of demons and healings and a delegation on its way from Jerusalem. And his family gets up and comes.

They went out to seize him. The verb is strong and physical — to take hold of, to arrest. It is the same word used later of the mob that comes for him in the garden (14:46). They are not coming to encourage him. They intend to take him home by force, and to do it before he embarrasses the family any further or gets himself killed.

He is out of his mind. That is their diagnosis, and Mark reports it without softening. His own people concluded he was mad.

Now stay with the sharpest edge of this, because verse 31 will tell you exactly who came, and the first name on the list is his mother.

Mary, who had heard the angel; who had said let it be to me according to your word; who had been told her son would be called the Son of the Most High and reign forever; who had kept the shepherds' words and treasured them in her heart (Luke 1:26–38; 2:19). And here she is on the road to Capernaum with her other sons, to take this one home before it gets worse.

This is not a detail to smooth over, and it says something worth holding on to. Mary was not a woman of flawless, finished faith standing serenely above the confusion of ordinary disciples. She was a real disciple, and like every real disciple she had to grow — her understanding stretched, corrected and deepened, sometimes painfully. His brothers were further back still: not even his brothers believed in him (John 7:5).

And that is finally an encouragement rather than a scandal, because of where her story goes. The Mary who is standing outside the crowd here is the Mary who stands at the foot of the cross when eleven of the Twelve have run (John 19:25), and who is found in the upper room praying with the believers after the resurrection (Acts 1:14). She moved from outside to inside; from misunderstanding to worship — which is precisely the journey this passage is about to define as belonging to the true family: not perfect comprehension, but doing the will of God.

So if your own coming to Christ has been uneven, with long stretches where you did not understand him at all, you are in the company of his mother.

And if it is your own family who now think your faith excessive — who say you have taken this too far, that it has become unhealthy, that somebody should have a word with you — then hear this carefully. Your Lord felt that wound first, and from the people who knew him best. He did not harden against them, and he did not let it turn him aside from the will of God. He kept doing what his Father sent him to do, and he stayed tender toward them while he did it. By the end, his brother James is writing a letter to the church as a servant of the Lord Jesus Christ, and his mother is in the prayer meeting.

verseByVerse.quote: And the scribes who came down from Jerusalem were saying, "He is possessed by Beelzebul," and "by the prince of demons he casts out the demons."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The second verdict arrives from the opposite direction, and this one has credentials.

The scribes who came down from Jerusalem. Not local critics. A delegation from the capital, sent up to Galilee to assess this man officially. Mark says they came down, which is how a Jew always spoke of leaving Jerusalem regardless of the map, because the city was up whatever the compass said. These are the professionals, the men whose judgement carries weight, and they have travelled ninety miles to render it.

And here is what they cannot do: deny the exorcisms. That option is not on the table for them, and it is worth pausing over, because it is often assumed that Jesus's opponents thought the miracles were tricks. They did not. The people best placed to expose a fraud, with every professional motive to do so, concede the events and dispute only the power behind them. The evidence was not in question in Galilee. The explanation was.

He is possessed by Beelzebul. The name has a sneer built into it. It appears to go back to Baal-zebul, lord of the exalted house — a Philistine god whose name the Israelites bent into Baal-zebub, lord of the flies (2 Kgs. 1:2), a piece of holy mockery: your great lord is a god of the dunghill. By Jesus's day the word had settled as a title for the prince of the demons.

So the charge is as bad as a charge can be. Not that he is mistaken. Not even that he is a fraud. That the power visibly operating in him is the power of hell, and that the man himself is occupied by it.

Notice the two accusations Mark has set side by side. His family says he is mad; the theologians say he is evil. Between them they cover the ground that people have covered ever since, because there have only ever been three available verdicts on Jesus of Nazareth and the third one is expensive. He is deluded, or he is dangerous, or he is what he says he is. What is not on the menu — never was, not in Capernaum and not now — is the comfortable modern option of a wise and gentle teacher whom everyone can admire. Nobody who actually met him thought that. They loved him or they wanted him dead.

And there is a hard word here for anyone who assumes that more information would settle the matter. These scribes had the best religious education available in the world at that time. They had the Scriptures largely by memory. They had walked ninety miles and stood in the room and watched the power of God set human beings free with their own eyes — and they went home and wrote it up as demonic.

The problem was never the evidence. When a heart has decided, it will build a theology to house the decision, and the better educated it is, the better the theology it can build. That is why Jesus answers them, in the next verses, with logic first and mercy second — and why the warning that follows is the most frightening thing he ever said.

verseByVerse.quote: And he called them to him and said to them in parables, "How can Satan cast out Satan? If a kingdom is divided against itself, that kingdom cannot stand. And if a house is divided against itself, that house will not be able to stand. And if Satan has risen up against himself and is divided, he cannot stand, but is coming to an end.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And he called them to him. Before a word of the argument, notice this. They have just accused him of being possessed by the devil, and his response is to invite them closer. He does not shout it across the room or dismiss them behind their backs. He calls the men who have slandered him into conversation.

How can Satan cast out Satan? Then he takes the charge apart, and he does it with cold logic rather than outrage. This is worth noticing in itself: when the most serious accusation in the Gospel is laid against him, Jesus reasons. He does not merely assert. There is a place for argument in the defence of the faith, and the Lord uses it.

The argument runs in three steps, and it is airtight.

A kingdom divided cannot stand. Everyone in that room knew the history of a divided kingdom. Israel had split in two after Solomon and never recovered; the northern half was gone forever. And they were living in the aftermath of Rome's own civil wars. This is not an abstract principle for them; it is the story of their nation.

A house divided cannot stand. Smaller and closer — a household at war with itself comes apart. Anyone who has watched a family tear itself in half over money or a grievance knows the proof without needing the argument.

If Satan has risen up against himself, he cannot stand, but is coming to an end. And there is the trap closing. The scribes' theory requires that the devil has begun a systematic campaign of expelling his own troops from the people he had captured — that he is dismantling his own operation, in public, with visible success. If that were true, then their theory has just announced the end of the kingdom of darkness, which is precisely what they came to deny.

Their explanation cannot be salvaged. Either the exorcisms are not from Satan, or Satan is finished. There is no third position.

Two things to take away from how he does this.

First, he grants them what is true. Jesus does not say there is no devil, no kingdom of darkness, no organised opposition. He concedes the whole framework and shows that it will not carry the weight they have put on it. That is how a Christian should handle an argument — take what is right in it seriously, and press the part that fails.

Second, and more searchingly: an unanswerable argument changed nobody in that room. Jesus wins the exchange completely, and the scribes go home unmoved and their verdict stands. Keep that in mind when you are burning to win an argument about the faith with someone you love. Argument can clear away an obstacle, and it is worth making well. It has never yet, on its own, changed a heart. That work belongs to the Spirit — which is exactly the Person these men are about to be warned against resisting.

verseByVerse.quote: But no one can enter a strong man's house and plunder his goods, unless he first binds the strong man. Then indeed he may plunder his house.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now Jesus stops defending and goes on the attack, and he does it with one picture that turns the accusation inside out.

No one can enter a strong man's house and plunder his goods, unless he first binds the strong man. A house. A strong owner. Goods stacked inside that belong to him and are secure because he is strong enough to keep them. And a burglar who wants what is in there.

Notice first what Jesus concedes. He does not deny that there is a strong man, or that the house has been securely held, or that the goods are genuinely in his possession. The picture takes the kingdom of darkness completely seriously. There is an owner, and the property is his by right of conquest.

And the goods are people. That is the whole force of it. Every possessed man in Galilee, every soul in the crowd on the beach, every reader of this page before Christ came for them, is inventory in a strong man's house.

Now the question the scribes have to answer: which man in this story is Jesus? They have said he is an agent of the owner. But nobody breaks into a house he already owns, and nobody carries out goods that are already his. Jesus is not in the house as the owner's servant. He is in it as the thief, and the owner is on the floor with his hands tied.

Unless he first binds the strong man. The order is exact and it is the point. Binding first; plundering afterwards. You cannot walk off with a strong man's property while he is standing.

Which means that every deliverance in this Gospel is not a skirmish but a removal van. Every demon that comes out, every fever that breaks, every leper made clean, is furniture being carried out of a house whose owner has already been dealt with. The New Testament keeps the same picture when it describes what happened to you: God delivered us from the domain of darkness and transferred us to the kingdom of his beloved Son (Col. 1:13) — and transferred is a word for moving property.

So when was the strong man bound?

Here is the thing that no one in the room could have guessed, and it is the strangest and best turn in the faith. He was bound by a stronger man who let himself be bound first. In a garden, a few miles from where the scribes lived, soldiers put their hands on Jesus and tied them, and he did not resist. They led him away bound to a high priest, bound to a governor, and finally fastened him to a cross with his arms open and immovable, which is the posture of a man who can plunder nothing.

And that was the binding of Satan. He disarmed the rulers and authorities and put them to open shame, by triumphing over them in him — in the cross (Col. 2:15). That through death he might destroy the one who has the power of death, that is, the devil (Heb. 2:14).

The strongest man who ever lived walked into the house, and instead of overpowering the owner he let the owner tie him up, and died — and that is how the ropes went onto the other pair of wrists.

So if you are in Christ tonight, understand what you are. You are not a volunteer who signed up. You are stolen goods. You were in that house, and the owner had every legal claim on you, and you had no way out. Somebody broke in and carried you out over his shoulder, and the price of the raid was his life.

verseByVerse.quote: "Truly, I say to you, all sins will be forgiven the children of man, and whatever blasphemies they utter, but whoever blasphemes against the Holy Spirit never has forgiveness, but is guilty of an eternal sin"— for they were saying, "He has an unclean spirit."
verseByVerse.commentary:
He begins with the widest promise in the Gospel, and it is important to take it at full strength before anything else is said.

Truly, I say to you, all sins will be forgiven the children of man, and whatever blasphemies they utter. The word behind truly is amen — the formula Jesus uses to put his own authority behind a statement. And what he puts it behind is this: all of them. Not most. Not the respectable ones. All sins, and every blasphemy men speak — the things said in rage, the things said in a hospital corridor at three in the morning, the years spent mocking him, the words you would not repeat to another human being. All forgivable.

Do not hurry past that on the way to the exception. This is the most sweeping sentence about mercy that Jesus ever spoke, and he spoke it to men who had just called the Holy Spirit a devil.

But whoever blasphemes against the Holy Spirit never has forgiveness, but is guilty of an eternal sin. And then the one exception, stated with the same solemnity, and there is no getting around how serious it is.

Mark, to his enormous credit, tells us immediately what it refers to, and this is the key that unlocks the whole passage: for they were saying, He has an unclean spirit (v. 30). Mark does not leave it floating as an abstract category. He anchors it in the specific thing happening in that room.

So here is what it is. Men are watching the Spirit of God set human beings free in front of their eyes. They cannot deny the events; they have travelled ninety miles and seen them. And with full knowledge of what they are looking at, they call it the work of hell. That is the sin: not doubt, not confusion, not a hasty word, but the settled, informed, deliberate decision to look straight at the light and name it darkness — and to keep saying so. Mark's tense is worth noting: they were saying it. It is not a slip. It is a position they are maintaining.

Now the pastoral question, because a great many tender Christians read this verse at night and cannot sleep. Have I committed it?

Let the answer be given straight, because you are living inside this question and you do not need a survey of opinions. If you are afraid you have committed the unforgivable sin, you have not committed it.

Look at why that is not a comforting fiction. The sin in question is the terminal hardening of a heart against the Holy Spirit — a heart so calcified that it can see God at work and call it the devil without a tremor. Now consider what fear of this sin actually requires: it requires that you want to be forgiven, that you care what God thinks of you, that the possibility of being cut off from him horrifies you. Where did that come from? Not from a hardened heart. Hardened hearts do not lie awake worrying about their standing with God; they sleep extremely well. The scribes went home untroubled. Your distress is itself the evidence of a conscience still alive under the Spirit's hand — and the Spirit does not trouble a man he has abandoned.

R. C. Sproul put it about as plainly as it can be put: the person who fears he has committed this sin almost certainly has not, because the capacity for that fear is the very thing the sin destroys. The hardness that commits it does not tremble. It calculates.

And if you want a test you can run tonight rather than a doctrine to hold at arm's length, here it is. Can you say, honestly, that you want Christ — that if he would have you, you would come? Then come, because he has never once turned away anyone who did. Whoever comes to me I will never cast out (John 6:37), and there is no clause in that sentence excepting people who are afraid they have gone too far.

The unforgivable sin is unforgivable because it is unrepented, and it is unrepented because the man committing it has no intention of repenting and no wish to be forgiven. A person who wants pardon is by definition not in that position. Your fear is not your danger. It may well be the Spirit's own work in you, dragging you toward the only place where fear is answered.

verseByVerse.quote: And his mother and his brothers came, and standing outside they sent to him and called him. And a crowd was sitting around him, and they said to him, "Your mother and your brothers are outside, seeking you."
verseByVerse.commentary:
And now, after all that, they arrive.

Mark has been building to this since verse 21. The family set out to seize him; the delegation from Jerusalem accused him; the argument about Satan and the strong man has been made; the terrible warning has been given. And into that room, at that moment, a message comes in from the door: your mother and your brothers are outside.

And standing outside they sent to him and called him. Mark places them with two words and they carry the whole scene. Outside. The house is packed with people sitting on the floor around him, close enough to touch him, and his own mother is on the pavement sending a message in.

They do not come in. They send for him, which is what you do when you expect to be obeyed. It is the summons of family authority — a mother and four grown brothers, standing together, requiring the eldest to come out to them. And we know from verse 21 what they intend to do when he does.

It is a picture of something very common and very sad: people who have every natural claim on Jesus, positioned as near to him as it is possible to be without being inside, calling him out rather than coming in.

Your mother and your brothers are outside, seeking you. The crowd relays it, perhaps helpfully, perhaps enjoying the interruption. And here is the geography of the whole chapter in one sentence, and it is worth naming plainly: proximity is not the same as belonging. You can be his mother and be outside. You can have carried him, fed him, watched him grow, known him better than anyone alive — and be in the street while a crowd of strangers sits at his feet.

Which is the most searching thing in the passage for religious people, and it is not really about Mary. It is about anyone whose connection to Christ is a matter of nearness rather than surrender. Raised in it. Related to it. Married into it. Employed by it. On the rota, in the building, known by name to everyone in the congregation — and functionally outside, sending messages in, wanting Christ to come out and fit into a life that has been organised without him.

So it is worth asking, without panic but without dodging it either: am I in the room, or at the door? Not have I been around this a long time — the family had been around him for thirty years. The question is whether you have sat down in front of him as one of the people who wants what he says more than you want him manageable.

And there is real hope in the fact that Mark names Mary here, because she does not stay outside. The woman on the pavement in Capernaum is at the cross when the disciples have scattered (John 19:25), and in the prayer meeting after the resurrection (Acts 1:14). The brothers standing with her do not believe in him at all at this point (John 7:5); one of them will write the letter of James and open it by calling himself the servant of the Lord Jesus Christ, and another will write Jude.

Nobody in that street is beyond the reach of the man in that house. It took them a resurrection, but they came in.

verseByVerse.quote: And he answered them, "Who are my mother and my brothers?" And looking about at those who sat around him, he said, "Here are my mother and my brothers! For whoever does the will of God, he is my brother and sister and mother."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Who are my mother and my brothers? Read as a snub, it is shocking. It is not a snub. It is a question asked in order to be answered, and the answer is one of the most extraordinary things Jesus ever said about ordinary people.

And looking about at those who sat around him. Mark keeps giving us the eyes of Jesus in this chapter. In verse 5 he looked around at hard men with anger and grief. Here he looks around at a floor full of nobodies — fishermen, a reformed tax collector, a former Zealot, and whoever else had got into the house that morning — and takes his time about it. It is a deliberate sweep of the room, face by face, before he says the words.

Here are my mother and my brothers. He said it while his actual mother was standing in the street. He was not making a point at her expense; the whole New Testament forbids that reading. He honoured her from the cross, arranging her care with almost his last breath (John 19:26–27), and he is the one who said that setting aside your duty to your parents for a religious excuse makes void the word of God (7:11–13). This is not the demotion of the natural family. It is the announcement of a second one.

For whoever does the will of God, he is my brother and sister and mother.

Take the sentence apart slowly, because every word in it is doing work.

Whoever. No pedigree. Not whoever is descended from Abraham, not whoever has the education, the record, the family, the reputation. Whoever.

Does the will of God. Not whoever admires it, or believes the correct things about it — the demons on the beach had the doctrine right and were no relation of his. This is the chapter's own dividing line, and Jesus draws it at the door: not what you can recite, but whether you have come in and sat down under his word. And lest anyone make that into a performance to be earned, John records the Lord's own definition of the work God requires: this is the work of God, that you believe in him whom he has sent (John 6:29).

My brother and sister and mother. And here is the tenderness of it. He does not say my followers, or my servants, or even my friends, though he says that elsewhere. He reaches for the closest words the language has. And he says sister, in a room where a rabbi's disciples were men, which is not an accident.

Now feel the weight of what is on offer, and measure it against what is broken. Some people reading this had a father who was never satisfied. Some have a family that has gone quiet since they became a Christian — the empty seat at Christmas, the brother who does not call. Some have no family left alive at all; they are the last one, and there is nobody now who remembers them as a child.

To all of them, the Lord Jesus Christ looks round a room and says: here. These are mine, and if you do the will of God, so are you — brother, sister, mother. Not a metaphor for a support group. A family with a Father, a firstborn brother who is not ashamed to call you his own (Heb. 2:11), and a household you will still belong to when every other name on your family tree has been forgotten.

That is why the awkward, mismatched congregation you sit among on a Sunday is not a social arrangement you could improve on by finding people more like yourself. It is your family, given to you by Christ, and he named them before you did.

And this is the man who said it: the one who was called mad by his own mother and demonic by the theologians on the same afternoon, who was on his way to being deserted by every man in that room, and who went to the cross to make a family out of people who had none — so that a room of strangers on a dirt floor in Capernaum could be looked at, one face at a time, by the Son of God, and called his mother and his brothers.

3.theology:
Two of the most-asked questions in Mark sit in this chapter, and both deserve a straight answer.

Was Jesus's anger sinful? No — and v. 5 shows how to tell, because it gives the anger and the grief in one breath. He looked around at them with anger, grieved at their hardness of heart. Sinful anger wants the other person diminished and would be quietly disappointed by their repentance; righteous anger grieves, wants the wrong put right and the wrongdoer restored, and would be glad to be made unnecessary. Be angry and do not sin (Eph. 4:26) is a command with a boundary, not a contradiction.

What is the unforgivable sin? Mark answers it himself in v. 30 and the answer is anchored, not abstract: for they were saying, He has an unclean spirit. It is the settled, informed, deliberate attribution of the Holy Spirit's unmistakable work to Satan by men who have seen it with their own eyes and chosen their verdict. It is not a slip, a doubt, or a season of confusion. And the pastoral corollary is firm: the person terrified of having committed it has not, because the fear itself requires a conscience still responsive to the Spirit, and that is precisely what this sin destroys. The hardness that commits it does not tremble; it calculates.
3.examples:
The chapter's two great alliances are worth setting side by side, because they explain a great deal about churches.

Then: Pharisees and Herodians — strict separatists and worldly courtiers, men who despised each other on religion, politics and money — in a room together within minutes, agreeing perfectly on one thing: how to destroy him. Nothing on earth unites people like a shared hatred of the light. Pilate and Herod became friends the day they both condemned him (Luke 23:12).

And then: Matthew the tax collector and Simon the Zealot on the same list of twelve, walking the same roads for three years. In any other year of the world, Simon's politics would have called for a knife in Matthew's ribs. Nothing reconciled them except the man in the middle.

Now: both are still in operation. A congregation can be welded together by what it is against, and it will feel like unity and it will not be. Or it can be a collection of people with nothing whatever in common except Christ — which is more than everything they had against each other. If your church contains people you would never otherwise have chosen, that is not a defect to be managed. It is the evidence.

4.title: Seed, Soil, and the Sleeping Lord
4.text: <sup>1</sup>Again he began to teach beside the sea. And a very large crowd gathered about him, so that he got into a boat and sat in it on the sea, and the whole crowd was beside the sea on the land. <sup>2</sup>And he was teaching them many things in parables, and in his teaching he said to them: <sup>3</sup>“Listen! Behold, a sower went out to sow. <sup>4</sup>And as he sowed, some seed fell along the path, and the birds came and devoured it. <sup>5</sup>Other seed fell on rocky ground, where it did not have much soil, and immediately it sprang up, since it had no depth of soil. <sup>6</sup>And when the sun rose, it was scorched, and since it had no root, it withered away. <sup>7</sup>Other seed fell among thorns, and the thorns grew up and choked it, and it yielded no grain. <sup>8</sup>And other seeds fell into good soil and produced grain, growing up and increasing and yielding thirtyfold and sixtyfold and a hundredfold.” <sup>9</sup>And he said, “He who has ears to hear, let him hear.” <sup>10</sup>And when he was alone, those around him with the twelve asked him about the parables. <sup>11</sup>And he said to them, “To you has been given the secret of the kingdom of God, but for those outside everything is in parables, <sup>12</sup>so that they may indeed see but not perceive, and may indeed hear but not understand, lest they should turn and be forgiven.” <sup>13</sup>And he said to them, “Do you not understand this parable? How then will you understand all the parables? <sup>14</sup>The sower sows the word. <sup>15</sup>And these are the ones along the path, where the word is sown: when they hear, Satan immediately comes and takes away the word that is sown in them. <sup>16</sup>And these are the ones sown on rocky ground: the ones who, when they hear the word, immediately receive it with joy. <sup>17</sup>And they have no root in themselves, but endure for a while; then, when tribulation or persecution arises on account of the word, immediately they fall away. <sup>18</sup>And others are the ones sown among thorns. They are those who hear the word, <sup>19</sup>but the cares of the world and the deceitfulness of riches and the desires for other things enter in and choke the word, and it proves unfruitful. <sup>20</sup>But those that were sown on the good soil are the ones who hear the word and accept it and bear fruit, thirtyfold and sixtyfold and a hundredfold.” <sup>21</sup>And he said to them, “Is a lamp brought in to be put under a basket, or under a bed, and not on a stand? <sup>22</sup>For nothing is hidden except to be made manifest; nor is anything secret except to come to light. <sup>23</sup>If anyone has ears to hear, let him hear.” <sup>24</sup>And he said to them, “Pay attention to what you hear: with the measure you use, it will be measured to you, and still more will be added to you. <sup>25</sup>For to the one who has, more will be given, and from the one who has not, even what he has will be taken away.” <sup>26</sup>And he said, “The kingdom of God is as if a man should scatter seed on the ground. <sup>27</sup>He sleeps and rises night and day, and the seed sprouts and grows; he knows not how. <sup>28</sup>The earth produces by itself, first the blade, then the ear, then the full grain in the ear. <sup>29</sup>But when the grain is ripe, at once he puts in the sickle, because the harvest has come.” <sup>30</sup>And he said, “With what can we compare the kingdom of God, or what parable shall we use for it? <sup>31</sup>It is like a grain of mustard seed, which, when sown on the ground, is the smallest of all the seeds on earth, <sup>32</sup>yet when it is sown it grows up and becomes larger than all the garden plants and puts out large branches, so that the birds of the air can make nests in its shade.” <sup>33</sup>With many such parables he spoke the word to them, as they were able to hear it. <sup>34</sup>He did not speak to them without a parable, but privately to his own disciples he explained everything. <sup>35</sup>On that day, when evening had come, he said to them, “Let us go across to the other side.” <sup>36</sup>And leaving the crowd, they took him with them in the boat, just as he was. And other boats were with him. <sup>37</sup>And a great windstorm arose, and the waves were breaking into the boat, so that the boat was already filling. <sup>38</sup>But he was in the stern, asleep on the cushion. And they woke him and said to him, “Teacher, do you not care that we are perishing?” <sup>39</sup>And he awoke and rebuked the wind and said to the sea, “Peace! Be still!” And the wind ceased, and there was a great calm. <sup>40</sup>He said to them, “Why are you so afraid? Have you still no faith?” <sup>41</sup>And they were filled with great fear and said to one another, “Who then is this, that even the wind and the sea obey him?”
4.overview:
Chapter 4 is Mark's great block of teaching, and it is built to answer one question the previous chapter forced: if Jesus really is the King, why does this look so small and go so badly? The professionals have called him demonic, his family thinks he is unwell, and the kingdom of God at this point consists of a preacher in a borrowed boat and twelve unimpressive men.

The answer comes in seed. A sower broadcasts across ground he cannot see into, and three-quarters of it appears wasted — and the harvest is still thirty, sixty, a hundredfold, when a Galilean farmer expected five or ten (vv. 3–20). A man scatters seed and goes to bed, and it grows while he sleeps and he does not know how (vv. 26–29). The smallest speck in the garden becomes the largest plant in it, with room in its branches for the birds of the air — which in Ezekiel and Daniel means the nations (vv. 30–32).

Then the teaching stops and the test begins. He says let us go across, and the crossing nearly kills them. The chapter that has been about hearing the word ends with the word spoken to a hurricane, and with a question left deliberately unanswered: Who then is this, that even the wind and the sea obey him?

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–25 — The Sower and the Purpose of Parables
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The pulpit (vv. 1–2). The crowd is so large that Jesus pushes a boat out a few yards and preaches from the water, with the people banked up the shore. The setting is itself a picture: one voice, one seed, going out over a great many different kinds of ground.

The parable (vv. 3–9). A sower walks a field and the seed lands in four places — a trodden path, a shelf of rock under thin soil, a patch of thorn roots, and open ground. Three losses and one harvest so large it would have made a Galilean farmer laugh.

Why parables at all (vv. 10–12). The hardest paragraph in the chapter, and Jesus does not soften it. He quotes Isaiah's commission to a nation that had already shut its eyes, and says the stories both shelter the seeker and confirm the scorner.

The explanation (vv. 13–20). The only parable Jesus takes apart line by line in this Gospel. Four soils, four fates, and the third one is the one most of us are living in.

The lamp and the measure (vv. 21–25). The hiding is temporary — a lamp goes under a basket for a moment, not for a life. And what you do with what you have heard determines what you will be given next.
verseByVerse.theology:
Verses 11–12 are the hardest words in the chapter, and they should not be smoothed over. Matthew's version says Jesus speaks in parables because people do not see (Matt. 13:13); Mark's says he speaks so that they may not see, lest they should turn and be forgiven. Read flatly, that sounds as though the Lord veils truth deliberately to stop people repenting.

Three things dissolve the difficulty. First, the words are a direct quotation of Isaiah 6:9–10 — God's charge to a prophet sent to a nation that had already, for generations, shut its own eyes. This is not fresh cruelty; it is the settled judgement of God on hardened refusal. Second, the so that carries the weight of fulfilment as much as bare purpose: the parables come to a people who have chosen blindness and confirm the choice, which is how God deals with those who insist — he gives them over to the dark they preferred (cf. Rom. 1:24). Third, and decisively, the door is never bolted. Those around him with the twelve understood nothing either. The difference between them and the outsiders is one thing only: they asked.

So the same parable is judgement and mercy at once. It hardens the scornful and shelters the seeker — hiding the truth from the mouth that would only spit on it, while keeping it within arm's reach of anyone who will turn and ask.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: a farmer broadcasting seed by hand across ground he has not sorted in advance, some of it landing where it has no chance at all.

Now: every faithful preacher, parent and friend who keeps sowing without being able to see the soil. The sower in the parable does not test the ground first, and he is not blamed for the path, the rock or the thorns. That is a real relief for anyone who has taught a class for years, or raised children in the faith, and cannot see a harvest. Your job was the sowing.

And a hundredfold is not a rounded-up figure. Ordinary yields in that country ran five- or tenfold, and a farmer who got thirty would have talked about it for the rest of his life. Jesus names thirty as the lowest of the three good outcomes. Three-quarters of the field appears to fail, and the harvest is still absurd. Whatever the losses look like from where you are standing, the ledger at the end is not in doubt.

verseByVerse.quote: Again he began to teach beside the sea. And a very large crowd gathered about him, so that he got into a boat and sat in it on the sea, and the whole crowd was beside the sea on the land. And he was teaching them many things in parables, and in his teaching he said to them:
verseByVerse.commentary:
Picture the arrangement, because Mark has gone to the trouble of describing it and it is a striking image.

The crowd is too large for the shore. So Jesus gets into a boat — the one he had asked for back in 3:9 — and has it pushed out a few yards, and sits down in it. Sitting is the posture of a teacher in that world; a rabbi sat and the class stood. And the whole crowd is beside the sea on the land, packed along the beach and up the slope behind it.

Anyone who has stood on the shore of Galilee near Capernaum knows what that means. The ground rises from the water in a natural curve, and the water in front carries sound. A man in a boat can be heard by thousands on that hillside without shouting. He is using the shape of the world his Father made as a sound system.

And the setting is already the sermon. One voice, from one fixed point, going out across a crowd of hundreds — landing on farmers and fishermen, on Pharisees who came to listen for errors, on women at the back with children pulling at them, on people who walked ninety miles from Judea and people who wandered down from the village because there was a commotion. One seed. Many kinds of ground.

Again he began to teach. Mark keeps saying it because it keeps needing saying. We remember the miracles; Mark records that the bulk of the Lord's time went on talking. Teaching is what he was doing when the roof came in (2:2), and it is what he is doing here.

He was teaching them many things in parables. A parable is not a children's illustration and it is not a code with a decoder ring. The word covers a wide range in the Bible — a proverb, a riddle, a comparison thrown alongside something to explain it. What they all share is that they make you work.

And that is deliberate. A parable will not let you file it away as information. A straight proposition — people respond differently to the word of God — is easy to agree with and easier to forget; you can nod at it without a flicker of self-suspicion. But tell a man about a field, and hand him a picture with four kinds of ground in it, and he will find himself walking round the edge of it wondering which patch he is standing on. He has to enter the story to understand it, and once he is inside it, it has him.

Which is why the Lord's teaching keeps ambushing people who thought they were merely listening. A story gets under the guard that an argument goes straight into. Nathan did not open with you are the man. He opened with a poor man and one little ewe lamb, and let David pass sentence on himself first (2 Sam. 12:1–7).

So read this chapter expecting to be handled the same way. Jesus is not about to give you information about four types of hearer. He is about to walk you out into a field and ask you where you are standing.

verseByVerse.quote: "Listen! Behold, a sower went out to sow. And as he sowed, some seed fell along the path, and the birds came and devoured it.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Listen! He opens with a command, and it is the first word out of his mouth. Not consider or imagine. Listen — and he will end the same parable with he who has ears to hear, let him hear (v. 9). The story is bracketed by warnings about how you are receiving it, which is a fair sign of what it is about.

Behold, a sower went out to sow. Now the picture, and it helps enormously to know how it was actually done, because a modern reader imagines neat drills and a man walking a straight line.

He did not. A Galilean farmer carried the seed in a fold of his cloak or a bag at his hip and threw it in a wide arc, walking, broadcasting it across the whole surface of the field. In much of that country the ploughing came after the sowing, not before — you scattered the grain over the ground and then turned it in. And the field was not fenced. Paths ran across it where people had walked for generations; limestone shelf lay a few inches under the surface in places; last year's thorn roots were still in the ground at the edges.

So the sower is not careless. This is simply what sowing looked like. He throws it everywhere because he cannot see, from up there with a bag on his hip, what is six inches under the surface of any given yard of his field.

Hold on to that, because it is the first comfort in the chapter and it is for anyone who has ever taught, preached, raised children in the faith, or talked about Christ to a friend and watched nothing happen. You are not asked to survey the soil first. You could not do it if you tried; you cannot see into another human being. Sow. The results were never the part assigned to you.

Some seed fell along the path. The path is not bad ground. It is ground that has been walked on so often that it has set like a floor. Nobody decided to make it hard. It was made hard by traffic — by the same feet going over it, day after day, until nothing could get in.

And the birds came and devoured it. Immediately. The seed does not even get the dignity of failing slowly. It lies on a surface it cannot penetrate, in plain view, and it is gone before the sower has reached the end of the row.

Jesus will tell us in verse 15 who the birds are, and it is worth knowing in advance so that you feel the weight of the picture: Satan comes at once and takes the word away. Which means that the most ordinary religious experience in the world — sitting through a sermon and remembering none of it by lunchtime — is not always a neutral failure of concentration. Something can be at work in it.

And the path is the soil nobody worries about being. That is its danger. The rocky-ground hearer has a crisis; the thorny-ground hearer feels the squeeze. The path feels nothing at all. The word arrives, lies there, and is carried off, and the man goes home to his lunch entirely undisturbed and slightly bored.

verseByVerse.quote: Other seed fell on rocky ground, where it did not have much soil, and immediately it sprang up, since it had no depth of soil. And when the sun rose, it was scorched, and since it had no root, it withered away.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Other seed fell on rocky ground. Not stony soil with rocks scattered through it — that would be a nuisance rather than a death sentence. Mark means a shelf of limestone bedrock lying a few inches beneath the surface, with a thin skin of earth over the top. From above, standing in the field, it looks exactly like the rest.

And here is the cruelty of it: this is the ground that performs best at first.

Immediately it sprang up, since it had no depth of soil. Read the logic, because it is the opposite of what you would expect. It came up fast because the soil was shallow. Warmth collects in a thin layer over rock; the seed cannot go down, so everything it has goes up. The fastest, greenest, most impressive growth in the whole field is the growth that is going to die.

Anyone who has been in church life for twenty years has watched this. The new convert whose enthusiasm makes everyone else feel lukewarm; who is at everything, telling everyone, radiant — and who is not there in three years and nobody can quite say when they stopped coming. The rate of early growth told you nothing. It never does.

And when the sun rose, it was scorched. Notice the sun is not an enemy. The sun is what ripens the harvest in the good soil in the same field. The identical heat that kills one plant matures another, and the only difference is what is happening underground where nobody can see.

That is worth saying plainly, because it reframes the hard seasons of a Christian life. Trouble is not sent to destroy you; trouble is the weather in which real growth is finished and shallow growth is exposed. The same bereavement, the same diagnosis, the same run of humiliating years, will make one believer and break another, and the difference was decided long before the heat arrived.

Since it had no root, it withered away. There is the whole verdict in five words. Not attacked. Not argued out of it. Withered — dried up from underneath, from a place nobody was looking.

So the practical question is not how green you look this month. It is what is happening in the dark. Roots are grown in private and in the boring stretches: the unimpressive half-hour with a Bible on a wet Tuesday when nothing in you wants it; the prayers that feel like talking to the ceiling; the Sundays you attend when you would rather not; the doctrine you take the trouble to actually understand before you need it.

None of that shows. That is precisely the point of it. And the honest test is this: if the heat came this year — if the illness, the redundancy, the public embarrassment for being a Christian arrived in March — what exactly would you be drawing on? If the answer is a feeling you had at a conference, you have been told in advance, kindly, while there is still time to dig.

verseByVerse.quote: Other seed fell among thorns, and the thorns grew up and choked it, and it yielded no grain.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Other seed fell among thorns. This is the soil most readers of this page are standing in, so read it slowly.

Understand what the field actually looked like. The thorns are not visible when the sowing happens. What is in the ground is a root system — last season's thorn bushes, cut down or burned off at the surface, entirely dormant, with the earth above them looking as good as any other part of the field. A man could walk that ground and see nothing wrong with it.

Then the rains come, and both things grow at once. That is the whole picture: not a field of thorns with a bit of wheat in it, but wheat and thorns coming up together in the same soil, drawing on the same water, the same light, the same few inches of earth.

And the thorns grew up and choked it. The verb means to strangle — it is used of the demon-possessed pigs drowning in the next chapter (5:13) and of a man taking a debtor by the throat (Matt. 18:28). Nothing about it is gradual or gentle, though it is silent. There is no moment of decision. Nobody digs up the wheat. It is simply crowded, shaded and starved by things that are also alive, also growing, also using the ground.

And it yielded no grain. And that is the outcome that ought to stop us. The plant is still there. It is green, it is standing, it has leaves. Walk past that corner of the field in June and you would say the wheat is doing fine. It simply never produces anything.

Now here is what makes this the most searching of the three failures, and Jesus will spell it out in verse 19: the thorns are not sins. They are the cares of the world, the deceitfulness of riches, and the desires for other things. Not adultery, theft or blasphemy — worry, money and the wanting of ordinary stuff.

Which means this soil cannot be diagnosed by examining your conduct. A man in this field is not doing anything he would need to confess to his minister. He is doing what everyone does: worrying about the mortgage, working hard for a promotion he does not really need, extending the house, taxiing children between activities, watching the pension, keeping up with the news and the group chat and the series everyone is talking about. None of it is wicked. All of it is alive, and all of it drinks.

And the tell-tale sign is not a sin you have committed but a fruit you cannot find. The prayer that has quietly stopped happening. The Bible that gets opened on Sunday because someone else opens it. The conversation about Christ you have not had with anyone in a year — not because you decided against it, but because there has genuinely been no room.

So try the honest version of the question. Not is there anything bad in my life? There may well not be. Ask instead: what has crowded out what? If you laid your week beside your Bible, which of the two would look like the thing you actually organise your life around? The wheat and the thorns are still growing in the same field, and only one of them is going to yield anything in September.

verseByVerse.quote: And other seeds fell into good soil and produced grain, growing up and increasing and yielding thirtyfold and sixtyfold and a hundredfold." And he said, "He who has ears to hear, let him hear."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Three failures, and now the harvest — and Jesus deliberately overwhelms the arithmetic.

And other seeds fell into good soil. Note that the good soil does nothing to become good. It does not clear itself of stones or grub out its own thorn roots. It simply receives what falls on it and lets it go down. Whatever this parable is asking of you, it is not asking you to manufacture your own fertility; the field is worked on, not self-improving.

And produced grain, growing up and increasing. Mark alone gives the process in three stages, and it is the quiet answer to the shallow soil. That plant sprang up immediately. This one grows up and increases — it takes its time. Fast is not the same as fruitful, and slow is not the same as dead.

Thirtyfold and sixtyfold and a hundredfold. And now the numbers, which a Galilean farmer on that beach heard very differently from the way we do.

An ordinary yield in that country was somewhere around fivefold to tenfold — you sowed a measure and harvested five, out of which next year's seed had to come. A good year might give you more. A man who brought in thirtyfold would have been talking about it for the rest of his life and the village would have remembered the season.

Jesus names thirty as the worst of his three good outcomes. Then sixty. Then a hundred — which in normal farming does not happen at all.

So do the sum the parable wants you to do. Three-quarters of the field appears to be a total loss. Seed gone to birds, seed withered on rock, seed strangled in thorns. And the harvest is still ludicrous — the kind of harvest that fills every barn in the village and leaves the farmer standing in the yard laughing.

That is the answer to the question the whole chapter is quietly addressing, and it was a live question for the twelve men listening. It looked, in Galilee in that year, as though this was going badly. The professionals had declared him demonic, his family thought he was mad, the crowds wanted healings and not much else, and the kingdom of God consisted of a preacher in a borrowed boat and a dozen unimpressive men. Jesus tells them what the accounts will say at the end, and they are not close.

Which is worth holding when you look at your own field and see mostly loss — the children who are not walking with God, the years of teaching that seemed to change nobody, the church that is smaller than it was. The losses in this parable are real and they are named honestly. They are also not the story. He who supplies seed to the sower is the one who will supply and multiply your seed for sowing and increase the harvest (2 Cor. 9:10).

He who has ears to hear, let him hear. And then the refrain — the same words that will sound seven times over the churches in Revelation (Rev. 2–3). Everyone on that beach had ears. That is exactly why the sentence is not a tautology but a warning: the hearing that saves is not the hearing that everybody in the crowd was already doing. Physical hearing is universal. Spiritual hearing is a gift, and the man who wants it has only to ask the one in the boat for it.

verseByVerse.quote: And when he was alone, those around him with the twelve asked him about the parables. And he said to them, "To you has been given the secret of the kingdom of God, but for those outside everything is in parables, so that they may indeed see but not perceive, and may indeed hear but not understand, lest they should turn and be forgiven."
verseByVerse.commentary:
And when he was alone. The crowd goes home. The beach empties. And a smaller group stays behind — those around him with the twelve — and asks him what he meant.

Hold on to that detail, because it turns out to be the hinge of the whole passage. The insiders are not insiders because they understood. They did not understand a word of it; verse 13 makes that painfully clear. They are insiders because when the sermon was over they did not go home. They stayed and asked.

To you has been given the secret of the kingdom of God. The word is mystērion, and in the Bible it never means a puzzle to be cracked by clever people. It means something God had kept hidden and has now disclosed. It is given — the verb is passive, and there is only one person doing the giving. Nobody works this out. It is handed over.

And the secret, in Mark, is a Person: that the kingdom of God has arrived in a carpenter from Nazareth who is going to a cross.
