But for those outside everything is in parables, so that they may indeed see but not perceive... lest they should turn and be forgiven.

Now the hardest sentence in the chapter, and it must not be smoothed over, because a thoughtful reader will feel the difficulty immediately. It sounds as though Jesus is speaking in stories precisely so that people will not repent and be saved.

Three things dissolve it.

First, these are not new words. They are a quotation of Isaiah 6:9–10 — God's commission to a prophet sent to a nation that had already, for generations, shut its own eyes. Isaiah is not sent to a curious people who are wrongly denied the truth; he is sent to a people who have refused it for so long that the preaching itself will now confirm them in it. This is not fresh cruelty. It is the settled judgement of God on hardened refusal, and it is the very passage the New Testament reaches for again and again to explain unbelief (Matt. 13:14–15; John 12:40; Acts 28:26–27).

Second, the so that is the language of fulfilment as much as of bare intention. Mark writes with the Old Testament in his hand, and the sense is: this happens, and in it Isaiah's word comes true. It is the pattern Paul describes as God giving people over to what they have already chosen (Rom. 1:24, 26, 28) — the darkness they preferred, finally granted.

Third, and decisively: the door is never bolted. The proof is sitting in the room. The men who received the secret had understood exactly nothing thirty seconds earlier. The only thing separating them from the crowd walking home along the shore is that they asked. And the invitation never closes: ask, and it will be given to you; seek, and you will find (Matt. 7:7).

So the parable is judgement and mercy in the same breath. To the man who has already decided, it is one more story he can shrug at — and every shrug sets the ground harder. To the man who is troubled by it, it is a door left open, a truth kept just out of reach so that he has to come and ask for it, and the asking is the beginning of everything.

Which puts one question to you, and it is not a difficult one. This chapter has been strange to you in places. Did you notice, and go and ask him about it? Or did you read it, find it obscure, and go and get on with the day?

The people who stayed behind on that beach did not have better minds. They had a habit of not leaving. Everything they eventually understood came out of that.

verseByVerse.quote: And he said to them, "Do you not understand this parable? How then will you understand all the parables? The sower sows the word. And these are the ones along the path, where the word is sown: when they hear, Satan immediately comes and takes away the word that is sown in them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Do you not understand this parable? How then will you understand all the parables? There is a sigh in that, and Mark is not embarrassed to record it. It is worth noticing what kind of rebuke it is: not a refusal to explain, but a comment made in the middle of explaining. He says do you not understand? — and then tells them.

Which is a mercy for slow disciples, and that is all of us. The men who were with him three years were, by any honest reading of this Gospel, consistently baffled. They will be worse in chapter 8. The Lord Jesus keeps teaching people who are not quick.

The sower sows the word. Four words, and they set the terms for everything that follows. The seed is not a general religious influence, an experience or a mood. It is the word — a message, in sentences, that can be spoken and heard.

That matters more than it may seem. It means the kingdom of God comes to human beings by an ordinary means, one that anyone can use. Faith comes by hearing, and hearing through the word of Christ (Rom. 10:17); we are born again through the living and abiding word of God (1 Pet. 1:23). This is why an unremarkable sermon in a half-empty building on a wet Sunday is not a low-grade activity. It is the sowing. The only thing that has ever produced a harvest is being done.

And these are the ones along the path. Now the first soil, and Jesus takes the birds and names them.

Satan immediately comes and takes away the word that is sown in them. Three things in that sentence deserve attention.

Satan. Jesus attributes it to a person, not to a process. He does not say the word evaporates or that people are naturally forgetful. Someone comes and takes it. The New Testament says the same thing elsewhere without flinching: the god of this world has blinded the minds of the unbelievers, to keep them from seeing the light of the gospel of the glory of Christ (2 Cor. 4:4).

Immediately. Mark's word again. The theft is not a slow leak over months. It happens at once — in the car park, in the walk home, in the first conversation afterwards. Anyone who preaches knows how fast a sermon can be gone.

Takes away. Which means the loss is a theft rather than a verdict. The word did not fail to be good; it was removed before it could get in.

And remember what made the path hard. Nobody chose it. It was traffic — the same feet crossing the same ground until it set like a floor. That is how a heart hardens in real life: not by a decision to reject God, but by years of the same routines going over the same ground, until the sound of the gospel is simply a sound you have heard before.

If you have started to find it dull, take that seriously and take it to God tonight, in exactly those words. He has never once refused a man who asked him to break up his own hard ground: I will remove the heart of stone from your flesh and give you a heart of flesh (Ezek. 36:26). The path cannot plough itself. It does not have to.

verseByVerse.quote: And these are the ones sown on rocky ground: the ones who, when they hear the word, immediately receive it with joy. And they have no root in themselves, but endure for a while; then, when tribulation or persecution arises on account of the word, immediately they fall away.
verseByVerse.commentary:
They immediately receive it with joy. And there is nothing wrong with the joy. That is the first thing to say, because this soil frightens sensitive people and it is often misread. Jesus does not criticise the gladness. Real conversion is glad — the man who found treasure in a field went and sold everything in his joy (Matt. 13:44). The problem here is not that they were happy. It is that happiness was all there was.

And they have no root in themselves. Look at the last two words, because they are the diagnosis. Not no root in the church, or no root in good teaching. No root in themselves. Something was never internalised. The faith was held at the level of atmosphere — the music, the friendships, the feeling in the room, a preacher they admired — and never went down into the private ground of the man himself where nobody could see it.

But endure for a while. Which is why it takes time to tell. This soil looks identical to good soil, and looks better than good soil at first, and keeps looking fine for a season. Mark gives no timescale. It might be two years.

Then, when tribulation or persecution arises on account of the word. Now notice precisely what the heat is. Jesus does not say when trouble comes — he specifies trouble that arrives on account of the word. It is the cost of the faith itself: the friendships that cool once you are known as a Christian, the joke at work you are now on the wrong side of, the family that has become careful with you, the promotion that goes elsewhere, and in much of the world today far worse than any of that.

This is the soil that discovers Christianity is expensive and had assumed it was free.

Immediately they fall away. The word is skandalizontai — they are tripped up. It is the same root as the stumbling block Peter becomes to Jesus (8:33) and the offence the cross itself gives (1 Cor. 1:23). And Mark uses immediately for the third time in two verses: fast in, fast up, fast out. The whole story of this soil is speed.

So the practical question is the only one that matters here, and it has to be asked while the weather is fine: what are you doing this month that will still be holding you in ten years?

Roots go down in the unglamorous places. They are grown on the Tuesday morning when you open the Bible with no appetite for it and read anyway; in the trouble taken to actually understand a doctrine before you need it, so that when the diagnosis comes you are not starting from nothing; in the prayer that feels like talking to a ceiling and is offered up anyway; in belonging properly to a church rather than attending one, so that other people know you well enough to hold you.

None of it produces a visible inch of growth. That is what makes it root.

And here is the encouragement, because this parable is not a sentence passed on you. Rocky ground in a field cannot do anything about the rock. You can. You are the one soil in the story that is able to go to the Farmer and say: there is something hard underneath me, and I cannot shift it. Ask him now, in the cool of an ordinary week. That prayer, in my experience of Scripture, has never once been declined.

verseByVerse.quote: And others are the ones sown among thorns. They are those who hear the word, but the cares of the world and the deceitfulness of riches and the desires for other things enter in and choke the word, and it proves unfruitful.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Here is the soil that describes most Christians in a comfortable country, and Jesus names its three weeds precisely. Take them one at a time.

The cares of the world. Worry. Not wickedness — worry. The word is the ordinary one for anxiety, the same one Peter uses when he says casting all your anxieties on him, because he cares for you (1 Pet. 5:7). The mortgage. The scan result. The child who is not doing well. The parents who are getting frail and the decisions that are coming. The news, checked six times a day, about disasters you cannot affect.

These are not sins. Most of them are duties. And they will strangle the word, because worry is not passive — it works. It takes the time and the mental room that hearing God requires, and it does it while you are asleep.

The deceitfulness of riches. Not riches. The deceitfulness of them — which means the lie money tells rather than the money itself, and the lie is always the same: a little more will make you safe. That lie is told to the man with very little as loudly as to the man with a great deal, which is why this weed grows in every income bracket. Jesus does not say wealth is evil. He says it is dishonest company. It promises a security it has never once delivered to anybody, and the promise is enough to organise a whole life around.

And the desires for other things. And this is the most devastating phrase of the three, because it is so casual. Literally, the desires concerning the rest — everything else. Jesus does not even bother to name them. The other stuff. The extension. The bike. The holiday you are researching in the evenings. The series everybody is watching. The hobby that has quietly become the thing you think about while other people are talking.

None of it is wrong. That is the entire point of this soil, and why it is so hard to see from the inside. There is nothing here you would need to confess to anyone.

Enter in and choke the word. The verb is strangulation — silent, gradual, and total. And notice the direction of travel: they enter in. Nothing was pushed out. Things were let in, one reasonable thing at a time, and the word was crowded to the edge of a life it had once been the centre of.

And it proves unfruitful. Not dead. Not renounced. The plant is standing there, green, with leaves on it — and there is nothing on it in September.

So test it, and do not test it the easy way. Do not ask is there anything bad in my life? There may be nothing. Ask two harder questions.

First: what has been crowded out? Name what used to happen and has quietly stopped. The praying. The reading. The hospitality. The conversation about Christ you have not had with anybody for a year — not because you refused, but because there was no room.

Second: where does the overflow go? When your week has a spare hour and your mind has a spare half-hour, where do they go, automatically, without a decision being made? Whatever answers that question is what is actually growing in your field.

And then do the only thing that works with thorns, which is not to feel bad about them but to cut them. Thorns are never cleared in general; they are cleared one at a time, with a name attached. The specific anxiety, handed over in specific words. The specific spending, stopped. The specific evening, given back. That is unglamorous, and it is the whole job, and it wants doing before the September when you go out to the field and find nothing on the stalk.

verseByVerse.quote: But those that were sown on the good soil are the ones who hear the word and accept it and bear fruit, thirtyfold and sixtyfold and a hundredfold."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Three verbs, in an order that cannot be rearranged: hear, accept, bear fruit.

Hear the word. The path heard it too. Hearing is where everyone starts and where three of the four stop.

And accept it. This is the verb that separates this soil from the others, and it is worth knowing what it means. The word is paradechomai — to welcome, to take something in as your own, the way you receive a guest rather than the way you receive a leaflet. The rocky ground received the word too, with joy, but the word Mark uses there is the ordinary one for taking something; here it is the warmer word, and the difference is between a man who takes a letter at the door and a man who opens it, reads it, and does what it says.

And notice what accepting is not. It is not agreeing that the sermon was true. Everybody in the boat's hearing agreed that God should be obeyed. Accepting the word means letting it in with authority — allowing it to contradict you and change what you do on Monday.

And bear fruit. Then the outcome, and the order is enormously important pastorally, because it is the order in which the Christian life actually runs and it is constantly reversed.

Fruit is not the price of acceptance. It is the result of it. No plant in any field in the world produces grain by straining to produce grain. It receives — light, water, whatever the soil gives it — and the fruit is what comes out of that. Jesus says the same thing plainly elsewhere: abide in me, and I in you. As the branch cannot bear fruit by itself, unless it abides in the vine, neither can you, unless you abide in me (John 15:4).

Which is the answer to a way of living that exhausts a great many sincere Christians: trying to squeeze fruit out of themselves by effort, and concluding they are failures when they cannot. You are not asked to manufacture. You are asked to receive, and to keep receiving, and to let it go down.

Thirtyfold and sixtyfold and a hundredfold. And here is the pastoral kindness in the last clause, which is easy to read straight past: the yields are different, and all three are good soil.

Jesus could have said a hundredfold and left it there. He did not. He put thirty in the same category as a hundred. There is no suggestion that the thirtyfold Christian is a second-class one; the soil is the same soil, the harvest is a harvest, and a farmer who brought in thirty in that country would have been the talk of the village.

So do not spend your life measuring your field against somebody else's. Some believers are given health, gifts, years and opportunity, and their lives are visibly fruitful. Some are ill, or poor, or obscure, or worn down by circumstances they did not choose, and what they produce is thirty — a marriage held together, a few people prayed for by name for decades, a faith kept in a hard place where nobody applauded. Both are in this verse. Both were sown by the same hand, and the barn does not sort them.

What God requires of a field is not that it should be the best field. It is that it should be honest ground, taking in what falls on it — and the Sower who scattered that seed across your life knew exactly what was under the surface when he threw it, and threw it anyway.

verseByVerse.quote: And he said to them, "Is a lamp brought in to be put under a basket, or under a bed, and not on a stand? For nothing is hidden except to be made manifest; nor is anything secret except to come to light. If anyone has ears to hear, let him hear."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The tone changes, and the change is a relief. After a paragraph about seeing and not perceiving, Jesus picks up a domestic object and asks a question a child could answer.

Is a lamp brought in to be put under a basket, or under a bed, and not on a stand? The lamp is a small clay dish of olive oil with a wick, giving about as much light as a candle. The basket is the household grain measure, a bushel bowl. The bed is a low pallet. And the question is faintly comic on purpose: nobody lights a lamp in order to hide it. You would put the lamp out and save the oil. Everyone in the crowd knew that; the answer is obvious, which is exactly why he asks it.

And it answers the worry the last paragraph raised. If the parables conceal, has God gone into the business of hiding things from people? No. Concealment in the kingdom of God is always temporary and always for the sake of a later revealing. A lamp goes under a basket for a moment while somebody carries it across a room. It does not live there.

For nothing is hidden except to be made manifest; nor is anything secret except to come to light. Read that carefully, because it is a stronger claim than it first appears. It does not say that hidden things sometimes come out. It says that the whole purpose of the hiding was the eventual showing. The concealment is a stage in the disclosure.

And that is precisely what happens in this Gospel. Jesus silences demons, hushes the healed, tells the disciples to say nothing — and then dies in public on a hill outside a city wall at the busiest week of the year, and a Roman officer says out loud what nobody was allowed to say (15:39). The secret was always going to be shouted. It was being protected until it could be understood, the way you shield a flame with your hand while you are carrying it, not because you want the room dark but because you want it lit.

Which is a real comfort for the parts of your own life that make no sense yet. There is a great deal God is doing in the dark at the moment — in you, and in situations you have prayed about for years with nothing to show for it. This verse does not promise that you will get an explanation next Tuesday. It promises that the darkness is not the point. Nothing in the hands of God is hidden for the sake of being hidden. Now we see in a mirror dimly, but then face to face. Now I know in part; then I shall know fully, even as I have been fully known (1 Cor. 13:12).

There is also a searching side to the same saying, and the New Testament does not let it go unmentioned: what is true of God's purposes is true of our secrets. Nothing is covered up that will not be revealed (Luke 12:2). The Christian's comfort is that the things he most dreads coming to light were dealt with at the cross before they were ever brought up.

If anyone has ears to hear, let him hear. The refrain returns, and by now it has an edge. He has just said that everything hidden is destined to be revealed. The only question left is whether you are the kind of person who goes and asks.

verseByVerse.quote: And he said to them, "Pay attention to what you hear: with the measure you use, it will be measured to you, and still more will be added to you. For to the one who has, more will be given, and from the one who has not, even what he has will be taken away."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Pay attention to what you hear. Or, closer to the Greek, watch how you hear. And that is the point of the whole chapter arriving as a command: it turns out that listening is not a passive activity you either succeed or fail at by accident. It is something you do, and can do well or badly, and will be held responsible for.

With the measure you use, it will be measured to you, and still more will be added to you. Picture the transaction, because it is a market-stall image. A man brings his own container to be filled — and what he gets depends on the size of the vessel he brought. Bring a thimble to the merchant and you will carry home a thimbleful, however generous he is.

Then Jesus breaks the picture open at the end, and this is the part people miss: and still more will be added to you. The merchant does not merely fill your container level. He heaps it over. This is God we are dealing with, not a shopkeeper, and the arrangement is not strict reciprocity — it is a generosity that outruns the vessel.

For to the one who has, more will be given, and from the one who has not, even what he has will be taken away.

Now the sentence that sounds unjust, and it is worth facing squarely, because it reads at first like a description of the worst thing about the world — the rich get richer and the poor lose the little they had. Anyone who has watched money or opportunity work knows that pattern and hates it.

But Jesus is not describing money. He is describing spiritual capacity, and there it is not cruelty but simple truth about how understanding works. Everything you actually take in and act on enlarges the vessel you bring back next time. Everything you hear and shelve does not stay neutral — it quietly diminishes your capacity to hear at all.

You know this from ordinary life. The man who learns a little music hears more in the next piece; the man who learns a little of a language hears words in the noise where he used to hear only noise. Use expands the organ. Disuse shrinks it. And a truth heard and never obeyed does not sit patiently waiting to be obeyed later; it hardens, and next time it comes past it will be a little easier to ignore.

That is why even what he has will be taken away is not a punishment arbitrarily imposed. It is the path in verse 15, described from the inside. The ground got hard by traffic.

So run the test, and be specific. Think of the last clear thing God said to you through Scripture or a sermon — not the last interesting thing, the last thing you knew you were meant to do. The conversation to have. The habit to stop. The person to forgive. The money to give.

Did you do it?

If yes, expect more. That is the promise of this verse and it is not stingy — still more will be added. If no, then understand what is actually at stake: the danger is not that God is annoyed with you. It is that the next thing he says will be fainter, and the one after that fainter still, and there will come a day when you sit through the reading of the very words that once moved you and feel nothing at all.

Which is why the Lord ends the section as he began it: pay attention to what you hear. He is not asking for concentration. He is asking for obedience, because obedience is the only container that ever gets bigger.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 26–41 — The Growing Seed, the Mustard Seed, and the Storm
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The seed that grows while you sleep (vv. 26–29). A parable found only in Mark, and it is the most relaxing thing in the chapter. A man scatters seed and then goes to bed, gets up, goes to bed, gets up — and the seed grows, and he knows not how. The growth is not his doing and never was.

The mustard seed (vv. 30–32). The proverbially smallest thing in the garden becomes the largest plant in it, with branches enough for birds to nest in. Spoken to twelve unimpressive men whose movement looked like nothing at all.

As they were able to hear it (vv. 33–34). Mark tells us the teaching was calibrated: parables to the crowd, everything explained in private to the disciples. God gives truth at the rate a person can take it.

The storm (vv. 35–41). And then the chapter stops talking about the word and puts them in a boat. It was his idea to cross. The storm was not an interruption of obedience but the road it went down. He is asleep on a cushion; they are bailing; and the question they ask at the end — who then is this? — is the question the whole Gospel has been walking toward.
verseByVerse.theology:
The stilling of the storm is not a nature miracle among others; it is a disclosure of who is in the boat, and the disciples' own Scriptures gave them the answer to their question the moment they asked it.

In the Old Testament, mastery of the sea belongs to God and to nobody else. You rule the raging of the sea; when its waves rise, you still them (Ps. 89:9). He made the storm be still, and the waves of the sea were hushed (Ps. 107:29) — in a psalm about sailors at their wits' end who cried to the LORD in their trouble. It was God who shut in the sea with doors and said thus far shall you come, and no farther, and here shall your proud waves be stayed (Job 38:8–11). To the ancient mind the sea was chaos itself, the one thing no king could command.

So who then is this, that even the wind and the sea obey him? has exactly one possible answer, and it should have frightened them more than the weather did.

And hold the two halves of the scene together, because the chapter will not let you have one without the other. He was asleep because he was exhausted — a real man, worn out, on a boat cushion, so tired that a storm did not wake him. And he silenced the sea with two words. Fully man in his exhaustion, fully God in his voice, in the same four feet of a fishing boat.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: experienced fishermen, on their own lake, in their own boat, bailing with their hands and certain they were about to die — while the Lord of wind and wave slept four feet away.

Now: the same accusation, in the same words, from every believer in a storm — do you not care? And it is worth noticing that Mark preserved the accusation. The Gospel does not tidy up the prayer of frightened men into something more reverent. There is a place in Scripture for saying exactly that to God, and the Psalms are full of it: Awake! Why are you sleeping, O Lord? (Ps. 44:23).

Two things follow. First, he answered the panicked prayer before he corrected the panic — the storm was stilled, and then the question about faith was asked. He is not waiting for you to pray well before he acts. Second, their fear did not end when the danger did; Mark says they were filled with great fear after the calm. They were more frightened of the man in the boat than of the wind. That is not a failure. That is the beginning of knowing who he is.

verseByVerse.quote: And he said, "The kingdom of God is as if a man should scatter seed on the ground. He sleeps and rises night and day, and the seed sprouts and grows; he knows not how. The earth produces by itself, first the blade, then the ear, then the full grain in the ear. But when the grain is ripe, at once he puts in the sickle, because the harvest has come."
verseByVerse.commentary:
This little parable belongs to Mark alone, and it is the most restful thing in the chapter.

A man should scatter seed on the ground. Same as before: he sows. And then Jesus tells us what he does next, and it is the surprise of the story — nothing.

He sleeps and rises night and day. Four ordinary words for a man's whole life. He goes to bed; he gets up; he goes to bed; he gets up. The rhythm of a completely unremarkable existence. There is no watching over the field at night, no anxious digging up of seed to see how it is doing, no technique.

And the seed sprouts and grows; he knows not how. There is the heart of it, and it is a phrase worth memorising. Not he does not control it — he does not even understand it. And notice that his ignorance does not slow the crop down by a single day. The wheat does not wait for the farmer to comprehend it.

Now feel who this was spoken to. Twelve men who had just been handed a mission and were, on any reasonable assessment, unqualified for it. In a few chapters they will be sent out two by two with no money and no spare tunic, and told to preach. Everything in them will want to know how it works, and whether they are doing it right, and what to do when it does not seem to be working.

Jesus tells them: you scatter, and then you sleep. The power was never in the sower.

That is not a licence for laziness — the man in the parable still sows, and still turns up with a sickle at the end. It is a release from a burden nobody was ever asked to carry. You cannot make a seed germinate. You cannot argue a person into the kingdom, or engineer a revival, or produce growth in your own soul by force of will. Paul, who worked harder than anyone, says it exactly: I planted, Apollos watered, but God gave the growth (1 Cor. 3:6).

So the practical shape of it is this. Do your sowing, honestly and generously — the conversation, the teaching, the years with your children, the invitation, the faithful ordinary Sunday. Then go to bed. Actually go to bed. The anxious sleeplessness that so often passes for spiritual seriousness is not in this parable at all, and the crop is not depending on it.

The earth produces by itself. The word is automatē — of itself, automatically. Not without God, obviously; this is a picture of how God works, not a picture of God's absence. But without the farmer.

First the blade, then the ear, then the full grain in the ear. And this is the tenderest line for anyone worried about their own slowness, or somebody else's. Growth has stages, and the stages cannot be skipped or hurried. A blade is not a failed ear; it is a blade, which is exactly what a healthy plant looks like in April. God is not disappointed with a young Christian for not being an old one, and he is not finished with an old one either.

But when the grain is ripe, at once he puts in the sickle. And then the ending, which is quietly enormous. The words are lifted from Joel: Put in the sickle, for the harvest is ripe (Joel 3:13) — a text about the final judgement of the nations.

So this is not merely a story about patience. There is a harvest, and it is fixed, and it comes not when the field is exhausted but when the grain is ripe. The long, quiet, unimpressive middle of history — this stretch you are living in, where the kingdom looks small and slow and nothing seems to be happening — is not drift. It is growing season. And the man with the sickle knows the day.

verseByVerse.quote: And he said, "With what can we compare the kingdom of God, or what parable shall we use for it? It is like a grain of mustard seed, which, when sown on the ground, is the smallest of all the seeds on earth, yet when it is sown it grows up and becomes larger than all the garden plants and puts out large branches, so that the birds of the air can make nests in its shade."
verseByVerse.commentary:
With what can we compare the kingdom of God? He asks the question out loud, as a teacher does when he wants the class leaning in. And the answer he reaches for is deliberately, almost comically, small.

A grain of mustard seed... the smallest of all the seeds on earth. The mustard seed was the standard proverb for tininess in that world, the way we say a grain of sand; the rabbis used it that way. Jesus is not delivering a lecture in botany, and it is worth saying plainly for the reader who has heard this raised as an objection: he is not making a claim about the seed catalogue of the world. He is using the everyday proverb of the people in front of him, about the seeds a Galilean farmer actually handled, exactly as we say the sun rises without being wrong about astronomy.

What matters is the size of the thing in the hand. It is a speck. You could lose it in the creases of your palm.

Yet when it is sown it grows up and becomes larger than all the garden plants and puts out large branches. Black mustard in that climate goes up eight or ten feet in a season — tall enough to ride through, woody enough to hold weight. Nothing in the seed announces it.

Now hear who is listening. Twelve men and a handful of others, sitting on a beach in a provincial district of an occupied country, following a village carpenter whose own family thinks he is unwell and whose national religious leadership has ruled him demonic. Rome has legions and roads and an emperor. This has a boat.

And Jesus says: the kingdom of God is that speck in your hand.

So that the birds of the air can make nests in its shade. Then the last clause, and it is not decoration — it is a deliberate echo, and every Jew on that beach would have caught it. In Ezekiel, God takes a sprig from the top of a cedar and plants it on the mountain height of Israel, and it becomes a noble cedar, and under it will dwell every kind of bird; in the shade of its branches birds of every sort will nest (Ezek. 17:22–23). In Daniel, the great tree whose shade shelters the beasts and whose branches hold the birds of the heavens is a world empire (Dan. 4:12, 21).

The birds are the nations. That is the point of the picture: a kingdom big enough for the peoples of the earth to come and live in.

So set the two ends of the parable side by side, because that is the whole force of it. At one end: a speck, a dozen men, a borrowed boat, a preacher three years from a public execution. At the other: shade for the nations of the world.

And the distance between them is not covered by strategy or numbers or a change in the weather. It is covered by the nature of the seed. Small is not the same as weak, and slow is not the same as failing, and it is only ever in the hand that a mustard seed looks like nothing.

Which is worth taking home if the part of the kingdom you can actually see is discouragingly small — the congregation that is aging, the Sunday school class of four, the one believing member of a family, the years of prayer for a person who has not moved an inch. You are not looking at the tree. You are looking at the seed, and you were never given the ability to tell the difference by looking.

Two thousand years after that afternoon, the speck has put out branches on every continent on earth, and men and women of every language nest in its shade — and the seed has not finished growing.

verseByVerse.quote: With many such parables he spoke the word to them, as they were able to hear it. He did not speak to them without a parable, but privately to his own disciples he explained everything.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Mark steps back from the scene for two verses and tells us how the Lord Jesus taught, and both halves are worth having.

With many such parables he spoke the word to them, as they were able to hear it.

Stop on that last clause, because it is one of the kindest sentences in the Gospel. He measured what he said to what they could take. Not to what he could have said. Not to what was true — all of it was true. To what they could bear.

He does that all the way through. Late on, in the upper room, he says it in so many words: I still have many things to say to you, but you cannot bear them now (John 16:12). The Son of God, with everything worth knowing available to him, holds things back out of tenderness for the capacity of the people in front of him.

And that is worth applying in two directions.

To yourself, if you are impatient with your own understanding. There is a way of reading the Bible that turns into anxiety — the sense that you ought to have grasped more by now, that other people see things you do not, that your slowness is a mark against you. He is not withholding out of displeasure. He gives at the rate a person can receive, and that rate is not a judgement on you. A field gets the blade before it gets the ear, and the farmer is not disappointed in April.

And to how you handle other people. If the Lord calibrated what he said, so should we. There is a kind of zeal that unloads everything it knows onto a new believer, or a struggling one, or a person who has just been bereaved — every doctrine, every implication, every hard edge — and calls it faithfulness. It is not faithfulness; it is a failure to notice who is in the room. Say what they can hear. There will be more Tuesdays.

He did not speak to them without a parable, but privately to his own disciples he explained everything.

Two audiences, two levels — and the difference between them, once again, is not intelligence but proximity. The explanation happens privately, to those who stayed. Everything in this chapter keeps coming back to that: the crowd got the story, the ones who did not go home got the meaning, and the only qualification was that they were still there when the beach emptied.

Explained everything. He did not leave them with a riddle. Whatever else the parables were, they were not designed to keep his own people in the dark, and the door into the private room was never locked.

So take the plainest possible lesson from the plainest verse. The difference between a Christian who understands his Bible and one who does not is very rarely ability, and very often simply this: one of them keeps coming back to Christ with the bits he did not follow, and the other closes the book. Stay behind. Ask. He explains everything to the people who do.

verseByVerse.quote: On that day, when evening had come, he said to them, "Let us go across to the other side." And leaving the crowd, they took him with them in the boat, just as he was. And other boats were with him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
On that day, when evening had come. Mark ties it to the day of teaching — the long day in the boat with the crowd on the shore. He has been preaching since morning. He is finished, and it is getting dark.

He said to them, Let us go across to the other side. And here is the detail that changes how the whole storm is read, so fix it now: going out onto that lake was his idea.

Not theirs. They were not running away from anything, or taking a shortcut, or making a poor decision he then had to rescue them from. The Son of God said cross, and they crossed, and the storm that nearly killed them was met in the middle of doing exactly what he told them to do.

That is worth pressing, because a great deal of Christian thinking assumes the opposite. When the trouble comes we search backwards for the wrong turn — what did I miss, where did I disobey, is this because I stopped praying. Sometimes there is a wrong turn and it should be found. But this boat is in this storm because Jesus put it there, and the obedience was the route in.

Job did not suffer because he had drifted; the whole book opens by insisting he was blameless. Paul was in the will of God on the ship that broke up under him (Acts 27). The storm you are in may not be evidence of anything having gone wrong at all. It may simply be what the other side costs.

And leaving the crowd, they took him with them in the boat, just as he was.

That last phrase is one of those small Markan details that can only have come from a man who was there. Just as he was — no going ashore, no preparation, no meal, no change of clothes. He had been sitting in that boat teaching since the morning, and they simply pushed off with him still in it, exhausted where he sat.

Keep hold of that when you reach verse 38 and find him asleep. Mark has already told you why. This is a man at the end of a day's work who never got off the boat.

And other boats were with him. A single clause, easy to skip, and Mark alone records it.

Which means the storm did not fall on one boat. There were other people out on that water in the dark, in smaller craft than a fishing boat, with no one aboard who could still a wave. Mark says nothing about what happened to them, and the silence is its own comfort: when the calm came, it came over the whole lake. The men who benefited most from the miracle may have been people who never knew who had done it, in boats whose names nobody wrote down.

Some of what God does in answer to the church's terrified praying spills a long way past the church, and is never traced back.

verseByVerse.quote: And a great windstorm arose, and the waves were breaking into the boat, so that the boat was already filling. But he was in the stern, asleep on the cushion. And they woke him and said to him, "Teacher, do you not care that we are perishing?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
And a great windstorm arose. The word is lailaps — a hurricane, a squall that hits without warning.

The geography explains it, and these men knew it better than we do. The Sea of Galilee sits nearly seven hundred feet below sea level in a bowl, with the Golan heights rising steeply to the east and gullies running down to the water. Cold air off the heights funnels down those gullies onto warm air sitting on the lake, and the surface can go from glass to breaking waves in minutes. It is still notorious. Modern boats have been caught out on it.

And the waves were breaking into the boat, so that the boat was already filling. Not spray. Waves coming in over the side, one after another, and the boat going down under the weight of the water.

Take seriously who these men are. At least four of them are professional fishermen who have worked this lake since boyhood, in their own boat, on water they know as well as their own street. Their terror is not the panic of amateurs. When men like that conclude they are about to drown, they are almost certainly right.

But he was in the stern, asleep on the cushion.

Mark gives us three details nobody would invent: the stern, the cushion, and the sleep. The stern of a fishing boat had a small raised deck; the cushion is the helmsman's — a leather sandbag kept for ballast and used as a pillow. And Mark writes the cushion, the way a man remembers the exact object.

Now hold what that sleep means, because it is one of the great windows in the Gospels onto who Jesus actually is. He is asleep because he is worn out. He had been teaching since morning and they pushed off with him just as he was. The Son of God got tired — properly, physically tired, the tiredness that will not wake for a hurricane and freezing water breaking over you. He was hungry (11:12), he was thirsty (John 19:28), he wept at a graveside (John 11:35). Whatever else the doctrine of the incarnation means, it means this: there is a man in that boat, and he is exhausted.

And there is more in it than exhaustion. He can sleep in a storm on a lake he made. In peace I will both lie down and sleep; for you alone, O LORD, make me dwell in safety (Ps. 4:8).

And they woke him and said to him, Teacher, do you not care that we are perishing?

That is not a prayer request. It is an accusation, and Mark did not tidy it up.

Notice they do not ask him to do anything. They do not say save us — they say do you not care? Which is what fear does to us: it goes past the danger and attacks the character of God. The real terror in that boat was not the water. It was the sudden conviction that the person in charge had gone quiet and might not be bothered.

If you have prayed like that — if you have said something to God in a hospital corridor or at two in the morning that you would be ashamed to repeat in church — then take note of what Scripture does with this sentence. It preserves it. The Bible is full of it: Awake! Why are you sleeping, O Lord? Rouse yourself! Do not reject us forever! (Ps. 44:23). How long, O LORD? Will you forget me forever? (Ps. 13:1).

He would rather have that shouted at him from four feet away than have you drown politely at the other end of the boat. They got one thing right in the middle of getting everything else wrong: when they were sure they were dying, they went to him.

verseByVerse.quote: And he awoke and rebuked the wind and said to the sea, "Peace! Be still!" And the wind ceased, and there was a great calm.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And he awoke and rebuked the wind. No preparation. He does not take the helm, or tell them to bail harder, or pray to his Father for deliverance. He wakes up in a swamped boat and speaks to the weather as though it had been misbehaving.

And the verb is worth stopping on: rebuked. It is the same word Mark used in the synagogue at Capernaum when Jesus rebuked the unclean spirit (1:25). He addresses a storm the way he addresses a demon — as a hostile thing that has no business being here.

And said to the sea, Peace! Be still! The English is gentler than the Greek. The first word means be silent; the second is a perfect passive imperative that means, quite literally, be muzzled — and it is precisely the word he threw at the demon in 1:25. The sea is told to shut its mouth and stay shut.

You have to hear that against everything an ancient reader believed about the sea. To Israel the sea was not a beauty spot; it was chaos, the old enemy, the thing that swallows men and gives nothing back. Only one Person in their Scriptures ever gave it orders. You rule the raging of the sea; when its waves rise, you still them (Ps. 89:9). He made the storm be still, and the waves of the sea were hushed (Ps. 107:29). Thus far shall you come, and no farther, and here shall your proud waves be stayed (Job 38:11).

And this is a carpenter, standing in a fishing boat, wet through, speaking two words in Aramaic to a hurricane at midnight.

And the wind ceased, and there was a great calm.

Do not let familiarity flatten that. Wind does not stop; it drops away, and even when it does the sea keeps running for hours. Anyone who has been at sea knows that the swell outlives the storm — that is simply how water behaves. Here there is no interval at all. Wind gone, water flat, instantly, as though the lake had never moved.

Mark sets the two greats side by side deliberately: a great windstorm in verse 37, a great calm in verse 39, and one sentence between them.

And there is the whole difference between him and every other help you have ever had. Everything else that assists you works with the situation — manages it, mitigates it, gets you through it. He speaks to it. The gap between what he is and what we are is not a gap of degree.

Then hold this alongside the only other time in Mark that a great calm follows a great storm. On a hill outside Jerusalem the sky goes black at noon and stays black for three hours, and a man cries out that God has forsaken him, and then he dies (15:33–37) — and it goes quiet. That day nobody rebuked the storm. He went into it and let it break over him with nothing held back, and it was not muzzled and it did not stop until it had finished with him.

The voice that could have silenced anything said nothing at all — so that when the storms come for you, they come as weather and not as wrath.

verseByVerse.quote: He said to them, "Why are you so afraid? Have you still no faith?" And they were filled with great fear and said to one another, "Who then is this, that even the wind and the sea obey him?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Why are you so afraid? Have you still no faith?

It sounds hard, and a nervous reader flinches at it. Two things take the sting out of it without taking away the point.

First, look at the order of events. He stilled the storm and then asked the question. He did not sit up in the stern and require a better standard of praying before he would act. He dealt with the water first, because they needed the water dealt with, and only afterwards turned to what was wrong inside the boat. That order is worth remembering next time you are ashamed of how badly you prayed in a crisis. He is not waiting for you to pray well.

Second, hear what the question actually asks. Not why were you frightened by a hurricane? — any sane man is. The word is deiloi, timid, cowardly; and the issue is not the fear but its object. They had every reason to be afraid of the lake and no reason at all to be afraid with him in the boat. The rebuke is not you felt something. It is you forgot who was aboard.

Still no faith? The still is the sad word. They have watched a leper made clean, a paralytic walk, a withered hand restored, demons obey him in public. It has been in front of them for three chapters. What they had not yet done is take any of it into the one place where it would cost them something — the place where they thought they were dying.

That is a familiar distance, and it is worth naming honestly: the gap between what you believe on a Sunday and what you can lay hold of at three in the morning. Faith is not tested by whether you can affirm a doctrine. It is tested by whether the doctrine is load-bearing when the water comes over the side.

And they were filled with great fear.

And now the strangest thing in the chapter, and Mark reports it without explanation. The danger is over. The lake is like glass. And the disciples are more frightened than they were during the storm — the Greek is emphatic, they feared a great fear.

They had been afraid of drowning. Now they are afraid of the man who is standing in the boat with them, dripping wet, four feet away.

This is not a failure of faith; it is the beginning of understanding. When a man realises what has actually been sharing a boat with him all afternoon, terror is not an unreasonable first response. Isaiah saw the Lord and said Woe is me! For I am lost (Isa. 6:5). Peter, after another miracle on this same lake, fell down and said Depart from me, for I am a sinful man (Luke 5:8). The fear of the LORD is where knowledge begins, and it has to begin somewhere.

Who then is this, that even the wind and the sea obey him?

They ask it of each other, in the dark, on flat water. And they do not answer it. Mark leaves the question hanging at the end of the chapter, because the whole Gospel is the answer, and it will not be complete until a Roman soldier says it at the foot of a cross (15:39).

But their own Scriptures had already answered it, and they knew those Scriptures by heart. Who stills the sea? There is one name in the whole Old Testament that fits, and there is no second candidate.

So the sentence that ought to be forming in that boat is not a question at all. The man asleep on the helmsman's cushion, so worn out by a day's preaching that a hurricane could not wake him, is the One who said thus far and no farther to the ocean before there was a man alive to see it.

And that is who was in the boat. Not a good teacher who happened to be useful in an emergency — the Lord of the wind and the sea, tired out in the stern, having chosen to be there, in a body he took so that he could sleep, and thirst, and bleed, and die, for the men bailing water round his feet.

4.theology:
Why parables? Verses 11–12 are the hardest words in the chapter and they should not be softened. Matthew says Jesus speaks in parables because people do not see (Matt. 13:13); Mark says so that they may not see, lest they should turn and be forgiven. Three things resolve it. The words are a quotation of Isaiah 6:9–10, God's charge to a prophet sent to a nation that had already shut its eyes for generations — settled judgement on hardened refusal, not fresh cruelty. The so that carries fulfilment as much as bare purpose: the parables meet a people who have chosen blindness and confirm the choice, which is how God deals with those who insist (cf. Rom. 1:24). And the door is never bolted — those around him with the twelve understood nothing either, and the one thing that separated them from the crowd walking home was that they stayed and asked.

Who is in the boat? In the Old Testament, command of the sea belongs to God alone: you rule the raging of the sea; when its waves rise, you still them (Ps. 89:9); he made the storm be still, and the waves of the sea were hushed (Ps. 107:29); thus far shall you come, and no farther (Job 38:11). So the disciples' closing question has exactly one possible answer. And Mark holds the two natures within four feet of each other: asleep from sheer exhaustion on the helmsman's cushion, and muzzling a hurricane with two words.
4.examples:
The four soils are not four historical types but four live possibilities in any congregation on any Sunday, and the third is the one that describes most Christians in a comfortable country.

The path was not made hard by a decision; it was made hard by traffic — the same feet over the same ground until nothing could get in. That is how hearts harden in real life: not by rejecting God but by hearing about him so often that the sound becomes familiar.

The rocky ground grows fastest, and grows fastest because the soil is shallow. The heat that kills it is the same sun that ripens the harvest in the next furrow. Roots are grown in private, in the boring stretches, and the test is simple: if the trial came this year, what exactly would you be drawing on?

The thorns are not sins. Jesus names them — cares, riches, and the desires for other things. Worry, money, and the ordinary wanting of ordinary stuff. This soil cannot be diagnosed by examining your conduct, because there may be nothing in it to confess. It is diagnosed by what has quietly stopped: the praying, the reading, the conversation about Christ you have not had in a year — not refused, just crowded out.

And the good soil yields thirty, sixty, or a hundred — and all three are good soil. Jesus put thirty in the same category as a hundred. Some believers are given health and years and visible fruitfulness; some produce a marriage held together and a few names prayed for over decades in a hard place where nobody applauded. Both are in verse 20, and the barn does not sort them.

5.title: Legion, Daughter, and the Hand That Takes Hold
5.text: <sup>1</sup>They came to the other side of the sea, to the country of the Gerasenes. <sup>2</sup>And when Jesus had stepped out of the boat, immediately there met him out of the tombs a man with an unclean spirit. <sup>3</sup>He lived among the tombs. And no one could bind him anymore, not even with a chain, <sup>4</sup>for he had often been bound with shackles and chains, but he wrenched the chains apart, and he broke the shackles in pieces. No one had the strength to subdue him. <sup>5</sup>Night and day among the tombs and on the mountains he was always crying out and cutting himself with stones. <sup>6</sup>And when he saw Jesus from afar, he ran and fell down before him. <sup>7</sup>And crying out with a loud voice, he said, “What have you to do with me, Jesus, Son of the Most High God? I adjure you by God, do not torment me.” <sup>8</sup>For he was saying to him, “Come out of the man, you unclean spirit!” <sup>9</sup>And Jesus asked him, “What is your name?” He replied, “My name is Legion, for we are many.” <sup>10</sup>And he begged him earnestly not to send them out of the country. <sup>11</sup>Now a great herd of pigs was feeding there on the hillside, <sup>12</sup>and they begged him, saying, “Send us to the pigs; let us enter them.” <sup>13</sup>So he gave them permission. And the unclean spirits came out and entered the pigs; and the herd, numbering about two thousand, rushed down the steep bank into the sea and drowned in the sea. <sup>14</sup>The herdsmen fled and told it in the city and in the country. And people came to see what it was that had happened. <sup>15</sup>And they came to Jesus and saw the demon-possessed man, the one who had had the legion, sitting there, clothed and in his right mind, and they were afraid. <sup>16</sup>And those who had seen it described to them what had happened to the demon-possessed man and to the pigs. <sup>17</sup>And they began to beg Jesus to depart from their region. <sup>18</sup>As he was getting into the boat, the man who had been possessed with demons begged him that he might be with him. <sup>19</sup>And he did not permit him but said to him, “Go home to your friends and tell them how much the Lord has done for you, and how he has had mercy on you.” <sup>20</sup>And he went away and began to proclaim in the Decapolis how much Jesus had done for him, and everyone marveled. <sup>21</sup>And when Jesus had crossed again in the boat to the other side, a great crowd gathered about him, and he was beside the sea. <sup>22</sup>Then came one of the rulers of the synagogue, Jairus by name, and seeing him, he fell at his feet <sup>23</sup>and implored him earnestly, saying, “My little daughter is at the point of death. Come and lay your hands on her, so that she may be made well and live.” <sup>24</sup>And he went with him. And a great crowd followed him and thronged about him. <sup>25</sup>And there was a woman who had had a discharge of blood for twelve years, <sup>26</sup>and who had suffered much under many physicians, and had spent all that she had, and was no better but rather grew worse. <sup>27</sup>She had heard the reports about Jesus and came up behind him in the crowd and touched his garment. <sup>28</sup>For she said, “If I touch even his garments, I will be made well.” <sup>29</sup>And immediately the flow of blood dried up, and she felt in her body that she was healed of her disease. <sup>30</sup>And Jesus, perceiving in himself that power had gone out from him, immediately turned about in the crowd and said, “Who touched my garments?” <sup>31</sup>And his disciples said to him, “You see the crowd pressing around you, and yet you say, ‘Who touched me?’” <sup>32</sup>And he looked around to see who had done it. <sup>33</sup>But the woman, knowing what had happened to her, came in fear and trembling and fell down before him and told him the whole truth. <sup>34</sup>And he said to her, “Daughter, your faith has made you well; go in peace, and be healed of your disease.” <sup>35</sup>While he was still speaking, there came from the ruler’s house some who said, “Your daughter is dead. Why trouble the Teacher any further?” <sup>36</sup>But overhearing what they said, Jesus said to the ruler of the synagogue, “Do not fear, only believe.” <sup>37</sup>And he allowed no one to follow him except Peter and James and John the brother of James. <sup>38</sup>They came to the house of the ruler of the synagogue, and Jesus saw a commotion, people weeping and wailing loudly. <sup>39</sup>And when he had entered, he said to them, “Why are you making a commotion and weeping? The child is not dead but sleeping.” <sup>40</sup>And they laughed at him. But he put them all outside and took the child’s father and mother and those who were with him and went in where the child was. <sup>41</sup>Taking her by the hand he said to her, “Talitha cumi,” which means, “Little girl, I say to you, arise.” <sup>42</sup>And immediately the girl got up and began walking (for she was twelve years of age), and they were immediately overcome with amazement. <sup>43</sup>And he strictly charged them that no one should know this, and told them to give her something to eat.
5.overview:
Chapter 5 is three impossible cases in a row, and the arrangement is deliberate. A man no one could restrain, a woman no one could cure, and a child who has already died — the whole range of human helplessness, met in one day and a boat ride.

It is also a chapter about uncleanness, and a modern reader misses most of it without knowing that. Under the Law three things defiled by contact: a grave, a discharge of blood, and a pig. Mark has put all three in one chapter. Jesus lands in a graveyard among pigs to save a man who lives in the tombs; an untouchable woman takes hold of his clothes in a crowd; and he ends the day taking a corpse by the hand. Every one of those contacts should have made him unclean under the system he himself gave. Every one of them runs the other way instead.

The two halves are held together by twelve years — the length of the woman's suffering and the whole life of Jairus's daughter — and by one word. The father calls the girl his little daughter; Jesus calls the destitute, unclean woman in the street Daughter, the only time in the Gospels he addresses a woman that way. The chapter opens with a man nobody could chain and closes with a girl being handed something to eat.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The landing (vv. 1–5). The storm of chapter 4 was crossed to reach this beach, and the welcoming party is one man out of the tombs — chained, unchainable, screaming night and day, cutting himself with stones. Mark spends five verses establishing that this case is beyond every remedy human beings had.

The encounter (vv. 6–10). He runs and falls at Jesus's feet, and the voice that comes out of him tries to put Jesus under oath. Asked its name, it answers with the word for a Roman army: Legion.

The pigs (vv. 11–13). The demons beg to be sent into a herd, and are permitted — and the herd goes over the cliff. What they intended for the man is acted out on the hillside for everyone to see.

The town's verdict (vv. 14–17). The neighbours arrive, find the man dressed and talking sense, and are frightened. They do not ask Jesus to stay and do more. They ask him to leave, and he goes.

The commission (vv. 18–20). The one man who wants to come is told no — and given a district instead of a boat. He becomes the first missionary to the Gentiles, and his whole training was what had happened to him.
verseByVerse.theology:
This chapter turns on ceremonial uncleanness, and a modern reader misses most of its force without knowing that. Under the Law, three things made a person unclean by contact: a corpse or a grave (Num. 19:11–16), a discharge of blood (Lev. 15:25–27), and a pig (Lev. 11:7). Mark has put all three in one chapter, and the man in this scene is standing in all of them at once — living among tombs, on a hillside where pigs are grazing, in Gentile country.

The whole logic of the purity system ran one way: uncleanness is contagious and holiness is not. Touch a corpse and you are defiled; the corpse does not become clean. Which is why what happens next in this chapter is so startling. A woman whose bleeding has made her untouchable for twelve years puts her hand on Jesus, and she is healed rather than he defiled. He takes a dead girl by the hand, and she gets up. The current runs backwards.

That is not Jesus ignoring the Law. It is the Law's purpose arriving. The system taught Israel for centuries that sin and death spread and cleanness does not — so that when a man walked into Israel whose holiness was catching, they would know exactly what they were looking at. He is the one clean thing in the world that cannot be contaminated, and everything he touches is what changes.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: a Gentile town given a neighbour back — sane, dressed, sitting down — and a hillside of dead livestock, and it grieves the livestock and asks the Healer to go.

Now: the same trade is still on offer, and it is not usually made by wicked people. It is made by people who have counted the cost of Christ disrupting an arrangement that works — the business practice, the relationship, the private habit, the plans — and quietly concluded they would rather keep the pigs. Nobody in that town denied the miracle. They simply decided it was too expensive.

And note what he does when they ask. He does not argue, and he does not stay. He gets into the boat. That is one of the most sobering sentences in the Gospel: Jesus goes where he is asked to go, including away.

But he does not leave them without a witness. The man they had chained and could not hold is left behind in the district with nothing to offer but what had been done to him — and by chapter 7 the crowds on that side of the lake will come out to meet Jesus. One restored man, telling one town, and the ground was ready.

verseByVerse.quote: They came to the other side of the sea, to the country of the Gerasenes. And when Jesus had stepped out of the boat, immediately there met him out of the tombs a man with an unclean spirit.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Remember what it cost to get here. The last chapter ended with a hurricane at midnight and a boat filling with water, and this is the shore they were crossing to. Everything that happened on the lake happened on the way to this man.

That is worth sitting with if you are inclined to think of the storm as an accident. Jesus said let us go across to the other side, and the other side had one person on it who needed him. If the price of the crossing was a night that nearly killed twelve experienced sailors, he paid it, and he paid it for a man whose own town had given up on him.

To the country of the Gerasenes. This is Gentile ground — the region of the Decapolis, ten Greek cities east and south of the lake, pagan territory with pig farms on the hillsides. Jesus has left Israel. It is the first time in this Gospel he sets foot outside Jewish land, and he goes there to fight.

A reader with a map will notice a real puzzle here, and it is better dealt with than hurried past. Gerasa was a city some thirty miles from the lake — far too far for a herd to run down the steep bank into the sea. Matthew names the Gadarenes (Gadara, about six miles off, still not on the shore), and some manuscripts of all three Gospels read Gergesenes. The likeliest answer is that Gergesa — modern Kursi, a small place right on the eastern shore where the hills drop sharply to the water — is the actual spot, and that Gerasa and Gadara were the well-known cities whose districts reached down to that shore. Each writer named the region by the city his own readers would recognise, much as one might say a village lies in greater London.

The steep bank is still there. What looks like a contradiction is the ordinary looseness of naming a place by its nearest famous city, and the shoreline fits the story exactly.

Immediately there met him out of the tombs a man with an unclean spirit. He has one foot on the beach. There is no interval, no walk into town, no settling in — the boat grounds and the man is coming down at them out of the rocks.

And picture where he comes from. The limestone hills on that shore are full of cave tombs, cut into the rock, some of them big enough to stand in. That is his address. A man is living in a graveyard, and the town knows it, and nobody has come to get him.

Note also the word Mark uses for the spirit: unclean. Under the Law, a grave defiled anyone who went near it for seven days (Num. 19:16). This man has been living inside his own permanent uncleanness — outside the town, outside worship, outside every category human beings use to organise the living.

So Mark has arranged the meeting with great care. On one side of the beach: a man out of the tombs, unclean, unreachable, the property of something that hates him. On the other side: a man stepping out of a boat, wet through, who has just been asleep on a cushion in a hurricane.

Nothing in the scene says which of them is stronger. The next twenty verses are about that.

verseByVerse.quote: He lived among the tombs. And no one could bind him anymore, not even with a chain, for he had often been bound with shackles and chains, but he wrenched the chains apart, and he broke the shackles in pieces. No one had the strength to subdue him. Night and day among the tombs and on the mountains he was always crying out and cutting himself with stones.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Mark now slows right down. Three verses of pure description before a word is spoken, and every clause is doing the same job: establishing that this man was past help.

He lived among the tombs. Not hid there occasionally. Lived. A graveyard was his home, and the dead were his company.

And no one could bind him anymore, not even with a chain. The word anymore tells the whole history in four letters. They had tried. Repeatedly. There had been a time when the town still attempted something, and it had stopped.

He wrenched the chains apart, and he broke the shackles in pieces. Two different failures. Iron chains torn apart; the shackles — the metal cuffs on wrists and ankles — smashed. Mark, who has this from Peter, gives the detail like a man describing physical evidence he has seen.

No one had the strength to subdue him. And there is the town's final verdict, stated flatly. The word means to tame — the word you would use of an animal. They had reached the point of trying to tame a man, and failed at that too.

So here is where the community got to. Restraint had failed. Confinement had failed. There was no help available and nobody left who thought there might be. He was written off, and the writing off had been going on for years.

Night and day among the tombs and on the mountains he was always crying out. The screaming never stopped. Not a fit that came and went — night and day, on the hillsides where the sound carried down to the town. The people of that district went to sleep hearing him.

And cutting himself with stones. And here Mark says the thing that will land hardest on a modern reader, and it should be handled gently, because a great many people know exactly what this verse is describing.

Understand first what it tells us about the power in him. Everything the demons do to this man is aimed at his destruction. They have taken him out of his home, out of his town, out of human company, out of clothing, out of his own mind, and now they are using his own hands against his own body. That is the settled programme of the enemy wherever he is given room: not pleasure, not power, but ruin — and ruin worked, where possible, through the victim's own hands. The pigs in a few verses will act it out on a hillside for everyone to see; whatever gets hold of them runs straight for the water.

And if you are a person who hurts yourself, or you love one, take this from the passage carefully and take the whole of it. This verse is not here to give you a diagnosis, and it would be wrong to read every case of self-harm as a case of possession — Scripture distinguishes plainly between the demonised and the ill (1:32–34), and pain, shame and illness are enough to explain most of what human beings do to themselves. Go to a doctor; that is an ordinary mercy from God and not a failure of faith.

What this passage does tell you is the direction the story runs. The man in the tombs, whom nobody could hold and nobody could help, is sitting quietly in a few verses, dressed, talking, in his right mind, with the marks of the stones still on his arms. And the one who put him back together did not flinch at meeting him at his worst, in a graveyard, screaming, bleeding, and out of control.

He came to that beach on purpose. That is who Jesus went out of his way, and through a storm, to find.

verseByVerse.quote: And when he saw Jesus from afar, he ran and fell down before him. And crying out with a loud voice, he said, "What have you to do with me, Jesus, Son of the Most High God? I adjure you by God, do not torment me."
verseByVerse.commentary:
And when he saw Jesus from afar, he ran and fell down before him.

The whole tragedy of the man is in that sentence, and you have to read it twice to feel it. He ran. Across broken ground, from a distance, to get to Jesus — and then went down on his face in front of him.

Who did the running? Mark does not tell us, and probably it cannot be separated. There is a man in there who has wanted help for years and has never once been able to get to it. And there is a power in there that has to come, because it cannot do anything else in the presence of the Son of God. Both are true, and they arrive at the same feet.

The posture is the posture of worship. It is not willing worship — this is the same involuntary prostration as on the beach in chapter 3 — but it is the rehearsal of a day when everything that has ever opposed him will do this: at the name of Jesus every knee should bow (Phil. 2:10).

And crying out with a loud voice. The screaming that the district has heard for years, aimed now at one person.

What have you to do with me, Jesus, Son of the Most High God?

The theology is flawless, and it is the second time in Mark that the best confession in the district comes out of a demon (cf. 3:11). Son of the Most High God — the title El Elyon, God Most High, is the name for God used by Gentiles in the Old Testament; it is Melchizedek's name for him (Gen. 14:18–20), and Nebuchadnezzar's. On the pagan side of the lake, even the demons use the local vocabulary. And they use it correctly.

It still does them no good. That is the point Mark keeps making and it will not go away: you can have the doctrine exactly right, use the right name, take the right posture, and be no nearer to being saved than you were before. The difference between this cry and a Christian's is not accuracy. It is that this one means keep away from me.

I adjure you by God, do not torment me.

Now look closely at what is happening here, because it is remarkable and easily missed. To adjure someone is to put them under oath — and that was the standard technique of the professional exorcist in that world. You named a higher power and bound the spirit by it. The formula was the trade.

So the demon is attempting an exorcism. It is trying to use the exorcist's own tools on the exorcist, invoking God to stop the Son of God. It is the last resort of something that has understood, in the first three seconds, that it is completely outmatched, and it does not work for even a moment.

Do not torment me. And there is the fear underneath. Matthew gives the sentence in full: Have you come here to torment us before the time? (Matt. 8:29).

Before the time. They know there is a time. They know what is fixed for them, and they know who fixed it, and their only argument is about the schedule. The kingdom of darkness in this Gospel is not confidently opposing Christ. It is a defeated thing negotiating for a delay.

So if the powers of evil frighten you — and there is no shame in that — notice who is on the ground and who is standing. The demons in Mark are never once calm in the presence of Jesus. They shout, they beg, they bargain, they go. He has not yet had to raise his voice.

verseByVerse.quote: For he was saying to him, "Come out of the man, you unclean spirit!" And Jesus asked him, "What is your name?" He replied, "My name is Legion, for we are many." And he begged him earnestly not to send them out of the country.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For he was saying to him, Come out of the man, you unclean spirit. Mark drops the tense back a step to tell us what had already been happening: the whole exchange in verse 7 was the answer to a command Jesus had already given. The screaming and the bargaining are what a thing does on its way out.

And notice the command itself. Six words. No ritual, no formula, no invoking of a higher name — which is exactly what every exorcist in the ancient world needed, and precisely what the demon had just tried to use on him. Jesus does not appeal to an authority. He is one.

And Jesus asked him, What is your name?

This is the only time in the Gospels that Jesus asks a demon its name, and it is worth asking why, because he plainly does not need the information. Two things are being done.

The first is for the man. Everything that has happened to him has happened in the dark, unnamed and unexplained, for years. The thing that owned him is about to be forced to identify itself out loud, in front of witnesses, before it is thrown out. What has been destroying you is made to say what it is.

The second is for the record. Mark wants his readers to grasp the scale of what they are watching, and only the enemy can supply that figure.

My name is Legion, for we are many.

The word lands like a boot. A legion was a Roman army unit of around six thousand men — not a metaphor to anybody in that district but the thing that had marched up their road. A legion arrives, occupies, and stays. It cannot be resisted, cannot be negotiated with, and does not leave.

That is the word these spirits choose for themselves, and it describes exactly what they had done to this man: moved in, taken possession, held territory. And it tells you why nothing had worked. The town had been trying to chain a man. The man was a garrison.

So Mark quietly sets two occupations side by side. There is the one everybody in that country could see, with soldiers on the road and taxes to Caesar. And there is the one nobody could do anything about at all. Jesus walks up the beach and evicts the second with a sentence — and he will deal with the first in his own way and at his own cost, when Rome nails him to a post outside Jerusalem and finds it cannot hold him either.

And he begged him earnestly not to send them out of the country.

Begged. It is the third time in five verses that the strongest power in the district has been reduced to asking, and it will beg again in verse 12. Luke tells us what they were most afraid of: that he would order them into the abyss (Luke 8:31).

Weigh the whole encounter, then, as the man on the ground would have heard it. He had been held by six thousand, and he was worth a storm and a crossing to the one who came for him — and the six thousand spent the entire conversation pleading.

verseByVerse.quote: Now a great herd of pigs was feeding there on the hillside, and they begged him, saying, "Send us to the pigs; let us enter them." So he gave them permission. And the unclean spirits came out and entered the pigs; and the herd, numbering about two thousand, rushed down the steep bank into the sea and drowned in the sea.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now a great herd of pigs was feeding there on the hillside. Mark mentions them almost as scenery, and the detail confirms where we are. No Jewish district would have two thousand pigs on a hillside; under the Law the animal is unclean (Lev. 11:7). This is Gentile country, and the pigs are somebody's livelihood.

And they begged him, saying, Send us to the pigs; let us enter them. Begging again. The Legion cannot go anywhere, or do anything, without permission — which tells you exactly how much of what happens in this world is unsupervised. Nothing.

So he gave them permission. Three words, and they raise every hard question in the chapter at once.

And the herd, numbering about two thousand, rushed down the steep bank into the sea and drowned in the sea.

Two thousand animals over a cliff. And a reader who cares about God's justice — and about somebody's ruined business — is entitled to ask what on earth this was for.

Three things answer it, and none of them requires pretending the loss did not happen.

First, the demons did this, not Jesus. He permitted their request; they drove the herd. And in permitting it, he let their intention show itself in the open. For five verses we have been told what they were doing to a man — the tombs, the chains, the screaming, the stones. Now the whole district gets to watch what that programme looks like when it runs unhindered: everything it enters goes straight over the edge and into the water. The pigs are the man's story, acted out in eight seconds on a hillside, so that nobody has to take Mark's word for it.

Second, the arithmetic of heaven is not the arithmetic of the market. One tormented man, restored to his mind, his clothes, his family and his town, and sent out as a herald of mercy, is worth more than any number of animals. Jesus had already said it in a synagogue argument: of how much more value is a man than a sheep! (Matt. 12:12). And a man than a pig. God's care for animals is real — he feeds the ravens, he counts the sparrows, and the righteous man regards the life of his beast (Prov. 12:10). But when the two are set against each other, there is no contest, and there never was.

Third, the reaction of the town settles the matter. Presented with a neighbour raised out of a living death and a hillside of dead livestock, they will grieve the livestock and ask the Healer to leave.
