Which is the uncomfortable question this scene puts to us, and it is not about pigs. There are still people who would rather keep their herd than lose their sins. The cost of Christ is always visible and always countable — the money, the relationship, the ambition, the private arrangement that works. What he gives is a man in his right mind, and that never appears in the accounts until later.

The town did the sum on the day and came out against him. It is worth being honest about how often we have done the same sum, and got the same answer, over something considerably less than two thousand pigs.

verseByVerse.quote: The herdsmen fled and told it in the city and in the country. And people came to see what it was that had happened. And they came to Jesus and saw the demon-possessed man, the one who had had the legion, sitting there, clothed and in his right mind, and they were afraid.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The herdsmen fled and told it in the city and in the country. Of course they ran. They have two thousand animals at the bottom of a cliff and somebody is going to want an explanation. Mark notes that they told it everywhere — town and countryside both. Within an hour the whole district knows.

And people came to see what it was that had happened. They come out in numbers, and Mark lets us watch them arrive at the scene.

And they came to Jesus and saw the demon-possessed man. Notice how they still describe him, even now. That is his name in this town: the demon-possessed man. It is what he has been called for years, and there is no other way anyone here knows how to refer to him.

Then Mark gives three details, and they are three of the loveliest words in the Gospel.

Sitting there. Start with that, because it is the one people skip. This man has not sat down in years. He has been running the hills, tearing at chains, roaming the tombs night and day. Whatever was in him never let him be still. And now, in the middle of the whole town, he is sitting quietly on the ground. Luke adds where: sitting at the feet of Jesus (Luke 8:35) — which is the posture of a disciple in a classroom.

Clothed. He had been naked; Luke says so plainly. Somebody has given him a garment — and you might well ask who, because there are only twelve men and their Master on that beach, and one of them is now short of a cloak. The restoration of this man's dignity involved somebody handing over the clothes off his own back.

And in his right mind. The Greek is a single word meaning sound-minded, sane, self-possessed. He is here. He can hold a conversation. He knows his own name, and he can hear his own thoughts for the first time in years.

Take the measure of what has just happened in the space of a few minutes. No process. No gradual rehabilitation. No years of careful work. He came down out of the rocks screaming and he is sitting on the ground with a borrowed coat on, listening.

That is what Christ does with a case that everybody else has closed. And it is worth saying to anyone praying for a person who has been beyond reach for a long time — the addict, the one who is not in their right mind, the family member nobody knows how to help — that this town had reached the settled conclusion that nothing could be done. They were right about their own resources and wrong about the possibilities, and the difference arrived by boat.

And they were afraid.

And there is the turn nobody expects. Not relieved. Not delighted for him. Afraid.

It is the same fear that filled the boat after the storm (4:41) — the fear of a power you cannot classify or control. And it is not, in itself, a wicked reaction; awe in the presence of God is right. But what this town does with it in the next two verses is another matter entirely.

verseByVerse.quote: And those who had seen it described to them what had happened to the demon-possessed man and to the pigs. And they began to beg Jesus to depart from their region.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And those who had seen it described to them what had happened to the demon-possessed man and to the pigs.

The eyewitnesses give their report, and Mark's summary of it is quietly devastating: the man and the pigs. Both items, in one account, presented for the town's consideration.

And the town weighs them up.

And they began to beg Jesus to depart from their region.

That is the third begging in this chapter, and it is the one that should stop us. The demons begged not to be sent away. The demons begged to go into the pigs. And now the people beg for the same thing the demons wanted — for Jesus to go somewhere else.

Read it slowly, because it is one of the most sobering verses in the Gospel. Nobody in that district disputes what has happened. Nobody says it was a trick. They have the facts, they have the eyewitnesses, and they have their neighbour sitting in front of them in his right mind. And their considered, unanimous request is that the man who did it should get back in his boat.

Why? Mark does not explain, and he does not need to. They had just watched a hillside of assets go into the water, and they had understood something about Jesus that many people who admire him never grasp: he is not safe, and he does not stay within the budget. A man who can do that to a herd of pigs might do it to anything. Better to have the misery you have priced than the mercy you cannot.

So they chose the graveyard they knew. And the terrible thing is that the choice is not exotic. It is the most ordinary transaction in the world.

Ask it plainly of yourself, because this is what the passage is for. What in your life is currently more expensive to lose than Christ is to have? Not in theory — in fact. The relationship you know he would not sanction. The way you make your money. The evening habit. The plan for the next ten years you have never once put in his hands. Everybody has an answer, and the honest test is what you do when he walks up the beach and touches it.

And he goes. That is the most frightening thing here, and Mark states it without comment in the next verse: as he was getting into the boat. No argument, no second attempt, no sermon on the shore about what they were throwing away. They asked him to leave and he left.

He does not force himself on a town that has counted the cost and declined. Ephraim is joined to idols; leave him alone (Hos. 4:17) is a real sentence in the Bible, and it is the most terrifying kind of answered prayer there is.

Yet do not close the account there, because he does not. He is going — and he leaves the district the one thing it cannot chain, cut, or drive away. He leaves a man with a story.

verseByVerse.quote: As he was getting into the boat, the man who had been possessed with demons begged him that he might be with him. And he did not permit him but said to him, "Go home to your friends and tell them how much the Lord has done for you, and how he has had mercy on you." And he went away and began to proclaim in the Decapolis how much Jesus had done for him, and everyone marveled.
verseByVerse.commentary:
As he was getting into the boat, the man who had been possessed with demons begged him that he might be with him.

Fourth and last begging in the chapter, and this one is a prayer any Christian would recognise. He has one request. He wants to go with Jesus.

And look at the words Mark chooses: that he might be with him. That is not a wish for a boat ride. It is the exact phrase used of the appointing of the Twelve — he appointed twelve so that they might be with him (3:14). The man is asking to be a disciple in the strictest sense. It is the best request in the whole chapter, made by the only person on that beach who has understood anything.

And he did not permit him.

Stay with that, because it is one of the hardest sentences in Mark. He permitted the demons. He did not permit the man.

The finest prayer offered on that shore, by the man with the most reason to offer it, asking for nothing but Jesus himself — and the answer is no.

So if you have prayed the best prayer you know how to pray and been refused, you are in extremely good company, and this is the passage for you. Paul asked three times to have the thorn removed and was told no (2 Cor. 12:8–9). Jesus himself asked in a garden that the cup pass, and it did not (14:36). A no from Christ is not a sign that you asked badly or that he has stopped caring. Sometimes it is a redeployment.

But said to him, Go home to your friends and tell them how much the Lord has done for you.

Because look what he is given instead. Not a place in the boat — a district. Not proximity — a commission.

And notice where he is sent. Home. To his friends, to the town that chained him, to the neighbours who had heard him screaming on the hills for years and had done nothing, to the family that gave up. That is the hardest mission field on earth and it always has been. These are people who knew him before, who will remember what he was, and who cannot be impressed by a stranger's testimony because they were there.

Which is exactly why they are the ones who cannot argue with it.

And note what the whole of his training consisted of. He has no theological education, no years with Jesus, no Scriptures at his fingertips. He has one thing: what happened to him. That is the entire content of his commission — tell them how much the Lord has done for you, and how he has had mercy on you. If you have ever thought you were not equipped to say anything about Christ to anybody, this man is the answer, and he had been out of his mind that morning.

And he went away and began to proclaim in the Decapolis how much Jesus had done for him.

Now catch what he has done with his instructions, because it is the most beautiful thing in the passage and almost everybody reads past it.

Jesus said: tell them what the Lord has done. He went out and told them what Jesus had done.

He made the substitution himself. Nobody taught him that. He had been a Christian for about ten minutes, in a pagan district, with no Bible and no instruction — and he had already worked out that the man who had spoken to him on the beach and the Lord God of Israel were not two subjects. His first sermon was better than the disciples' theology, and they had been in the boat for months.

And everyone marveled. Ten cities. One man, with no qualifications, telling the only story he had.

And when Jesus returns to that side of the lake in chapter 7, the crowds come out to meet him and bring him their sick. The town that begged him to leave got him back — because the man they could not chain would not stop talking.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 21–43 — Jairus’s Daughter and the Woman with the Bleeding
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The father (vv. 21–24). A synagogue ruler — a man of standing, from the very institution that has been building a case against Jesus — comes through the crowd and goes down on his face. His twelve-year-old is dying. Jesus goes with him, and there is not one word of negotiation.

The interruption (vv. 25–34). On the way, a woman who has been bleeding for twelve years, ruined by doctors' fees, ceremonially untouchable, gets close enough to take hold of his clothes from behind. She is healed instantly — and then Jesus stops the entire procession to find her. Jairus stands and watches while his daughter dies.

The news (vv. 35–36). Your daughter is dead. Why trouble the Teacher any further? — and Jesus overhears the sentence and speaks over the top of it: Do not fear, only believe.

The house (vv. 37–43). Professional mourners in full cry, and a man who says the child is sleeping, and a room that laughs at him. He puts them all out, takes a dead girl by the hand, and says two words in the language a mother would have used.
verseByVerse.theology:
Mark has interleaved these two stories deliberately — his habitual sandwich — and the links are not decoration. Both turn on twelve years: the girl's whole life, and the length of the woman's suffering. The year that family received a daughter is the year this woman's life began to come apart. Both are called daughter — the one by her father, the other by Jesus. Both are healed by touch: she takes hold of his garment, he takes hold of her hand. And the same Greek verb, sōzō, runs through both — made well, and saved, are the same word.

Set side by side, they say one thing between them. The woman had exhausted every human resource over twelve years; the father had run out of time in an afternoon. Slow ruin and sudden catastrophe, and the same answer to both.

And the interruption is the point of the arrangement. From where Jairus is standing, the delay is fatal — Jesus stops to talk to a woman who is already healed, and while he talks, a child dies. But the delay is what Jairus is given to watch. He hears a desperate woman told your faith has made you well before he hears the words your daughter is dead. God's delays are not always the absence of an answer. Sometimes they are the school in which faith is taught the thing it is about to need.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: a woman who had tried everything else and everyone else, coming from behind, in a crowd, hoping to take what she needed without being seen.

Now: everybody who comes to Christ as a last resort, after the money, the specialists and the years have all run out — and finds that the last resort was the first and only real one all along. She had no right to be in that crowd and she knew it; her condition made her contagious under the Law, and every person she brushed against on the way through was defiled by her. She came anyway.

And notice that Jesus was not content to heal her anonymously. He stopped everything, in public, and drew her out — not to shame her, since she had done nothing wrong, but because he wanted more for her than a cure. She got a conversation, a word about her faith, a blessing of peace, and a name: Daughter, the only time in the Gospels he calls a woman that. She came for a healing and went away with a relationship. He always gives more than was asked, and it is never the part you were focused on.

verseByVerse.quote: And when Jesus had crossed again in the boat to the other side, a great crowd gathered about him, and he was beside the sea. Then came one of the rulers of the synagogue, Jairus by name, and seeing him, he fell at his feet and implored him earnestly, saying, "My little daughter is at the point of death. Come and lay your hands on her, so that she may be made well and live." And he went with him. And a great crowd followed him and thronged about him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Back across the lake, and the crowd is waiting on the beach. Then a man comes through it who should not be there.

One of the rulers of the synagogue, Jairus by name. Mark names him, which he rarely does, and that is probably because Jairus was known in the church afterwards — a man people could go and ask.

Understand what his position was. The ruler of a synagogue was not a preacher; he was the senior layman who ran it — appointed the readers, kept the building, held the respect of the town. He is the establishment. And the establishment, in this Gospel, has already held a meeting about how to destroy Jesus (3:6), and scribes have come from Jerusalem to declare him demon-possessed (3:22).

Every professional instinct and every social pressure in this man's life points away from the beach he is walking down.

And seeing him, he fell at his feet. In front of everyone. A dignitary on his face in the sand before an itinerant preacher his colleagues have written off.

Desperation has stripped his standing off him, and he has not tried to hold on to any of it. That is what a dying child does to a man: it burns away everything he was worried about the week before. There is a mercy hidden in it — the very grief that is destroying him has got him to the only place where help was.

My little daughter is at the point of death. The Greek is a diminutive — my little daughter, the word a father uses. She is twelve, which Mark will tell us at the end almost as an afterthought; old enough in that world to be nearly a woman, and still his little girl.

Come and lay your hands on her, so that she may be made well and live. Notice the theology in a panicking man's request. He has a method in mind — come, and lay hands on her. He assumes Jesus must be physically present and must touch her. He is about to discover that this is not remotely the limit of it, and that the delay he is about to endure is not the disaster it looks like.

That is worth knowing about your own praying. Most of us come with the mechanism already specified: do it this way, by this date, through this means. God is not offended by that — he did not correct Jairus. He simply intends to answer more largely than the request was framed.

And he went with him.

Four words, and they are the gospel in miniature. No conditions. No questions about whether a synagogue ruler had been at the meeting in chapter 3. No lecture about coming sooner. No delay while the crowd is dismissed. Jesus goes where desperate faith brings him, and he goes at once.

And a great crowd followed him and thronged about him. And here Mark starts winding the tension. The crowd is not a backdrop; it is an obstacle. They are pressing in on all sides, and a man with a dying child at home is now moving at the pace of a mob through a village street.

Every step is slower than it should be. And it is about to stop altogether.

verseByVerse.quote: And there was a woman who had had a discharge of blood for twelve years, and who had suffered much under many physicians, and had spent all that she had, and was no better but rather grew worse.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Mark now does something novelists do: he stops the clock mid-journey and turns the camera on somebody else. A man with a dying daughter is left standing in the street while we are told about a woman in the crowd.

A woman who had had a discharge of blood for twelve years.

Twelve years. And here is the thing to notice first, because Mark has built it in deliberately: Jairus's daughter is twelve years old (v. 42). The year that family received a child is the year this woman's life began to fall apart. One household had been counting birthdays while, somewhere in the same district, another woman had been counting the same years and losing everything.

Now understand what her condition actually meant, because a modern reader hears only a medical problem, and it was very much more than that.

Under the Law, a woman with a chronic discharge of blood was ceremonially unclean for as long as it lasted (Lev. 15:25–27). And the uncleanness was contagious: anything she sat on was unclean, anyone who touched her bed or her chair was unclean until evening. In practice that meant she could not enter the temple courts or worship with the congregation; she could not be touched without making the other person unclean; and if she was married, twelve years of this had almost certainly ended the marriage.

So she has spent twelve years untouched. No embrace, no hand on the shoulder, no worship, no place at anyone's table. Whatever the bleeding was doing to her body, the loneliness had been doing something worse.

And who had suffered much under many physicians. Mark's word is strong: she suffered under them. Ancient remedies for this complaint were degrading and often painful — the Talmud preserves a list of them, and they include carrying the ash of an ostrich egg in a linen rag and drinking wine mixed with rubber and alum. Twelve years of that, each new man with a new theory, each course of treatment a fresh humiliation.

Luke, who was a doctor, records the same history and cannot quite bring himself to phrase it as bluntly (Luke 8:43).

And had spent all that she had. Everything. Whatever her family had, it is gone. She is not merely ill; she is destitute, and destitute in the specific way that leaves a person feeling foolish — she paid for all of it herself, one hopeful appointment at a time.

And was no better but rather grew worse.

There is the sentence, and it is the one that will find some readers exactly where they live. Not merely that nothing worked. That the whole twelve-year campaign of effort, money, hope and humiliation left her further down than she started.

If you have a chronic illness, or a chronic anything — a marriage that every attempt has made colder, a child who has moved further away with each intervention, a besetting sin you have fought with every weapon you own and are visibly losing to — this verse is in your Bible on purpose. Mark takes two full verses to say that she had tried everything and was worse for it, and he does not soften it or hurry past it to the good part.

And then, having established that there was no help anywhere, he tells you what she heard.

verseByVerse.quote: She had heard the reports about Jesus and came up behind him in the crowd and touched his garment. For she said, "If I touch even his garments, I will be made well." And immediately the flow of blood dried up, and she felt in her body that she was healed of her disease.
verseByVerse.commentary:
She had heard the reports about Jesus. That is all she has. Not a meeting, not an introduction, not a promise made to her personally. She has heard what people are saying, and she acts on it.

Faith, at its beginning, is very often no more than this: something you have heard about Christ, taken seriously enough to move on. Faith comes from hearing, and hearing through the word of Christ (Rom. 10:17).

And came up behind him in the crowd and touched his garment.

Every word there is loaded, and you have to know the Law to feel it.

Behind him. She will not come at him face on. She cannot. To approach openly would mean explaining, in front of a street full of people, what was wrong with her — and it would mean admitting that she had no business being in that crowd at all.

Because that is the real risk she is running, and it is not embarrassment. Under Leviticus 15 her uncleanness passed on by contact. Every single person she pushed past on her way through that press was defiled by her, and none of them knew it. If she were recognised, this would not be a scene; it would be a riot.

She came anyway. Think what twelve years of being untouchable does to a person, and then think what it took to walk into a crowd.

Touched his garment. Matthew and Luke specify the fringe — the tassel at the corner of the outer cloak that every Jewish man wore under the command of Numbers 15:38–39, to remind him of the commandments of the LORD. The furthest, lowest, most trailing edge of him. She is not reaching for his hand.

For she said, If I touch even his garments, I will be made well. Mark lets us hear her talking herself into it. And her theology is imperfect — there is something almost superstitious in it, as though the power were in the cloth. Jesus does not correct that. He never once, in this Gospel, refuses somebody for coming to him with a poor grasp of how it works.

Which is a considerable comfort. What saved this woman was not the accuracy of her understanding. It was that she put out her hand.

And immediately the flow of blood dried up.

Twelve years, stopped mid-street, in the time it takes to touch a piece of cloth. No process, no convalescence, and — this is the point of the whole scene — the current ran the wrong way.

Every law of uncleanness in Israel ran one direction: what is unclean contaminates what is clean, and never the reverse. Touch a corpse and you are defiled; the corpse is not raised. That is how it had worked for fifteen centuries. This woman put her hand on a clean man and, by every rule she had been taught, she should have made him unclean.

Instead she was made clean. The contagion went backwards.

That is not Jesus breaking the Law. It is the Law's whole purpose arriving. Israel had been taught for centuries that sin and death spread and holiness does not — precisely so that when a man walked into their villages whose holiness was catching, they would know what they were looking at.

And she felt in her body that she was healed of her disease. Mark's word for her disease is the one he used on the beach in chapter 3: a scourge, a whip. She had been flogged by this thing for twelve years. And she felt it stop.

verseByVerse.quote: And Jesus, perceiving in himself that power had gone out from him, immediately turned about in the crowd and said, "Who touched my garments?" And his disciples said to him, "You see the crowd pressing around you, and yet you say, 'Who touched me?'" And he looked around to see who had done it.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And Jesus, perceiving in himself that power had gone out from him.

This is a strange verse and it is worth being careful with, because it can be read as though healing were an electrical charge that leaked out of him without his knowledge. Two things rule that out.

The first is that he asks the question at all. He stops, turns, and looks for the person — and Mark says at the end of the section that he looked around to see who had done it. A power that simply drained away would not go looking for anybody.

The second is what he says to her in a moment: your faith has made you well. Not my cloak has. The healing was not mechanical, and it was not a transaction she managed to complete without him noticing. It was personal from both ends.

What Mark is describing is the cost of it. Something went out of him. He is God in the flesh, and the giving is not free even to him — which is why, at the end of this Gospel, the giving will take everything he has.

Immediately turned about in the crowd and said, Who touched my garments?

And now the scene stops dead. A crowd in a village street, a man with a dying child beside him, and Jesus turning round to ask an apparently unanswerable question.

And his disciples said to him, You see the crowd pressing around you, and yet you say, Who touched me?

You can hear the exasperation, and Mark has never minded making the twelve look foolish. It is a fair objection: dozens of people are in physical contact with him. Everyone in that street has touched him.

But they have missed the distinction the whole Gospel turns on. The crowd was pressing against him. One woman took hold of him. Contact is not faith. There were hundreds of hands on Jesus that afternoon and exactly one of them got anything.

Which is worth putting to yourself in the plainest terms, because it is possible to spend a lifetime in the press. You can be in the crowd around Christ — in the building, in the congregation, in the family, brushing against him week after week — and never once have reached out for him on your own account. The people jostling him went home exactly as they came. The woman went home well.

And he looked around to see who had done it.

He is not going to let this be anonymous. And that is the surprising kindness of the passage, though it will not have felt like kindness to her.

She had what she came for. The bleeding had stopped; she could have slipped out of that crowd and gone home cured, and nobody would ever have known. From her point of view, being found out is the worst thing that could happen.

Jesus refuses to leave it there — and he is willing to hold up a dying child's rescue in order to refuse it. He has something for this woman that she did not think to ask for, and it is worth the delay.

verseByVerse.quote: But the woman, knowing what had happened to her, came in fear and trembling and fell down before him and told him the whole truth. And he said to her, "Daughter, your faith has made you well; go in peace, and be healed of your disease."
verseByVerse.commentary:
But the woman, knowing what had happened to her, came in fear and trembling and fell down before him.

She could have stayed silent. The crowd was enormous, the question was unanswerable, the disciples had all but told him to drop it. She had only to stand still.

She comes forward instead, and Mark tells us exactly what it cost: fear and trembling. She is physically shaking. She is expecting to be exposed as the woman who had made half the street unclean, and rebuked in front of everybody for taking what she had no right to take.

And told him the whole truth.

All of it. Not a summary. The twelve years, the doctors, the money, the marriage if there was one, the reason she came from behind, what she had been hoping — the entire humiliating history, said out loud, in a public street, to a man she had just met.

That is what confession is, and it is why we avoid it. Not the general admission that we are sinners; the whole truth, in particular words, to the one person entitled to hear it.

And notice that nothing was owed. She was already healed. Jesus does not draw her out because the cure was incomplete or because he needed to check her credentials. He draws her out because he will not have a relationship with her that consists of her taking something from behind and running away.

And he said to her, Daughter.

Stop there, because that one word is the reason he stopped the procession.

It is the only time in all four Gospels that Jesus calls a woman daughter. She has been nobody's anything for twelve years — untouchable, unwelcome in worship, a name people lowered their voices about. And the first word out of his mouth gives her a place in a family.

Remember what Mark is doing with this chapter. Jairus is standing three feet away with his own daughter dying at home. And Jesus turns to a destitute, unclean, middle-aged woman that nobody in that street would have looked at twice, and calls her the same thing.

Your faith has made you well. He locates the power correctly, and it is worth noting for anyone with a superstitious streak: not the fringe, not the technique, not the crowd, not her boldness. Faith — which was, in her case, small, frightened, theologically muddled, and reaching from behind. That is all it has ever taken. Faith saves not because it is impressive but because of who it takes hold of.

Go in peace. The Hebrew behind it is shalom, and it means far more than the absence of trouble. It is wholeness — everything in its place, the whole person put right. She came for a body and is being sent away with a life.

And be healed of your disease. The final clause is a word of permanence, and it settles her forever. She had felt the bleeding stop and might well have spent the rest of her life waiting for it to start again — as anyone would, after twelve years. He tells her, out loud, that it is over.

And then, into the silence at the end of that sentence, the messengers arrive from Jairus's house.

verseByVerse.quote: While he was still speaking, there came from the ruler's house some who said, "Your daughter is dead. Why trouble the Teacher any further?" But overhearing what they said, Jesus said to the ruler of the synagogue, "Do not fear, only believe."
verseByVerse.commentary:
While he was still speaking. Mark's timing is exact and merciless. The word about the woman's peace is barely out of his mouth when the men from the house arrive, and Jairus, who has been standing through the whole delay, hears what he has been dreading for the last ten minutes.

Your daughter is dead. Why trouble the Teacher any further?

Two sentences, and they are the world's entire philosophy about death, delivered kindly by people who mean no harm.

Your daughter is dead. A fact. They are not wrong; she has died. Mark will not let anyone soften this later — the professional mourners are already at the house, and they will laugh at the suggestion that she is anything but dead.

Why trouble the Teacher any further? And there is the conclusion drawn from the fact, and it is the sentence to look at hard. Note what they call him: Teacher. That is their estimate of him and it is the reason for their advice. A teacher is a fine thing to bring to a sickbed and no use at all at a graveside. Their theology is not hostile; it is simply too small, and it produces the most reasonable pastoral advice in the world: stop praying about this one. It is finished. Do not bother him.

And that advice still gets given, in exactly that tone, by people who are trying to be kind. The marriage is over; stop praying for it. He is seventy-eight and hardened; leave it. That door is closed. It is always said gently, and it is always based on a true fact and an inadequate estimate of Christ.

Notice also what the delay has done. If Jesus had not stopped for the woman, he would have been at that house in time. From where Jairus is standing, the interruption killed his daughter — a stranger's twelve-year complaint, which could have waited an hour, cost him everything.

Hold that, because it is one of the hardest things about the way God works. His delays are real, they cost real people real things, and they are not accidents.

But overhearing what they said. Some translations render it that he ignored what they said, and the Greek can carry that: he heard it and refused to let it stand. He does not wait for the message to be relayed to Jairus, and he does not let it settle. He speaks over the top of it.

Jesus said to the ruler of the synagogue, Do not fear, only believe.

Five words in English, three in Greek, and they are commands rather than comfort. He is not saying do not worry, it will be fine. He is telling a man whose child has just died what to do with the next ten minutes.

Do not fear. Stop. The tense is a command to cut off a fear already in progress.

Only believe. And this one is present and continuous: go on believing. Keep doing what you were doing when you came down that beach and fell in the sand. Nothing has changed about who I am.

Only is the tender word. He is not asking Jairus to feel confident, or to produce an emotion he does not have, or to understand why the woman came first. Just this one thing, and nothing else is required of you.

And now see what the delay was actually for. Jairus has just watched, at point-blank range, a woman with a hopeless twelve-year case be healed by touching a piece of cloth, and heard her called Daughter, and heard her told to go in peace. He did not know it at the time, but he was being given the last lesson he would need, in the ten minutes before he needed it.

God's delays are not always the absence of an answer. Sometimes they are the school.

verseByVerse.quote: And he allowed no one to follow him except Peter and James and John the brother of James. They came to the house of the ruler of the synagogue, and Jesus saw a commotion, people weeping and wailing loudly.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And he allowed no one to follow him except Peter and James and John.

The crowd is dismissed. Whatever is about to happen in that house is not going to be a public demonstration, and the great press of people that has followed him all the way from the shore is left in the street.

This is the first time in Mark that these three are taken apart from the others, and it will not be the last: they are the three on the mountain at the transfiguration (9:2) and the three taken deeper into the garden at Gethsemane (14:33). So this is the beginning of an education, and notice the syllabus. The men who will be taken to watch him in glory, and taken to watch him in agony, are first taken to watch him in a dead child's bedroom.

And one of them tells the story to Mark years later, with the furniture still in it.

They came to the house of the ruler of the synagogue, and Jesus saw a commotion, people weeping and wailing loudly.

The word Mark uses is the ordinary one for an uproar — the same root used of a rioting crowd. That is what the house sounded like from the street.

Understand what was going on inside, because it is not what a modern reader pictures. Mourning in that culture was loud, immediate and professional. Even the poorest family was expected to hire at least two flute players and a wailing woman; a man of Jairus's standing would have had a houseful. Matthew's account mentions the flute players by name (Matt. 9:23). They come fast — burial was the same day in that climate — and their job was to make grief audible.

So there is nothing false about the sorrow of the family, and nothing contemptible about the mourners either; this was simply how a village buried its children. But it does tell you one thing beyond dispute, and it settles a question that will come up in two verses. The professionals had already arrived. Nobody sends for the mourners while there is a pulse.

And into that noise walks a man who is about to say something that will stop it and then start it up again as laughter.

Before he does, though, notice what Mark says he did first: Jesus saw the commotion. He did not push through it or shout over it. He stood in the doorway of a house full of people making the loudest sound human beings make, and looked at it.

He has looked at a graveside once before in the Gospels and wept at it (John 11:35), knowing perfectly well that he was about to empty the tomb. The knowledge that he can undo it has never once made him indifferent to it. He is not embarrassed by grief and he does not hurry anyone through it — which is worth knowing if you are in a house like this one, or have been.

verseByVerse.quote: And when he had entered, he said to them, "Why are you making a commotion and weeping? The child is not dead but sleeping." And they laughed at him. But he put them all outside and took the child's father and mother and those who were with him and went in where the child was.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Why are you making a commotion and weeping? The child is not dead but sleeping.

This sentence has been seized on for two hundred years, and it deserves a straight answer, because a reader who has heard the objection needs to be able to put it down.

The claim is that she was never really dead — a coma, a faint, a lucky misdiagnosis — so this is no resurrection at all.

The reading collapses the moment you look at it. Everyone present was certain she had died: the messengers reported it as fact, and the house was already full of professional mourners in full cry. Those people made their living recognising death. They laughed at Jesus precisely because they knew a corpse when they saw one, and they had seen this one. Luke, who was a physician, states plainly what happened when Jesus spoke: her spirit returned (Luke 8:55).

So what does sleeping mean? It is not a second opinion on her pulse. It is his settled way of speaking about the death of people he intends to raise.

Of Lazarus — four days in the tomb, and his sister objecting that by now there would be an odour — he said our friend Lazarus has fallen asleep, and when the disciples took it literally he told them plainly: Lazarus has died (John 11:11–14). Paul uses the same word for Christians in the grave: those who have fallen asleep, and Christ the firstfruits of them (1 Thess. 4:13–14; 1 Cor. 15:20). It is where our word cemetery comes from — the Greek for a sleeping place.

So the word is not a smaller claim than resurrection. It is a far larger one. To the mourners in that house, death was the end of the sentence. To the one standing in the doorway, it was as temporary as a night's sleep, and waking this child would cost him no more effort than a parent leaning over a bed in the morning.

He does not deny that she died. He announces that death, in his presence, has just become something you get up from.

And they laughed at him.

The verb is contemptuous — they ridiculed him. And the swing is worth noticing: these people were wailing thirty seconds ago and they are jeering now, which tells you something about how thin professional grief can be.

It also tells you what the world does with the resurrection. It is not usually argued against. It is laughed at, and the laughter feels like sophistication. That room contained the only person present who knew what he was talking about, and he was the one being mocked.

But he put them all outside. Firmly. Mark's word means to throw out — the same verb used of casting out demons. The mourners, the flute players, the neighbours, the crowd of opinion: all of them out the door.

And took the child's father and mother and those who were with him and went in where the child was.

Five people go in. Peter, James, John — and a father and a mother.

Notice that the parents are not left in the corridor. Whatever is about to happen, they are going to see it, and they are going to be standing there when it happens. This is not a private miracle performed on their daughter and reported to them afterwards. He takes them in with him, into the room they had presumably been unable to leave.

And the mother appears here for the first and only time in the story, unnamed, having been in that house all afternoon.

verseByVerse.quote: Taking her by the hand he said to her, "Talitha cumi," which means, "Little girl, I say to you, arise." And immediately the girl got up and began walking (for she was twelve years of age), and they were immediately overcome with amazement.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Taking her by the hand.

Before a word is spoken, he takes hold of a dead child.

Do not read past that. Under the Law, contact with a corpse made a man ceremonially unclean for seven days and required a specific rite of purification (Num. 19:11–13). Everyone in that room knew it. To take a dead girl's hand was to walk out of that house defiled.

And it is the third time in this one chapter that Jesus has gone straight to the place where uncleanness lives. He landed in a graveyard and dealt with a man who lived among the tombs. He let an untouchable woman take hold of his clothes. And now he takes a corpse by the hand.

Every one of those contacts should have run one way, and every one of them ran the other. The tombs did not defile him; the man came out of them. The bleeding did not contaminate him; it dried up. And death does not get its seven days out of him. He takes hold of it, and it lets go.

There is also, quite simply, the tenderness of it. He could have spoken from the doorway; he had stilled a hurricane from the stern of a boat without getting up. He goes and takes her hand — because that is what you do for a frightened twelve-year-old, and because her mother and father are watching.

He said to her, Talitha cumi.

And here Mark does something he does only a handful of times: he keeps the actual Aramaic. He is writing in Greek for readers in Rome and he stops to give them the sound of it, and then translates.

He does that because Peter never forgot it. This is a man remembering the exact syllables he heard in a small room thirty years earlier.

And they are gentle, domestic words. Talitha is a diminutive from the word for a lamb — the affectionate thing a parent in that house would have called her every morning of her life. It is not a formula. It is closer to up you get, lamb.

Which means, Little girl, I say to you, arise. No prayer. No invocation. No struggle. He does not ask the Father to raise her; he tells her to get up. And the authority in I say to you is the same authority that told a hurricane to be quiet.

And immediately the girl got up and began walking.

Not sat up weakly and was tended. She got up and started walking about the room, in front of her mother.

(For she was twelve years of age.) Mark drops it in as a bracket, almost apologetically, to explain why a raised child could walk rather than needing to be carried. It is exactly the kind of detail nobody invents, and it quietly ties the two halves of the chapter together: twelve years of a girl's life, twelve years of a woman's suffering, and both of them ended on the same afternoon by the same hands.

And they were immediately overcome with amazement. Mark's phrase is enormous — they were beside themselves with a great ecstasy. There is no adequate reaction to this and they did not manage one.

Two words in a child's ear. That is what it cost him here.

It will cost more than that at the end. When he stands outside another tomb and calls another name, it will be on his way to a grave of his own — and the hand that took this girl's hand will be opened by a nail, so that everyone who sleeps in him can be told, one morning, to get up.

verseByVerse.quote: And he strictly charged them that no one should know this, and told them to give her something to eat.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Two instructions close the chapter, and they could hardly be less alike.

And he strictly charged them that no one should know this.

The command is emphatic — Mark's verb is forceful, the same kind of charge he laid on the demons. And on the face of it, it is impossible. There is a street full of mourners outside who watched him go in, and a girl inside who is going to be seen in the village tomorrow. You cannot hide a resurrection.

So what is he doing? The same thing he has been doing since chapter 1. In Galilee at that moment, a man who raises the dead becomes a national event within a week — and the word Messiah in that year meant a king who would drive out Rome. Jesus will not be crowned before he is crucified. He keeps the lid on as long as he can, because the truth about him has to be defined by a cross or it will be misunderstood entirely.

But there is something else in it here, and it is worth seeing. He has just put the mourners out of the house and shut the door. He does not perform this. There is no crowd at the bedside, no audience, no demonstration. A father and a mother get their daughter back in a quiet room with four other people in it.

He is not using this family. He is helping them.

And told them to give her something to eat.

And there is the last sentence of the chapter, and it is one of the loveliest in the Gospel.

The room is full of people beside themselves with amazement. A twelve-year-old is walking about who was dead five minutes ago. Her parents are past speech. And the Lord of life, having just done the single most staggering thing anybody in that house will ever witness, turns to the mother and says: she will be hungry.

Nobody else in that room was capable of thinking about it. He was.

Consider what that tells you about him. The same care that raises the dead notices that a child has not eaten. There is no gap in him between the enormous and the domestic — the God who spoke the sea into place is the one who thought about the girl's breakfast, and it is the same tenderness in both directions.

He did it again after his own resurrection, incidentally. The risen Christ, having conquered death, lit a charcoal fire on a beach and cooked breakfast for seven tired fishermen (John 21:9).

So when you bring him something enormous — the diagnosis, the child, the grief that has flattened you — you are not distracting him from more important business. And when what you have is small and slightly embarrassing to mention, understand that he is the one who thought of the sandwich when nobody else did.

The chapter began with a man nobody could chain and ends with a girl being handed a plate. Between them a legion was evicted, a woman was called daughter, and death was told to let go of a child — and the same hands did all of it.

5.theology:
Legion, and two occupations. A legion was a Roman army unit of around six thousand men — the empire's instrument of occupation, the thing that arrives in your district and stays, that cannot be resisted and will not leave. That is the word the spirits choose for themselves, and it describes exactly what they had done to the man: moved in, taken possession, held territory. It also explains why nothing had worked. The town had been trying to chain a man; the man was a garrison. Mark sets two occupations side by side — the one everybody in that country could see, and the one nobody could touch — and Jesus evicts the second with a sentence, then deals with the first in his own way and at his own cost when Rome nails him up outside Jerusalem and finds it cannot hold him either.

Why the pigs? The demons drove the herd, not Jesus; he permitted their request, and in permitting it let their intention show itself in public. For five verses we have been told what they were doing to a man — the tombs, the chains, the stones. Now the district watches what that programme looks like unhindered: everything it enters goes over the edge. And the arithmetic of heaven is not the arithmetic of the market. Of how much more value is a man than a sheep! (Matt. 12:12) — and a man than a pig.

Not dead but sleeping. This is not a claim that the girl had merely fainted. The professional mourners were already in the house, and they laughed because they knew a corpse when they saw one; Luke, a physician, records that her spirit returned (Luke 8:55). Sleeping is the Lord's settled way of speaking about the death of those he intends to raise — of Lazarus, four days in the tomb, he said the same and then said plainly Lazarus has died (John 11:11–14). It is not a smaller claim than resurrection but a far larger one: death, in his presence, has become something you get up from.
5.examples:
Then: a man begging to get into the boat, and told no.

It is the fourth begging in the chapter and the best request in it — that he might be with him, the very phrase used of the appointing of the Twelve (3:14). He is asking to be a disciple. Jesus permitted the demons and did not permit him.

Now: anyone who has prayed the best prayer they know how to pray and been refused. Paul asked three times about the thorn and was told no (2 Cor. 12:8–9); Jesus asked in a garden that the cup pass, and it did not (14:36). A no from Christ is not evidence that you asked badly. Sometimes it is a redeployment — this man was given a district instead of a boat, and sent to the hardest mission field there is, which is home.

And notice his qualifications: none. No Scriptures, no training, no time with Jesus. One thing had happened to him, and that was the whole of his commission — tell them how much the Lord has done for you. Then watch what he did with it. Jesus said tell them what the Lord has done; he went out and proclaimed what Jesus had done. He made the substitution himself, ten minutes into the Christian life, in a pagan district with no Bible. His theology was ahead of the disciples' and they had been in the boat for months.

6.title: Refused at Home, Broken Bread, and a Prophet’s Head
6.text: <sup>1</sup>He went away from there and came to his hometown, and his disciples followed him. <sup>2</sup>And on the Sabbath he began to teach in the synagogue, and many who heard him were astonished, saying, “Where did this man get these things? What is the wisdom given to him? How are such mighty works done by his hands? <sup>3</sup>Is not this the carpenter, the son of Mary and brother of James and Joses and Judas and Simon? And are not his sisters here with us?” And they took offense at him. <sup>4</sup>And Jesus said to them, “A prophet is not without honor, except in his hometown and among his relatives and in his own household.” <sup>5</sup>And he could do no mighty work there, except that he laid his hands on a few sick people and healed them. <sup>6</sup>And he marveled because of their unbelief. And he went about among the villages teaching. <sup>7</sup>And he called the twelve and began to send them out two by two, and gave them authority over the unclean spirits. <sup>8</sup>He charged them to take nothing for their journey except a staff—no bread, no bag, no money in their belts— <sup>9</sup>but to wear sandals and not put on two tunics. <sup>10</sup>And he said to them, “Whenever you enter a house, stay there until you depart from there. <sup>11</sup>And if any place will not receive you and they will not listen to you, when you leave, shake off the dust that is on your feet as a testimony against them.” <sup>12</sup>So they went out and proclaimed that people should repent. <sup>13</sup>And they cast out many demons and anointed with oil many who were sick and healed them. <sup>14</sup>King Herod heard of it, for Jesus’ name had become known. Some said, “John the Baptist has been raised from the dead. That is why these miraculous powers are at work in him.” <sup>15</sup>But others said, “He is Elijah.” And others said, “He is a prophet, like one of the prophets of old.” <sup>16</sup>But when Herod heard of it, he said, “John, whom I beheaded, has been raised.” <sup>17</sup>For it was Herod who had sent and seized John and bound him in prison for the sake of Herodias, his brother Philip’s wife, because he had married her. <sup>18</sup>For John had been saying to Herod, “It is not lawful for you to have your brother’s wife.” <sup>19</sup>And Herodias had a grudge against him and wanted to put him to death. But she could not, <sup>20</sup>for Herod feared John, knowing that he was a righteous and holy man, and he kept him safe. When he heard him, he was greatly perplexed, and yet he heard him gladly. <sup>21</sup>But an opportunity came when Herod on his birthday gave a banquet for his nobles and military commanders and the leading men of Galilee. <sup>22</sup>For when Herodias’s daughter came in and danced, she pleased Herod and his guests. And the king said to the girl, “Ask me for whatever you wish, and I will give it to you.” <sup>23</sup>And he vowed to her, “Whatever you ask me, I will give you, up to half of my kingdom.” <sup>24</sup>And she went out and said to her mother, “For what should I ask?” And she said, “The head of John the Baptist.” <sup>25</sup>And she came in immediately with haste to the king and asked, saying, “I want you to give me at once the head of John the Baptist on a platter.” <sup>26</sup>And the king was exceedingly sorry, but because of his oaths and his guests he did not want to break his word to her. <sup>27</sup>And immediately the king sent an executioner with orders to bring John’s head. He went and beheaded him in the prison <sup>28</sup>and brought his head on a platter and gave it to the girl, and the girl gave it to her mother. <sup>29</sup>When his disciples heard of it, they came and took his body and laid it in a tomb. <sup>30</sup>The apostles returned to Jesus and told him all that they had done and taught. <sup>31</sup>And he said to them, “Come away by yourselves to a desolate place and rest a while.” For many were coming and going, and they had no leisure even to eat. <sup>32</sup>And they went away in the boat to a desolate place by themselves. <sup>33</sup>Now many saw them going and recognized them, and they ran there on foot from all the towns and got there ahead of them. <sup>34</sup>When he went ashore he saw a great crowd, and he had compassion on them, because they were like sheep without a shepherd. And he began to teach them many things. <sup>35</sup>And when it grew late, his disciples came to him and said, “This is a desolate place, and the hour is now late. <sup>36</sup>Send them away to go into the surrounding countryside and villages and buy themselves something to eat.” <sup>37</sup>But he answered them, “You give them something to eat.” And they said to him, “Shall we go and buy two hundred denarii worth of bread and give it to them to eat?” <sup>38</sup>And he said to them, “How many loaves do you have? Go and see.” And when they had found out, they said, “Five, and two fish.” <sup>39</sup>Then he commanded them all to sit down in groups on the green grass. <sup>40</sup>So they sat down in groups, by hundreds and by fifties. <sup>41</sup>And taking the five loaves and the two fish, he looked up to heaven and said a blessing and broke the loaves and gave them to the disciples to set before the people. And he divided the two fish among them all. <sup>42</sup>And they all ate and were satisfied. <sup>43</sup>And they took up twelve baskets full of broken pieces and of the fish. <sup>44</sup>And those who ate the loaves were five thousand men. <sup>45</sup>Immediately he made his disciples get into the boat and go before him to the other side, to Bethsaida, while he dismissed the crowd. <sup>46</sup>And after he had taken leave of them, he went up on the mountain to pray. <sup>47</sup>And when evening came, the boat was out on the sea, and he was alone on the land. <sup>48</sup>And he saw that they were making headway painfully, for the wind was against them. And about the fourth watch of the night he came to them, walking on the sea. He meant to pass by them, <sup>49</sup>but when they saw him walking on the sea they thought it was a ghost, and cried out, <sup>50</sup>for they all saw him and were terrified. But immediately he spoke to them and said, “Take heart; it is I. Do not be afraid.” <sup>51</sup>And he got into the boat with them, and the wind ceased. And they were utterly astounded, <sup>52</sup>for they did not understand about the loaves, but their hearts were hardened. <sup>53</sup>When they had crossed over, they came to land at Gennesaret and moored to the shore. <sup>54</sup>And when they got out of the boat, the people immediately recognized him <sup>55</sup>and ran about the whole region and began to bring the sick people on their beds to wherever they heard he was. <sup>56</sup>And wherever he came, in villages, cities, or countryside, they laid the sick in the marketplaces and implored him that they might touch even the fringe of his garment. And as many as touched it were made well.
6.overview:
Chapter 6 is the widest swing in the Gospel: a village that will not have him, a mission that works, a prophet murdered at a birthday party, a hillside fed until it could eat no more, and a man walking on water at three in the morning.

It opens at Nazareth, where the questions asked about Jesus are exactly the right ones — where did this man get these things? what is the wisdom given to him? — and the conclusion drawn is the worst in the book. They knew his trade, his mother, his brothers by name, and the knowing is precisely what stopped them.

Then Mark does something structurally deliberate. He sends the Twelve out (vv. 7–13), interrupts them with thirteen verses on the death of John the Baptist — by far the longest passage in this Gospel about anyone other than Jesus — and only then lets them come back (v. 30). Anyone reading to find out what following costs has just been told, and told at length: the greatest man born of women dies alone in a cellar because a girl danced well and a weak king could not bear to look foolish in front of his officers.

The second half answers the first. The crowd that ruins the disciples' day off is met with compassion rather than irritation, because he sees sheep without a shepherd; five loaves in his hands feed a district with twelve baskets over; and the men who could only do arithmetic are the ones who carry it out to the rows.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–29 — Rejection, Mission, and the Death of John
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Home (vv. 1–6). He goes back to Nazareth and preaches in the synagogue he grew up in, and the village is offended. They know his trade, his mother, his brothers by name and his sisters by sight, and the knowledge is exactly what stops them. Mark records that he could do no mighty work there, and that he marvelled at their unbelief.

The sending (vv. 7–13). Twelve men are sent out in pairs with authority over unclean spirits and instructions to carry almost nothing. They preach repentance, cast out demons, and anoint the sick with oil — and they are sent before they understand very much at all.

The dungeon (vv. 14–29). Then Mark stops the mission dead and tells, at length and out of sequence, how John the Baptist died: a birthday party, a dance, a rash oath, a girl sent to ask her mother, and a head brought in on a serving dish. Herod is not a monster. He is a weak man who liked listening to a preacher and would not be changed by him.

Note where Mark has put that story. He interrupts the sending of the Twelve with a martyrdom, and only then lets them come back. Anyone reading this Gospel to find out what following costs has just been told.
verseByVerse.theology:
Could he not, or would he not? Verse 5 is one of the most startling sentences in Mark — he could do no mighty work there — and it should not be softened into he chose not to. Mark wrote what he wrote.

But read the exception clause, because it settles the meaning: except that he laid his hands on a few sick people and healed them. Whatever the limitation was, it was not a failure of power; he healed people in Nazareth that afternoon. The impossibility is moral, not mechanical. In a village that had decided in advance what he was, mighty works would have been mere spectacle — and Jesus does not do spectacle for people who have already ruled out the conclusion. He had refused exactly that to the Pharisees (8:11–12) and would refuse it to Herod himself (Luke 23:8–9).

Faith is not a mechanism that generates miracles, as though God were a machine and belief the coin. It is the setting in which he ordinarily works, because he deals with persons and not with material. Unbelief does not disable God. It makes his help unwelcome, and he does not force it.

And he marvelled. There are only two things in the Gospels said to have astonished Jesus. He marvelled at the faith of a Roman officer who had no Bible and no upbringing in it (Luke 7:9), and he marvelled at the unbelief of the village that had raised him. The people with every advantage astonished him in the wrong direction.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Herod, who feared John, knew he was a righteous man, protected him from a wife who wanted him dead, was greatly perplexed by his preaching — and heard him gladly. Gladly. He enjoyed it. He came back for more of it.

Now: the most searching portrait in the chapter, because Herod is not a scoffer and never was. He is the rocky ground of chapter 4 given a name and a palace — the word received with real interest, real feeling, even real pleasure, and no root at all. Being moved by a sermon is not being changed by one, and the platter is the proof.

Everything was there in that man except the one thing that matters. He would not repent — and a man who will not repent will eventually have to silence the voice that keeps asking him to. It took a party, a dance and an audience to get it done, but it was decided long before the executioner was sent.

So the honest test is not whether you enjoy good preaching. Herod did. It is whether there is anything the preaching has actually cost you this year.

verseByVerse.quote: He went away from there and came to his hometown, and his disciples followed him. And on the Sabbath he began to teach in the synagogue, and many who heard him were astonished, saying, "Where did this man get these things? What is the wisdom given to him? How are such mighty works done by his hands?
verseByVerse.commentary:
He went away from there and came to his hometown. Mark does not name it, and does not need to — Nazareth, the village of a few hundred people where he had lived for something like thirty years.

Consider what going back meant. Everyone in that synagogue had known him since he was small. They had bought things from his workshop. Some of them had watched him at his father's funeral, whenever that was; Joseph has vanished from the record by now. He knew the seats they were sitting in.

And his disciples followed him. Mark mentions them because this is not a private visit. He has come home as a rabbi with a following, which is exactly the sort of thing a village finds hardest to swallow.

And on the Sabbath he began to teach in the synagogue. Luke tells us what he read that day: Isaiah 61, the year of the Lord's favour, and then the sentence today this Scripture has been fulfilled in your hearing (Luke 4:16–21). Mark gives only the reaction.

And many who heard him were astonished. It is the same verb used of the crowd in Capernaum in chapter 1, and there it opened into faith. Here it goes the other way, and Mark lets you watch it turn.

Listen to their questions, because every one of them is exactly right.

Where did this man get these things? A fair question, and the only fair question. He has had no rabbinic training. Nobody in Nazareth taught him this.

What is the wisdom given to him? They can hear that it is wisdom. They are not pretending it was a poor sermon. And note the word given — they have half the answer in their own question and do not follow it.

How are such mighty works done by his hands? They do not dispute the miracles either. News of Capernaum has reached them, and their objection is not that the reports are false.

So here is a village asking precisely the right questions about Jesus of Nazareth — where does this come from, what is this wisdom, how are these things done — and arriving at the worst answer anyone in this Gospel arrives at. They are one honest step from the truth and they will not take it, because the step costs too much.

That is worth watching closely, because it is not a first-century failure. It is entirely possible to acknowledge that the teaching of Jesus is extraordinary, that his influence is inexplicable, that something happened around him that ordinary categories do not cover — and to stop there, permanently, because the next sentence would rearrange your life.

These people were not fools and they were not liars. They were near. And the whole tragedy of this passage is that near is not the same as in.

verseByVerse.quote: Is not this the carpenter, the son of Mary and brother of James and Joses and Judas and Simon? And are not his sisters here with us?" And they took offense at him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Is not this the carpenter?

Here is where the astonishment curdles, and it turns on one word. This is the only place in the Gospels where Jesus himself is called a carpenter — Matthew's version has the carpenter's son (Matt. 13:55) — and the Greek tektōn means a craftsman in hard materials: wood, and in that stony country very often stone as well. Doors, roof beams, ploughs, yokes, window frames, furniture.

So for something like eighteen years the eternal Son of God did a trade in a village workshop, and the people in front of him had his work in their houses. There were roofs in Nazareth that afternoon that he had built.

And that is the offence, stated plainly: they had his furniture. You cannot easily worship a man who fixed your door.

The son of Mary. A small phrase with a barb in it. A Jewish man was always named as his father's son, even after the father's death. To call a grown man his mother's son in his own village was a slight, and the whisper behind it is not hard to hear: there had been a wedding, and a birth, and the arithmetic had never quite worked.

And brother of James and Joses and Judas and Simon? And are not his sisters here with us?

They name the brothers and gesture at the sisters, who are apparently sitting in the room. A reader is bound to ask whether these are Jesus's real siblings, and the question has divided the church, so it is worth answering plainly.

Rome and the Orthodox, holding that Mary remained a virgin all her life, take them as cousins (so Jerome) or as children of Joseph by an earlier marriage (so the Orthodox). But the words mean most naturally what they say: these are the later sons and daughters of Joseph and Mary, Jesus's younger half-brothers and half-sisters, born in the ordinary way. Matthew says Joseph knew her not until she had borne her son (Matt. 1:25), and calls Jesus her firstborn — a word that quietly waits for others to follow. Mary's honour is not a lifelong virginity. It is that she bore and raised the Son of God, and then mothered his brothers.

And there is gospel gold in that little family list, so do not walk past it.

During his ministry these brothers did not believe in him. John says it without softening: not even his brothers believed in him (John 7:5). Here in Nazareth they are among the offended, and two chapters back they were on the road to Capernaum to take him home as a madman (3:21, 31).

Then look where they are afterwards. In the upper room, praying with the believers after the resurrection (Acts 1:14). James becomes the pillar of the Jerusalem church, and writes the letter that bears his name, opening it James, a servant of God and of the Lord Jesus Christ. Judas — the Judas in this list — writes Jude.

What turns a scornful younger brother into a man who signs himself the servant of his own sibling, and dies for it? Nobody is fooled by a brother. You have seen him lose his temper as a boy, or you have not, and either way you are the last person on earth to be taken in by a reputation. Something happened between Nazareth and Acts 1, and Paul names it in a single line: then he appeared to James (1 Cor. 15:7).

And they took offense at him. The word is the root of our word scandal — he was a stumbling block to them, and the thing they tripped over was that they knew him.

Which is the warning this verse leaves lying about for anyone raised in a Christian home or a long-attended church. Familiarity does not produce faith. It is quite capable of producing the opposite: a settled, comfortable, unastonished acquaintance with the most extraordinary Person who ever lived, filed under things you have always known.

verseByVerse.quote: And Jesus said to them, "A prophet is not without honor, except in his hometown and among his relatives and in his own household." And he could do no mighty work there, except that he laid his hands on a few sick people and healed them. And he marveled because of their unbelief. And he went about among the villages teaching.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A prophet is not without honor, except in his hometown and among his relatives and in his own household.

He states it as a general rule, and it was probably a proverb already. But notice how the sentence narrows, step by step, and how it gets more painful as it goes: the town, then the extended family, then the house he grew up in. The closer you get, the worse it gets.

And he is speaking of himself. His own brothers are in the room, and they are among the offended.

So if your family think your faith is a phase, an embarrassment or a mild derangement — if you dread the Christmas table because of the sighs, or have a mother who talks about it as though you had joined something — take this verse seriously and let it do its work. He was not spared this. He was refused in the village where he had been a good neighbour for thirty years, by relatives who could name every one of his brothers.

And do not miss where his own brothers ended up. Nothing you can say to a family member will do what the risen Christ can do to them, and he had to rise from the dead to convince his.

And he could do no mighty work there.

Now one of the most startling sentences in Mark, and it should not be smoothed away. Matthew softens it slightly to he did not do many mighty works there (Matt. 13:58). Mark says could not, and he wrote it deliberately.

But read on, because the exception clause settles what it means: except that he laid his hands on a few sick people and healed them. Whatever the limitation was, it was not a failure of power. He healed people in Nazareth that day. Sick men and women in that village got up well.

The impossibility is moral, not mechanical. In a place that had already decided what he was, mighty works would have been mere spectacle — and Jesus does not perform. He refuses a sign to the Pharisees who demand one (8:11–12), and he will stand in silence in front of Herod Antipas, who wanted to see a miracle the way you would want to see a conjuror (Luke 23:8–9).

So faith is not a mechanism that produces miracles, as though God were a machine and belief the coin you put in. It is the setting in which he ordinarily works, because he is dealing with persons and not with material. Unbelief does not disable God. It makes his help unwelcome, and he does not force it on a town that has made up its mind.

And he marveled because of their unbelief.

Twice in the Gospels we are told that Jesus was astonished, and it is worth putting the two together.

He marvelled at a Roman officer — a Gentile soldier with no Bible, no upbringing in the covenant, no synagogue behind him — who said there was no need for him to come under the roof, only to say the word (Luke 7:9). And he marvelled here, at the village that had raised him, taught him the Scriptures, and heard him read them.

The people with none of the advantages astonished him in one direction. The people with all of them astonished him in the other.

And he went about among the villages teaching. No sulking, no long lament, no shaking of the Nazareth dust. He goes on to the next place and keeps preaching. Rejection at home did not stop him for a single day.

verseByVerse.quote: And he called the twelve and began to send them out two by two, and gave them authority over the unclean spirits. He charged them to take nothing for their journey except a staff—no bread, no bag, no money in their belts— but to wear sandals and not put on two tunics.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And he called the twelve and began to send them out.

The word behind send out is apostellō — from which comes apostle, a sent one. This is the moment the title starts to mean something. And it is worth pausing on how little they knew.

These men have not yet grasped who he is. In two chapters' time they will be in a boat asking each other who then is this? They will fail to understand the loaves before this chapter is out. And he sends them anyway, with real authority, to preach.

If you have been waiting to feel qualified before you say anything about Christ to anyone, notice that nobody in this group was.

Two by two. Never alone. There is practical wisdom in it — a road at night, the danger of accusation, the sheer weight of doing it by yourself. There is also a legal reason: only on the evidence of two witnesses or of three witnesses shall a charge be established (Deut. 19:15), and these men are bearing testimony. And it is how the church went on doing it: Paul and Barnabas, Paul and Silas, Barnabas and Mark.

It also means that every one of the Twelve went out with a colleague he had not chosen. Somebody was paired with Simon the Zealot and somebody was paired with Matthew the tax collector.

And gave them authority over the unclean spirits. Note that it is given. Not developed, not innate, not a technique they have learned by watching. Everything they are about to do runs on borrowed authority — which is exactly why it will fail in chapter 9 when they attempt it out of habit rather than dependence (9:28–29).

He charged them to take nothing for their journey except a staff — no bread, no bag, no money in their belts — but to wear sandals and not put on two tunics.

The list is deliberately stripped. No food. No bag — meaning either a travelling pack or, quite possibly, a beggar's collecting bag, which would have made them look like the wandering religious hucksters of the day. No money in the belt, where a man kept his coins. And one tunic: a second was the ordinary traveller's blanket, so they are being told to go without a change of clothes and without bedding.

This is not asceticism for its own sake. It is engineered dependence. They will eat only if somebody feeds them, and sleep only if somebody takes them in, which means the mission cannot be conducted at arm's length from the people it is for.

One detail here has been a favourite of sceptics for centuries, and a reader with Matthew open will spot it at once. Mark says take a staff and wear sandals; Matthew has Jesus forbid both (Matt. 10:9–10), and Luke also says take no staff (Luke 9:3). It looks like a flat contradiction over the smallest of things.

It dissolves the moment the verbs are examined. Matthew's word is acquire — do not procure, do not get hold of. Mark's is take, in the sense of carry along. One plain instruction stands behind both: do not equip yourselves for this journey. Do not go shopping for a new staff or a spare pair of sandals; go exactly as you are, with the stick already in your hand and the sandals already on your feet.

Every traveller in that country owned a staff and wore sandals, and neither writer is debating whether a man may walk shod. They are both forbidding the same thing — provisioning — which is the entire point of the paragraph. Matthew forbids the shopping trip; Mark permits the walking stick. Looked at closely, the collision turns out to be two men describing one scene from two sides.

verseByVerse.quote: And he said to them, "Whenever you enter a house, stay there until you depart from there. And if any place will not receive you and they will not listen to you, when you leave, shake off the dust that is on your feet as a testimony against them."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Whenever you enter a house, stay there until you depart from there.

A small instruction with a surprising amount in it.

Hospitality in that world was owed to travellers, and a visiting teacher with a following would attract offers. The temptation, once you were established in a village and word got round, was to move up — from the first house that took you in to a better one with a wealthier host and a more comfortable room.

Jesus forbids it. Take the first door that opens and stay behind it.

Two things are protected by that. The first is the poor family that risked something to receive them: they are not to be used as a stepping stone and then quietly left. The second is the message. A preacher who is visibly working his way toward the best address in town has already said something about himself that will drown out anything he says about Christ.

And it is not an obsolete rule. There is a version of climbing available in every church and every ministry — the cultivation of the useful people, the warmth that increases with a person's influence. The men who went out from this beach were told, before they preached a word, to stay in the house that had them.

And if any place will not receive you and they will not listen to you, when you leave, shake off the dust that is on your feet as a testimony against them.

Now the harder instruction, and it needs its background.

A devout Jew returning from Gentile territory would shake the dust off his feet at the border, so as not to carry pagan soil into the holy land. It was a deliberate, visible gesture, and everyone knew what it meant: what belongs to you stays with you; we are not bringing it home.

So to do that on the way out of a Jewish village was a shock. It said, in a sign anyone could read: you have put yourselves outside. We came with what was ours to bring, and the responsibility now rests with you.

And here is the practical mercy in it, which is why it is in the Bible for people like us. They are told in advance what to do when it does not work.

Jesus does not send these men out with the expectation of a clean sweep. He assumes refusal, names it, and gives them a way to leave that is neither bitter nor guilty. He does not say: try harder, stay longer, keep pressing until they yield. He says: say your piece, and if they will not have it, go — and do not carry the town away with you in your shoes.

That is worth taking to heart if you have talked to somebody about Christ for years and got nowhere, and have started to feel that their unbelief is a verdict on your competence. It may be, and it is worth examining. But this verse assumes the ordinary case is otherwise: the message was brought faithfully and was refused, and the refusal belonged to the hearer.

You are responsible for the sowing. You never were responsible for the soil, and a man who cannot shake the dust off will eventually stop going anywhere at all.
