verseByVerse.quote: So they went out and proclaimed that people should repent. And they cast out many demons and anointed with oil many who were sick and healed them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
So they went out and proclaimed that people should repent.

Mark gives their message in six words, and it is the same word Jesus opened with in chapter 1: repent and believe in the gospel (1:15).

Repentance is not the same as being sorry. Remorse looks at yourself and feels bad; repentance turns round and goes the other way. The Greek word is about the mind being changed, and the Hebrew behind it is about a road being reversed. It is a direction, not a mood.

And that is what twelve untrained men went from village to village saying. Not a technique for a better life. Not a defence of Jesus's credentials. Turn round.

And they cast out many demons. The authority given in verse 7 turns out to be real in their hands. Whatever they expected when they walked out of that village, this happened, and Luke records that they came back astonished at it (Luke 10:17).

And anointed with oil many who were sick and healed them.

This is the only place in the Gospels where anointing with oil accompanies healing, and it raises a fair practical question, because James tells the church to do the same thing: Is anyone among you sick? Let him call for the elders of the church, and let them pray over him, anointing him with oil in the name of the Lord (Jas. 5:14).

So what is the oil for?

It is not medicine, though olive oil was used medicinally (the Samaritan pours oil and wine on the wounds, Luke 10:34); these healings are plainly not pharmacological. And it is not magic — nothing in the New Testament suggests the oil has power in it. It is a sign: something visible and physical, laid on the body of a sick person, saying that God is being asked to act here, on this man, now. Oil in the Old Testament marked out a person as set apart for God — kings, priests, the tabernacle furniture. To be anointed is to be designated as belonging to him and claimed for his purposes.

Which is why James can tell an ordinary congregation to do it, and why it is a great pity that most churches have quietly dropped it. If you are seriously ill, the instruction in the New Testament is not to suffer privately and hope somebody remembers you in a service. It is to send for the elders of your church and ask them to come and pray over you and anoint you. That is a specific, concrete thing you are entitled to ask for, and it is in your Bible.

And notice, before anyone builds too much on the oil, where James puts the power: and the prayer of faith will save the one who is sick, and the Lord will raise him up. The Lord will. Not the oil, and not the elders.

Mark's summary is deliberately plain: they preached, they cast out, they anointed, people were healed. Twelve men who could not yet answer the question who then is this? went out and did all of that, on borrowed authority, because he sent them.

verseByVerse.quote: King Herod heard of it, for Jesus' name had become known. Some said, "John the Baptist has been raised from the dead. That is why these miraculous powers are at work in him." But others said, "He is Elijah." And others said, "He is a prophet, like one of the prophets of old." But when Herod heard of it, he said, "John, whom I beheaded, has been raised."
verseByVerse.commentary:
King Herod heard of it, for Jesus' name had become known.

The mission has worked. Twelve men in six pairs have covered the district, and the noise has reached the palace. Mark calls him King Herod, which is a courtesy and not a fact — Herod Antipas was a tetrarch, a Roman-appointed ruler of a quarter, and his ambition to be called king would eventually get him exiled. Mark uses the title the locals used.

Then Mark gives us three popular verdicts on Jesus, and they are worth laying side by side.

John the Baptist has been raised from the dead. He is Elijah. He is a prophet, like one of the prophets of old.

Every one of these is respectful. Every one is far too small. And every one will come back in chapter 8, word for word, when Jesus asks his disciples who people say that he is (8:28) — and then turns and asks them.

Note what the crowd is doing. It is reaching for the biggest category it already has. A prophet is the largest thing they can think of, so he must be one, or the greatest of them come back. It never occurs to anyone that a new category might be required.

That instinct has not aged at all. Ask people today who Jesus was and you will be offered the same shape of answer at a lower altitude: a great teacher, a moral genius, a mystic, a revolutionary. All respectful. All far too small. And the reason is the same: those categories cost nothing.

But when Herod heard of it, he said, John, whom I beheaded, has been raised.

And here is one of the most chilling sentences in the Gospel, because of one word in it.

Whom I beheaded. He could have said John, who was beheaded. He could have blamed his wife, who wanted it; or the oath, which trapped him; or the guests, who were watching. Every one of those excuses was available and he had used them all at the time.

Alone in his own head, months later, the sentence comes out in the first person, with the pronoun in it.

That is what a guilty conscience does. It keeps the accurate record. Herod has spent whatever time has passed managing this, and the moment he hears of miracles in Galilee his mind goes straight to the man he killed and produces a resurrection to explain it. He is not reasoning; he is haunted. He has become a man who cannot hear good news without hearing his own crime in it.

Which is worth knowing about the human machinery. Guilt does not fade because it is unaddressed; it goes underground and comes up sideways, in dreams, in irrational fears, in the inability to enjoy anything. A conscience that has not been dealt with does not stop working. It simply stops being useful and starts being a torment.

And there is only one place in the world where it can be dealt with. Herod had a prophet in his cellar who would have told him where, and he preferred to keep listening rather than obey. Now he has a ghost.

Mark now goes back and tells us how it happened, and it takes him thirteen verses — by far the longest account in this Gospel of anything that does not involve Jesus.

verseByVerse.quote: For it was Herod who had sent and seized John and bound him in prison for the sake of Herodias, his brother Philip's wife, because he had married her. For John had been saying to Herod, "It is not lawful for you to have your brother's wife."
verseByVerse.commentary:
For it was Herod who had sent and seized John and bound him in prison.

Mark now backs up to explain, and the flashback is the longest passage in his Gospel about anyone other than Jesus. Everything in it is compressed elsewhere; here he slows down and gives you the whole squalid business.

The setting, from the historian Josephus, is the fortress of Machaerus — a grim hilltop stronghold east of the Dead Sea, miles from anywhere. That is where John was held: the man who had baptised thousands in the open air of the Jordan valley, shut in a cell in a desert castle.

For the sake of Herodias, his brother Philip's wife, because he had married her.

The family arrangement takes a moment to lay out and is worth the trouble, because the mess of it is the point.

Herod Antipas was married. On a visit to Rome he stayed with his half-brother and formed an attachment to his half-brother's wife, Herodias — who was also his own niece, granddaughter of Herod the Great through another son. He came home, put away his first wife (the daughter of the Nabatean king Aretas, which would eventually cost him a war and an army), and married Herodias.

So: a man leaves his wife for his brother's wife, who is also his niece. And the Law of Moses is not ambiguous about it — you shall not uncover the nakedness of your brother's wife (Lev. 18:16; 20:21).

For John had been saying to Herod, It is not lawful for you to have your brother's wife.

The tense in the Greek is continuous: he kept on saying it. This was not one outburst that Herod overheard. John said it, and said it again, and went on saying it, to the ruler's face.

Look hard at what that sentence contains, because it is a model of something the church constantly gets wrong in one direction or the other.

It is short. John does not deliver a treatise on marriage. One sentence.

It is specific. Not a general denunciation of immorality in high places, which costs nothing and changes nobody. It names this man and this marriage.

It is addressed to the man himself. John says it to Herod. He does not preach it about him in the safety of the Jordan valley to a crowd who already agreed.

And it is about Herod's sin, not Herod's politics. John had no comment on the tetrarch's taxes or his building projects. He confronted him on the thing he was answerable to God for.

And it cost him his freedom and then his head.

That is the price of the fourth item on that list, and it always has been. It is perfectly safe to denounce sins in general, and sins that belong to people not present, and sins nobody in your circle is committing. The moment a name is attached, it becomes expensive — which is why the prophets are so few and the courtiers so many. A man who tells the king only what the king can bear is not a prophet. He is staff.

Two things keep this from being a licence for the sharp tongue. John was not rude, and he was not indiscriminate: he had a word for the crowds, the tax collectors and the soldiers too (Luke 3:10–14), and it was tailored to each. And he said it to the man's face, repeatedly, in a way that risked everything he had — which is a very different thing from criticising the powerful at no cost, from a distance, to an audience that will applaud.

verseByVerse.quote: And Herodias had a grudge against him and wanted to put him to death. But she could not, for Herod feared John, knowing that he was a righteous and holy man, and he kept him safe. When he heard him, he was greatly perplexed, and yet he heard him gladly.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And Herodias had a grudge against him and wanted to put him to death.

Mark's phrase is vivid — she had it in for him, held it against him, nursed it. This is not a flash of temper; it is a settled campaign, and she is waiting for her chance. Verse 21 will call it an opportunity, which means she had been looking for one.

And her reaction is worth noting for what it tells you about the effect of being told the truth. John's sentence was aimed at Herod, but it was Herodias who could not live with it, because it named her position exactly: she was not a wife. Every day that John stayed alive, that fact was alive in the kingdom.

Some people, when a sin is named, repent. Some argue. And some set out to destroy the person who said it, because if the witness can be discredited or removed then perhaps the fact goes with him. It never does — but the attempt is one of the most reliable behaviours in human life, and it is why speaking plainly to power has always been dangerous.

But she could not, for Herod feared John, knowing that he was a righteous and holy man, and he kept him safe.

And now Mark gives us the portrait of Herod Antipas, and it is the most searching thing in the chapter, because he is not a monster and everything in these two verses is to his credit until it isn't.

He feared John. Not in the sense of being frightened of a prisoner in his own dungeon. This is awe — the involuntary respect a slack man feels in the presence of a serious one.

Knowing that he was a righteous and holy man. Herod's assessment is correct. He is not deceived about John's character for a moment. He looks at the ragged preacher he has locked up and sees exactly what he is.

And he kept him safe. He protected him. Against his own wife, who wanted him dead, the tetrarch used his authority to keep John alive.

When he heard him, he was greatly perplexed. The word means thrown into confusion — John's preaching disturbed him, unsettled his mind, left him at a loss. So the word was getting through. This is not a man who was bored.

And yet he heard him gladly.

Gladly. He sent for him. He came back for more. Picture the scene, because it is extraordinary: the ruler of Galilee going down into his own prison to listen to the man he has chained there, being upset by what he hears, and returning to be upset again.

He enjoyed it.

And that is the most dangerous spiritual condition described anywhere in this Gospel, precisely because it looks so much like the real thing. Everything is present except one item. Interest, respect, emotion, protection of the preacher, genuine disturbance of conscience — and no repentance. The one thing John was actually asking for, week after week, was the one thing Herod would not do. Herodias stayed.

He is the rocky ground of chapter 4 given a name and a palace: the word received with real feeling and no root at all.

So take the test he offers, because it is a plain one and it cuts across every kind of Christian. It is possible to love good preaching — to seek it out, to be moved by it, to be genuinely stirred, to talk about it afterwards with real warmth — and to be, in the settled arrangements of your life, entirely unchanged by it. Herod would have said he had a high view of preaching. He did.

The question is not whether the sermon moved you. It is whether anything in your house is different because of it. Name one thing that has actually cost you something this year.

Because a man who will not repent must eventually silence the voice that keeps asking him to. Herod did not want John dead. He liked him. But the logic of an unrepented sin runs one way, and it took only a party, a dance and an audience to finish what had been decided long before.

verseByVerse.quote: But an opportunity came when Herod on his birthday gave a banquet for his nobles and military commanders and the leading men of Galilee. For when Herodias's daughter came in and danced, she pleased Herod and his guests. And the king said to the girl, "Ask me for whatever you wish, and I will give it to you." And he vowed to her, "Whatever you ask me, I will give you, up to half of my kingdom."
verseByVerse.commentary:
But an opportunity came. Mark's word is literally a good day — a well-timed day. Herodias has been waiting for one, and the calendar hands it to her.

When Herod on his birthday gave a banquet for his nobles and military commanders and the leading men of Galilee.

Note the guest list, because everything that follows turns on it. His nobles — the court. His military commanders — the army officers. The leading men of Galilee — the money and the influence of the province.

This is every man in the region whose opinion Herod cares about, in one hall, on his birthday. It is the most public night of his year, and by the end of it a man will be dead.

For when Herodias's daughter came in and danced.

Josephus names her Salome. Mark does not, and calls her the girl in the verses that follow — a word for a young girl, not a woman.

Understand what has happened here, because we have romanticised this scene for centuries and the reality is squalid. A royal princess does not dance at a stag banquet for a hall full of drunk officers. That is what hired entertainers were for, and their status was very low. Herodias sent her own daughter in to do the work of a dancing girl, in front of her stepfather and the entire military command of Galilee.

She was willing to use her child that way to get what she wanted. That is the measure of the grudge.

She pleased Herod and his guests. Mark leaves it there and does not need to say more.

And the king said to the girl, Ask me for whatever you wish, and I will give it to you. And he vowed to her, Whatever you ask me, I will give you, up to half of my kingdom.

Now the oath, and there are three things wrong with it.

It is theatre. Herod is performing for the room. This is a man buying a moment of admiration from his officers with a grand gesture, and the swearing is part of the show — he does not merely offer, he vows, and Mark says in verse 26 that it was oaths, plural. He said it more than once.

It is empty. He had no kingdom to give half of. He was a tetrarch holding his position entirely at Rome's pleasure, and he could not have alienated a square mile of it without permission. The most generous sentence he speaks all evening is one he has no power to keep.

And it is borrowed. Up to half of my kingdom is the line the Persian king Ahasuerus says to Esther, three times over (Est. 5:3, 6; 7:2). Every Jew in that hall would have caught it. And the echo is unbearable, because in Esther that offer is used by a brave woman to save a nation from slaughter. Here the same words are used by a girl to fetch a prophet's head on a plate.

The whole thing is a man who cannot say a small true sentence and cannot stop himself saying a large false one — and in about ninety seconds it will have him.

There is a plain warning in it that the New Testament makes explicit later: let your yes be yes and your no be no (Jas. 5:12; Matt. 5:37). The reason is exactly this scene. A man who inflates his words to impress a room will one day find himself standing behind a promise he never meant, in front of people he cannot bear to disappoint.

verseByVerse.quote: And she went out and said to her mother, "For what should I ask?" And she said, "The head of John the Baptist." And she came in immediately with haste to the king and asked, saying, "I want you to give me at once the head of John the Baptist on a platter." And the king was exceedingly sorry, but because of his oaths and his guests he did not want to break his word to her.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And she went out and said to her mother, For what should I ask?

She goes out. That detail is worth having: the girl does not know what she wants. She has been given, in front of the whole court, an open cheque from a ruler — and she has to leave the room and go and ask her mother.

Which tells you she was a child in every sense, and it tells you where the will in this story lives.

And she said, The head of John the Baptist.

No hesitation. No pause to think of anything else. Herodias has had the answer ready for months, and she gives it to her daughter in seven words.

Notice that she asks for nothing for herself and nothing for the girl. Not land, not money, not jewels, not a position — and the offer was half a kingdom. There is nothing in the world Herodias wants as much as she wants that voice stopped.

That is what a nursed grudge does to a person's appetites. It eats everything else. Given one wish, unlimited, this woman spends it on a man in a cell who has done her no injury except to tell the truth about her.

And she came in immediately with haste to the king. The girl runs back. Mark piles up the words — immediately, with haste — and you can see a child hurrying to deliver a message, pleased to have an answer.

And asked, saying, I want you to give me at once the head of John the Baptist on a platter.

And she has improved on it. Her mother said the head of John the Baptist. The girl adds two things: at once, and on a platter.

The platter is her own contribution. It is a serving dish — the word is used for the plates the food is coming round on. In a hall full of banqueting men, she asks for a man's head to be carried in on the crockery.

Mark does not comment. He does not need to. This is what happens to a child raised in that house.

And the king was exceedingly sorry. The word is strong — deeply grieved, cut up. It is the same word used of Jesus in Gethsemane (14:34). Herod's distress is entirely real. He does not want this.

But because of his oaths and his guests he did not want to break his word to her.

And there it is: the whole reason a man is beheaded tonight, stated in nine words.

Because of his oaths. He had sworn, loudly, twice. He was now the man who had said it.

And his guests. There they sit — the nobles, the officers, the leading men of Galilee, every one of them looking at him and waiting.

And here is the terrible piety of it. Herod keeps his word. He is scrupulous about an oath and murderous about a prophet, and he would have told you, quite sincerely, that a man must stand behind what he has sworn.

What he could not face was being the man who backed down in front of that room. Not conscience — he had already lost that argument, and he knew John was righteous and holy. Not law — every law he had said a prisoner should not be executed to settle a dinner-party bet. He could not bear to look foolish in front of people whose opinion he had spent his life courting.

Which is the most ordinary murder motive in the world, and the reason this passage is not really about ancient kings.

Almost nobody does the worst thing they ever do because they wanted to. They do it because backing out in front of the people watching was unthinkable. The joke you laughed at. The thing you went along with because the room had already turned. The stand you did not take because of who would have seen you take it. Peter is eight chapters away from denying he ever knew Jesus, in a courtyard, to a servant girl, for exactly this reason.

The fear of man lays a snare, but whoever trusts in the LORD is safe (Prov. 29:25). Herod was a king with an army, and a teenage girl and a room full of guests walked him into a murder he did not want to commit.

verseByVerse.quote: And immediately the king sent an executioner with orders to bring John's head. He went and beheaded him in the prison and brought his head on a platter and gave it to the girl, and the girl gave it to her mother. When his disciples heard of it, they came and took his body and laid it in a tomb.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And immediately the king sent an executioner with orders to bring John's head.

Immediately. The whole thing takes as long as it takes a soldier to walk down to the cells and back.

The word Mark uses for the executioner is a Latin loan-word — speculator, a member of the ruler's personal guard, the man kept for exactly this. There was such a man on the staff, and everybody knew what he was for.

He went and beheaded him in the prison.

Nine words, and Mark will not embellish them. He does not describe the cell, or whether John was asleep, or whether anything was said. There is a door opening in the dark and a soldier with an order, and that is all we are told.

Now stop and take in what has just happened, because it is one of the hardest things in the Gospel.

This is the man Jesus called the greatest born of women (Matt. 11:11). The forerunner. The voice crying in the wilderness. The man who baptised the Son of God and saw the heavens torn open and the Spirit descend, and who said behold, the Lamb of God, who takes away the sin of the world. The last and greatest of the prophets.

And he dies in a cellar, alone, unheard, with no last word recorded, because a girl danced well at a party.

There is no rescue. That is the thing to sit with, and the Gospel does not soften it. Jesus was alive and ten miles of lake away, healing strangers, and John — who had been shut in that fortress long enough to send messengers out asking are you the one who is to come, or shall we look for another? (Matt. 11:3) — was not delivered. The answer he got back was not I am coming to get you. It was a message about the blind seeing and the poor having good news preached to them, and a beatitude: blessed is the one who is not offended by me.

So John died with the question answered and the door still locked.

If you are serving God faithfully and your circumstances are getting worse rather than better, that is in your Bible on purpose, and it is not a sign that something has gone wrong. Faithfulness is not a contract with providence. Hebrews knows this: some by faith stopped the mouths of lions and escaped the edge of the sword — and others, by exactly the same faith, were sawn in two, they were killed with the sword (Heb. 11:33–37). The chapter puts them in the same list and calls it all faith.

And brought his head on a platter and gave it to the girl, and the girl gave it to her mother.

The dish comes into the hall. It passes to a girl, and the girl carries it to her mother, and Mark stops the sentence there. Herodias has what she wanted. What she does with it, we are not told.

When his disciples heard of it, they came and took his body and laid it in a tomb.

And here is the one clean act in the whole squalid story. John's own disciples — men with no power and everything to lose, walking into a Herodian fortress to ask for a headless corpse — come and take the body and bury it properly.

They could not save him. They could not avenge him. They could carry him, and they did.

Mark's readers, coming to the end of this Gospel, will meet that sentence again in almost the same words: another righteous man executed by a frightened ruler who knew he was innocent, and friends who came and took the body and laid it in a tomb (15:45–46).

The difference is what happened next. Herod's dungeon kept John. The tomb outside Jerusalem could not keep the one John had pointed to — and because it could not, the man in that cell is not finally a tragedy. He lost his head for telling one king the truth, and he will see the King, and the greatest born of women will find that the least in the kingdom of heaven was a very good thing to be.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 30–56 — The Feeding, the Walking, and the Healings
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The rest that never happened (vv. 30–34). The apostles come back full of what they have done, and Jesus's first instruction is not a debrief but a retreat: come away and rest. They get into a boat — and the crowd works out where they are going, runs round the head of the lake on foot, and is waiting when they land. His response to a wrecked afternoon off is compassion, because they were like sheep without a shepherd.

The feeding (vv. 35–44). The disciples do the arithmetic and propose dispersal. Jesus hands the problem back: you give them something to eat. Then he seats a crowd of thousands in ranks on the spring grass, takes five loaves and two fish, and there is more left at the end than there was at the start.

The lake at three in the morning (vv. 45–52). He sends them off ahead and goes up the mountain alone to pray — and from up there, in the dark, he sees them straining at the oars. He comes to them on the water, and he means to pass by, in the language the Old Testament reserves for God showing himself.

Gennesaret (vv. 53–56). And then a summary paragraph of pure mercy: whole villages carrying the sick out into the marketplaces, and everyone who touched even the edge of his clothing made well.
verseByVerse.theology:
He meant to pass by them (v. 48) is the strangest clause in the chapter, and it is not what it sounds like. He is not trying to overtake them or slip past unnoticed. Passing by is the Old Testament's own vocabulary for God making himself visible.

When Moses asked to see the glory of God, the LORD put him in a cleft of the rock and said while my glory passes by I will cover you with my hand (Ex. 33:22). When Elijah stood at the mouth of the cave, the word was behold, the LORD passed by (1 Kgs. 19:11). And Job, describing the God no man can lay hold of, says he alone stretched out the heavens and trampled the waves of the sea — and then, four verses later, behold, he passes by me, and I see him not (Job 9:8, 11).

Walking on the sea and passing by, in the same sentence, out of the same book. Mark's readers who knew their Scriptures were not being told about a shortcut.

And then, when they scream, he speaks: Take heart; it is I. Do not be afraid. The middle phrase is egō eimi — literally I am, the words from the burning bush (Ex. 3:14). It is the ordinary way to say it's me, and in this setting, on that water, from that Person, it is very much more.

Which makes verse 52 the saddest verse in the chapter: they did not understand about the loaves, but their hearts were hardened. Mark uses of the Twelve the very word he used of the men in the synagogue who watched a withered hand restored and went out to plan a murder (3:5). Hardness is not a disease of unbelievers only.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: twelve exhausted men doing sums in front of a hungry crowd — two hundred denarii, most of a year's wages, and it still would not be enough — and hearing you give them something to eat.

Now: anyone facing a need that is plainly larger than their resources. The parent who has run out of wisdom. The pastor of a small church looking at a large town. The person asked to care for someone whose needs exceed anything they have.

Jesus is not asking them to solve it. He asks a different question, and it is the practical one: how many loaves do you have? Go and see. Not how many do you need — how many have you got. Go and count it.

Five loaves and two fish is an embarrassing answer to give in front of five thousand people, and it was the right answer, because the multiplication happens in his hands and not in theirs. Bring what you actually have, including how little it is. And notice who ended up carrying the twelve baskets of surplus: the men who had nothing to give, one basket each.

verseByVerse.quote: The apostles returned to Jesus and told him all that they had done and taught. And he said to them, "Come away by yourselves to a desolate place and rest a while." For many were coming and going, and they had no leisure even to eat. And they went away in the boat to a desolate place by themselves.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The apostles returned to Jesus and told him all that they had done and taught.

This is the only place in Mark where the Twelve are called apostles, and it is exactly the right moment for it: they have just been sent and have just come back.

And they are full of it. You can hear the noise in the sentence — all that they had done, and all that they had taught, everything, at once, probably several of them at the same time. Demons had come out. Sick people had got up. It had worked.

Now watch what he does with that, because it is not what a modern ministry would do.

And he said to them, Come away by yourselves to a desolate place and rest a while.

No debrief. No strategy session about how to build on the momentum. No suggestion that the moment of maximum success is the moment to press the advantage.

Rest.

He does not even say pray, though he will go and do that himself in a few verses. He says come away, by yourselves, to an empty place, and rest a while — and the word for rest means to stop and be refreshed.

Take this seriously, because Christians are peculiarly bad at it. There is a way of serving God that treats tiredness as a badge and rest as a slightly shameful concession, and it is not in this Gospel. The Lord of the harvest, with a whole district newly stirred up and more open doors than he could walk through, took twelve effective men out of circulation and sent them for a rest.

For many were coming and going, and they had no leisure even to eat.

Mark gives the reason, and it is the same detail he gave in chapter 3 (3:20): the demand is so constant that meals are being missed. Not a hard week. A pattern.

And that is the diagnostic worth applying to your own life, because it is measurable rather than vague. Not do I feel busy — everybody feels busy. Are the ordinary human things being squeezed out? Meals eaten standing up. Sleep treated as the flexible item. Days off that quietly became half days and then nothing. When the basics start going, something has gone wrong that no amount of fruitfulness justifies, and Jesus treated it as a reason to stop rather than a sign of seriousness.

And they went away in the boat to a desolate place by themselves.

They actually go. And the last thing to notice in this little paragraph is that the rest was his idea, he arranged it, they obeyed it — and in three verses it will be completely ruined.

Which is worth knowing in advance. Planning rest is right, and it will still sometimes be taken from you. What matters is what a man does when it is, and that is the next verse.

verseByVerse.quote: Now many saw them going and recognized them, and they ran there on foot from all the towns and got there ahead of them. When he went ashore he saw a great crowd, and he had compassion on them, because they were like sheep without a shepherd. And he began to teach them many things.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now many saw them going and recognized them, and they ran there on foot from all the towns and got there ahead of them.

The plan fails immediately, and Mark tells you exactly how.

They are seen leaving. Somebody works out from the direction of the boat where they must be heading. Word goes out to the villages along the shore, and people set off round the head of the lake on foot — nine or ten miles of hot road at walking pace — and they get there first.

Picture the boat coming in. Twelve exhausted men who have been travelling and preaching for weeks, who were promised a quiet day, rowing toward an empty shore and seeing, as it comes into view, that the empty shore is covered with people. Thousands of them. Already waiting.

Anyone who has ever needed a day off knows what would rise in the chest at that moment.

When he went ashore he saw a great crowd, and he had compassion on them.

And there is the sentence that makes this passage what it is. He is tired. His plan for the day is destroyed. The people on that beach are the reason he had to leave in the first place, and they have chased him round the lake.

He looks at them and is moved with compassion.

The Greek word is one of the strongest in the language for pity — it is built on the word for the inward organs, the deep viscera, and means to be moved in the gut. It is not a decision to be nice. It is what happens inside him when he sees them.

Because they were like sheep without a shepherd.

Now hear what he actually saw, because this phrase is not a general remark about how lost people are. It is a quotation, and it comes loaded.

It is Moses's prayer at the end of his life, asking God to appoint a successor so that the congregation of the LORD may not be as sheep that have no shepherd (Num. 27:17). It is Micaiah's vision of Israel scattered on the mountains after the death of a bad king (1 Kgs. 22:17). And behind both stands Ezekiel 34, the great denunciation of Israel's leaders: shepherds who feed themselves and not the flock, who do not strengthen the weak or heal the sick or bring back the strays — and God's answer to it, I myself will search for my sheep and will seek them out... I myself will be the shepherd of my sheep (Ezek. 34:11, 15).

So he is not merely feeling sorry for a crowd. He is looking at a nation and seeing the ancient failure — people with no one to feed them, and every one of those texts has an answer, and he is it.

And he began to teach them many things.

And notice what the compassion produces first. Not the loaves. Not healing. Teaching.

That is a striking order, and Mark has done it before (2:2). Given a hungry, tired, spiritually starving crowd, the first thing he gives them is words — because the deepest thing wrong with sheep who have no shepherd is that nobody has been feeding them, and Ezekiel's complaint is about food.

He will get to their stomachs before the day is out. He starts with the thing they did not know they came for.

verseByVerse.quote: And when it grew late, his disciples came to him and said, "This is a desolate place, and the hour is now late. Send them away to go into the surrounding countryside and villages and buy themselves something to eat." But he answered them, "You give them something to eat." And they said to him, "Shall we go and buy two hundred denarii worth of bread and give it to them to eat?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
And when it grew late, his disciples came to him and said, This is a desolate place, and the hour is now late.

The disciples are being sensible, and it is worth granting them that before we watch them fail. They are right about the facts: it is an empty place, it is getting dark, and there are thousands of people here with no arrangements made.

Send them away to go into the surrounding countryside and villages and buy themselves something to eat.

And their solution is the obvious one. Disperse them while there is still light, and let everyone sort himself out.

Notice the shape of it, because it is the standard shape of religious problem-solving. The need is real, the resources are insufficient, therefore reduce the need. Send them away. It is not callous — they are trying to get people fed. It simply never occurs to them that the man standing next to them might be a factor in the calculation, and they have just come back from a mission trip on which they cast out demons.

But he answered them, You give them something to eat.

Five words, and the pronoun is emphatic in the Greek: you give them something.

It is not fair, and it is not meant to be. He is handing twelve tired men a responsibility that is plainly, mathematically beyond them, and standing there while they work out what to do with it.

He does this. It is one of his settled habits with his people — the command that cannot be obeyed out of your own resources. Stretch out your withered hand. Feed this crowd. Go and make disciples of all nations. Every one of them is impossible, and every one of them is an invitation.

And they said to him, Shall we go and buy two hundred denarii worth of bread and give it to them to eat?

And out comes the arithmetic.

A denarius was a day's wage for a labourer, so two hundred denarii is something like eight months' work. They have evidently done the sum on the spot — thousands of people, so much bread each, and the figure comes out at most of a year's income, which they do not have and could not spend in a village at dusk anyway.

You can hear the tone. It is not quite rude and it is not quite faith. It is a man showing his working to prove the thing cannot be done.

And here is what makes it painful rather than funny. These are the men who, a few days ago, were casting out demons in villages on borrowed authority. They have seen a paralytic walk, a leper cleaned, a girl raised from the dead, and a hurricane muzzled. They are standing next to the person who did all of it, and their considered response to a catering problem is a spreadsheet.

Before that is used as a stick, be honest about how normal it is. Most of us pray about the things we already half expect to manage and quietly do arithmetic about the rest. We have a category for what God might do, and a much larger category for what is realistically going to happen, and the second one runs our week.

The disciples' sum was not wrong. Two hundred denarii really would not have been enough. That is the point. They were correct, and completely beside the point, because they had left out the only variable that mattered.

verseByVerse.quote: And he said to them, "How many loaves do you have? Go and see." And when they had found out, they said, "Five, and two fish." Then he commanded them all to sit down in groups on the green grass. So they sat down in groups, by hundreds and by fifties.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And he said to them, How many loaves do you have? Go and see.

He does not answer the objection. He asks a different question, and it is the practical one.

Not how much do you need — they have already worked that out and it paralysed them. How many have you got? And then, gently: go and count it.

That is worth taking as a method, because it is exactly what to do when a need is obviously beyond you. Stop calculating the gap. Go and find out precisely what is in your hands, however little that is, and bring it to him. The gap is his business; the inventory is yours.

And when they had found out, they said, Five, and two fish.

Five small barley loaves — John tells us they came from a boy in the crowd, and that barley was the bread of the poor (John 6:9). The fish would have been small, salted, the relish you ate with bread rather than a meal.

It is an embarrassing thing to say out loud in front of five thousand hungry people. Five. And two fish. Somebody had to walk back and report that.

And it was the right answer. Christ has never once been hindered by the smallness of what was brought to him; he has often been hindered by its being kept back.

Then he commanded them all to sit down in groups on the green grass.

Two details here, and both are worth stopping for.

The green grass. That is Peter's eye, and nobody else's — Mark is the only Gospel that mentions the colour. In that country the hills are green for a few weeks in spring after the rains and brown for the rest of the year. It tells you the season (John says the Passover was near), and more than that, it tells you a man was standing there and remembered what it looked like.

It also puts a psalm into the scene without saying a word. The LORD is my shepherd; I shall not want. He makes me lie down in green pastures (Ps. 23:1–2). Mark has just called the crowd sheep without a shepherd. Now the shepherd sits them down on the green grass and feeds them.

In groups, by hundreds and by fifties. The word Mark uses for groups is vivid — it means garden plots or flower beds; from the air the crowd would have looked like a hillside laid out in rectangles.

And the arrangement is not crowd control. This is how Israel was organised in the wilderness: Moses appointed chiefs of thousands, of hundreds, of fifties, and of tens (Ex. 18:25; Deut. 1:15). A crowd seated in hundreds and fifties in a desolate place, about to be given bread from heaven at the hands of a leader, is Israel in the wilderness all over again.

Mark has been building this for two verses and expects his readers to see it. There is a new Exodus under way, and the man arranging the ranks is greater than Moses — who never made a loaf in his life, and only ever announced that the manna had arrived.

verseByVerse.quote: And taking the five loaves and the two fish, he looked up to heaven and said a blessing and broke the loaves and gave them to the disciples to set before the people. And he divided the two fish among them all. And they all ate and were satisfied.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And taking the five loaves and the two fish, he looked up to heaven and said a blessing and broke the loaves and gave them to the disciples to set before the people.

Four verbs, and every Christian reading this Gospel is meant to feel them land: he took, he blessed, he broke, he gave.

You will meet them again in chapter 14, in an upstairs room in Jerusalem: he took bread, and after blessing it broke it and gave it to them, and said, Take; this is my body (14:22). And the two disciples on the Emmaus road will recognise a stranger at their own table by exactly this sequence — he took the bread and blessed and broke it and gave it to them. And their eyes were opened (Luke 24:30–31).

So this is not the Lord's Supper. But Mark has laid the two scenes on top of each other on purpose. The man who feeds a hillside with broken bread is going to be broken himself, and the church has been eating from that ever since.

He looked up to heaven and said a blessing. The blessing in a Jewish home was not said over the food but to God for it — Blessed are you, LORD our God, King of the universe, who brings forth bread from the earth. He is not enchanting the loaves. He is thanking his Father, out loud, over food that is obviously not enough, before a single extra crumb exists.

That is a small thing with a long reach. Gratitude offered before the provision arrives is one of the plainest marks of faith there is, and it is very easy to test in your own house: do you thank God for what is in front of you when you can see it is not going to stretch?

And gave them to the disciples to set before the people.

And here is the mechanism, which is the most instructive thing in the verse. Jesus does not distribute. He hands it to the Twelve, and they carry it out to the ranks on the grass.

Which means the multiplication happened in their hands. Nobody records the moment; Mark does not describe bread swelling. Somewhere between the Lord's hands and the hundredth row, there kept on being more — and the men doing the carrying were the men who, ten minutes earlier, had proved by arithmetic that it could not be done.

That is how he still works. He does not usually rain provision directly onto the people who need it. He gives it to his church to carry, and the carriers discover the sufficiency by handing it out. You will not find out whether there is enough by standing still and calculating. You find out on the fourth row.

And he divided the two fish among them all. And they all ate and were satisfied.

Mark's word is emphatic and slightly comic: they were filled — the word you would use of an animal fed to fullness. Not sampled. Not given a token. Thousands of people on a hillside ate until they had had enough and stopped.

They had come out to that place with no food, chasing a man round a lake, and the day ended with every one of them full.

verseByVerse.quote: And they took up twelve baskets full of broken pieces and of the fish. And those who ate the loaves were five thousand men.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And they took up twelve baskets full of broken pieces and of the fish.

The gathering up of the fragments is not a detail Mark had to include, and John tells us it was commanded: gather up the leftover fragments, that nothing may be lost (John 6:12).

Which is worth a moment on its own. The one who has just created bread out of five loaves will not have scraps trodden into the grass. Abundance in the kingdom of God never licenses waste. There is no contradiction between believing that God's supply is endless and refusing to be careless with a slice of bread — and the man who made the supply is the one who gave the order.

Twelve baskets. The number is not accidental and Mark expects it to be counted.

Twelve disciples. Twelve tribes. Each man who went out among the ranks with an impossible task and a fraction of a loaf comes back at the end of the evening carrying a basket he cannot see the bottom of.

Do the arithmetic they did earlier and it comes out backwards. They began with five loaves and two fish. They ended with more food than they started with, after feeding a town. That is the accounting of the kingdom, and it is why the sum in verse 37 was the wrong question.

Paul says the same thing in a sentence: God is able to make all grace abound to you, so that having all sufficiency in all things at all times, you may abound in every good work (2 Cor. 9:8). And the widow of Zarephath, down to a handful of flour and a little oil and expecting to die after one last meal, found that the jar was not spent (1 Kgs. 17:14–16).

And those who ate the loaves were five thousand men.

Mark gives the number at the end, almost as a footnote, and specifies men — the word is andres, males, not the general word for people. Matthew makes the implication explicit: besides women and children (Matt. 14:21). So the real figure on that hillside was very much larger, quite possibly two or three times larger.

Five thousand men is roughly the size of a Roman legion, and considerably more than the population of any town in Galilee outside Tiberias and Sepphoris. This is the entire district, sitting on the grass in the dark, fed.

And it happened because a boy handed over his lunch and twelve men did what they were told with what they had.

The last thing to notice is what the crowd did not know. John records that they tried to make him king by force that night and had to be dispersed (John 6:15). They had eaten from his hands and concluded that a man who can do that should be running the country.

They were nearly right, and entirely wrong. He had not come to be the kind of king who keeps a nation fed. He had come to be the bread — and when he said so the next day, most of them left (John 6:66).

verseByVerse.quote: Immediately he made his disciples get into the boat and go before him to the other side, to Bethsaida, while he dismissed the crowd. And after he had taken leave of them, he went up on the mountain to pray. And when evening came, the boat was out on the sea, and he was alone on the land.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Immediately he made his disciples get into the boat and go before him to the other side.

The word is strong: he compelled them. Something is being cut short here in a hurry, and the disciples plainly did not want to go.

John tells us why. The crowd, having been fed, was about to take him by force and make him king (John 6:15). Five thousand men on a hillside in an occupied country, well fed and enthusiastic, is a rebellion looking for a leader — and twelve disciples who had spent the evening handing out miraculous bread were in no state to resist that mood. One of them was a Zealot.

So he breaks it up. He puts his men on a boat and sends them away, and then deals with the crowd himself.

Notice what he is refusing. This is a crown, offered freely, by acclamation, without a cross. It is the third time in this Gospel that the shortest road to glory has been laid in front of him and the first two were offered by the devil in a wilderness (1:13). He will not take a kingdom on those terms, because a king who feeds you is not the same as a king who saves you.

And after he had taken leave of them, he went up on the mountain to pray.

And here is the pattern of his life, and it is worth putting the pieces of this chapter together to see it.

He has had no rest. The retreat was ruined before it started. He has taught for hours, fed thousands, defused a political crisis, and dismissed a crowd of that size personally — after he had taken leave of them is a whole evening's work in a subordinate clause.

And what he does with the first free hour is climb a hill in the dark to pray.

This is the second of three times Mark shows him at prayer alone, and the placing of all three is the sermon. Before dawn, at the height of his popularity in Capernaum (1:35). Here, on the night the nation tried to crown him. And in Gethsemane, on the night they came to arrest him (14:32–39). Success, and the offer of glory, and the approach of death — and he handles all three the same way.

Which quietly exposes something. Most of us pray hardest at the third kind of moment and hardly at all at the first two. Prosperity is treated as a season that requires no prayer, and it is the season in which men are most often lost.

And when evening came, the boat was out on the sea, and he was alone on the land.

Mark paints the picture and then leaves it there for a moment: a boat somewhere out in the dark, and a man by himself on the mountain.

They are separated, and they cannot see him. He is on the land, they are on the water, and night has come down between them.

Which is exactly what a hard stretch feels like from inside the boat — and the next verse says something about it that changes everything.

verseByVerse.quote: And he saw that they were making headway painfully, for the wind was against them. And about the fourth watch of the night he came to them, walking on the sea. He meant to pass by them,
verseByVerse.commentary:
And he saw that they were making headway painfully, for the wind was against them.

Take that clause apart slowly, because it may be the most comforting sentence in the chapter.

He saw them. It is the middle of the night. He is up a mountain, on shore, and they are out on the lake in the dark — three or four miles out, John says (John 6:19). Whatever kind of seeing this was, he was watching them the whole time.

They did not know that. From inside the boat there was nothing but wind, black water, and a horizon with nobody on it. Every fact available to them said they were alone.

Making headway painfully. The Greek is literally that they were tormented in the rowing — the same root as the word for torture. This is not a storm that threatens to sink them, as in chapter 4. It is worse in a particular way: hours of grinding, exhausting, unrewarded effort. They row and the shore does not get closer.

For the wind was against them. And that is the whole trouble in five words, and it is worth remembering that they are out there because he sent them. He compelled them into that boat. Obedience put them in the wind.

So here is the shape of a great deal of Christian experience, laid out in one verse. You are where he put you. You are pulling as hard as you can. Nothing is moving. He appears to be somewhere else entirely, and it is dark.

And the verse tells you the one thing you cannot possibly know from inside the boat: he is watching, and he was watching the whole night, and he was praying while he watched. Verse 46 has him on that mountain praying, and verse 48 has him seeing them from it. Those two facts belong together, and they are still true: he always lives to make intercession for them (Heb. 7:25).

And about the fourth watch of the night he came to them, walking on the sea.

The fourth watch is between three and six in the morning. Mark told us they set out in the evening. They have been at the oars for something like nine hours.

He came. Not at the first hour, when it started to get hard. Not at midnight. At three in the morning, when men have stopped talking and are simply pulling.

He is never early, in the way we would arrange it. He has never yet been late.

He meant to pass by them.

And now the strangest clause in the chapter, which sounds on a first reading as though he intended to leave them to it.

He did not. Passing by is the Old Testament's own language for God making himself visible. When Moses asked to see his glory, God put him in a cleft of the rock: while my glory passes by I will cover you with my hand (Ex. 33:22). When Elijah stood at the mouth of the cave: behold, the LORD passed by (1 Kgs. 19:11).

And most exactly of all, Job — describing the God whom no man can lay hold of — says that he alone stretched out the heavens and trampled the waves of the sea, and then, three verses later: behold, he passes by me, and I see him not (Job 9:8, 11).

Trampling the waves of the sea, and passing by, in the same passage, about God. Mark's readers knew that book.

So this is not a man taking a shortcut past a struggling boat. It is a self-disclosure. He came out to them in the dark, on the water, doing the thing that Job says God alone does — and he did it in the language of every theophany in their Bible.

He was not passing them by. He was passing before them, so that they could see who had been watching from the mountain.

verseByVerse.quote: but when they saw him walking on the sea they thought it was a ghost, and cried out, for they all saw him and were terrified. But immediately he spoke to them and said, "Take heart; it is I. Do not be afraid."
verseByVerse.commentary:
But when they saw him walking on the sea they thought it was a ghost, and cried out.

Of course they did.

It is between three and six in the morning. They have been rowing for hours into a headwind, they are wet, exhausted and frightened, and there is a figure moving on the surface of the water beside the boat.

Mark's word is phantasma — an apparition. In that world, a shape on the sea at night meant a portent of death, and every sailor on that lake would have grown up on such stories.

So the first thing to say about the disciples here is the fair thing. The Lord of glory came to them in the exact form of their worst fear, and they did not recognise him. Their instinct was not stupid; it was human. The one thing that could actually save them looked, in the dark, like the thing most likely to kill them.

That is worth holding on to, because it is often the case. God has a way of coming to his people wearing the shape of what they most dread. Job did not recognise mercy when it arrived in a whirlwind. Joseph's brothers did not recognise their salvation in the man who had them arrested. The thing bearing down on you out of the dark this year may be the Lord, and you will not necessarily know it at the time.

For they all saw him and were terrified.

All of them. Mark closes off any possibility that this was one man's imagination or a trick of the light on a wave. Twelve men, including four professional fishermen who had spent their lives on that water at night, all saw the same thing and all reacted the same way.

But immediately he spoke to them.

Immediately. The moment they cry out, he speaks — and notice what comes first. Not the calming of the wind. Not getting into the boat. His voice.

Before anything about their circumstances changes, he tells them who he is. That is the order in which he deals with frightened people, and it has not altered.

Take heart; it is I. Do not be afraid.

Three short phrases, and the middle one carries more than the English can hold.

It is I is egō eimi in the Greek — literally, I am. In everyday speech it is simply how you identify yourself in the dark: it's me. But these are also the words God gave Moses at the burning bush when Moses asked for his name — I am who I am (Ex. 3:14) — and they run all through Isaiah on the lips of God: I am he; before me no god was formed (Isa. 43:10).

And they are spoken here by a man standing on water in the middle of the night, having come out to them across a sea that the Scriptures say God alone tramples.

Take the whole sentence, then, in the order he gives it. Take heart — courage, now, before anything changes. It is I — and here is the reason, and the reason is not the weather but a Person, and the name he uses for himself is the name from the bush. Do not be afraid — which follows, and only follows, from the middle phrase.

There is no argument in it. He does not tell them the wind will drop, or that they will reach the shore, or that the night is nearly over. He tells them who is with them, and treats that as sufficient.

It is sufficient. That is the whole of Christian comfort in three phrases, and every one of them was spoken from the middle of the water they were afraid of.

verseByVerse.quote: And he got into the boat with them, and the wind ceased. And they were utterly astounded, for they did not understand about the loaves, but their hearts were hardened.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And he got into the boat with them, and the wind ceased.

He gets in. After nine hours of rowing and a night of terror, the ending is almost domestic: a man climbs over the side and sits down with them, and the wind stops.

Mark does not even say he rebuked it this time. It simply stops, because he is aboard.

And they were utterly astounded.

The word is enormous — beside themselves, out of their senses with amazement. It is the same reaction as in the room where the little girl got up (5:42).

And then Mark says something about his own leaders that no church would ever have invented.

For they did not understand about the loaves, but their hearts were hardened.

Read that twice. This is the verdict of the Gospel on the twelve apostles, written by a man who got his information from the chief of them, and circulated in the church while most of them were still alive.

They did not understand about the loaves. That is the connection Mark wants made, and it is not the one we would expect. He does not say they failed to understand the walking on water. He says the walking on water astonished them because they had not understood the loaves.

Which means the bread was the lesson. That afternoon they had carried food out of his hands to five thousand people and come back with twelve baskets each, and they had drawn no conclusion from it about who he was. Had they understood the loaves, a man on the water would not have been an inexplicable horror. It would have been the same Person doing the same kind of thing.

God's past dealings with us are meant to be evidence. The reason a new trouble knocks us flat is very often that we drew nothing from the last deliverance — we were relieved, and we were grateful for about a fortnight, and we filed it as something that happened rather than as something we learned about him.

But their hearts were hardened.

And here is the word that should stop anyone reading this comfortably. Mark uses of the Twelve the identical term he used in chapter 3 for the men in the synagogue who watched a withered hand restored and walked out to arrange a murder (3:5). The word is the one for a callus — soft tissue that has thickened at the point of injury until it cannot feel.

These are not enemies. They are the apostles, mid-mission, fresh from casting out demons in his name, and their hearts are described with the vocabulary of his opponents.

So hardness is not a disease of unbelievers only, and it does not announce itself. It is not disbelief; the Twelve believed a great deal. It is the slow loss of the capacity to be affected — the state in which the same truths arrive and produce nothing, in which a man can carry the bread and never taste it.

The only mercy is that Mark tells us this without despair, because we know what these men became. The hardening was real and it was not final. He kept them, taught them, corrected them, was betrayed and denied by them, and after the resurrection he fed them breakfast on a beach and sent them out — and the man whose memory this Gospel preserves was the one who had denied him three times.

He does not give up on hard-hearted disciples. He gets into the boat with them.

verseByVerse.quote: When they had crossed over, they came to land at Gennesaret and moored to the shore. And when they got out of the boat, the people immediately recognized him and ran about the whole region and began to bring the sick people on their beds to wherever they heard he was. And wherever he came, in villages, cities, or countryside, they laid the sick in the marketplaces and implored him that they might touch even the fringe of his garment. And as many as touched it were made well.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When they had crossed over, they came to land at Gennesaret and moored to the shore.

Gennesaret is the fertile plain on the north-west shore, a few miles of unusually rich farmland — Josephus was lyrical about it. They had been sent to Bethsaida (v. 45) and the night has put them down somewhere else entirely, which is what happens when you row against a wind for nine hours.

And when they got out of the boat, the people immediately recognized him.

No rest again. The boat touches the shore and it starts.

And ran about the whole region and began to bring the sick people on their beds to wherever they heard he was.

Now picture what Mark is describing, because it is one of the most remarkable pictures in the Gospel and it goes by in a sentence.

Word spreads across the plain, and people start carrying. Not helping the sick to walk — carrying them, on the pallets they lie on, in from the villages and the farms. And they are chasing a moving target: to wherever they heard he was. He is walking, so the beds are being carried from place to place after him, all day, by relays of neighbours and relatives.

Whole communities are mobilised and there is not a word about any of them wanting anything for themselves.

And wherever he came, in villages, cities, or countryside, they laid the sick in the marketplaces.

The marketplace is the open square where everything happened — the shops, the courts, the gossip, the day-labourers waiting for work. And the sick are being laid out in rows in the middle of it, in public, in the way of everybody.

These people have stopped caring how it looks. There is a certain kind of desperation that has burned through embarrassment entirely, and it is the only kind that ever gets anywhere with Christ.

And implored him that they might touch even the fringe of his garment.

The fringe is the tassel that every observant Jewish man wore at the corners of his outer cloak, commanded in Numbers 15:38–39 as a reminder of the commandments of the LORD.

And the request has a history in this Gospel, one chapter old. A woman with twelve years of bleeding had said to herself if I touch even his garments, I will be made well, and reached from behind in a crowd, and it worked (5:28). She had told nobody in advance and had hoped to slip away unnoticed — and Jesus stopped everything and drew her out and called her Daughter.

Now a whole province is doing what she did.

That is what one healed woman's story did when it got out, and it is worth noticing, because it is exactly what one healed madman's story did on the other side of the lake (5:20). Mark keeps showing you the same mechanism: somebody tells what happened to them, and a district comes.

And as many as touched it were made well.

All of them. Mark does not qualify it, and he does not tell us that anyone's theology was corrected first.

Their understanding was thin and probably half superstitious — as hers had been. He does not lecture them about the tassel. He heals them. And the Greek behind made well is sōzō, the word for saved, which Mark has been quietly using throughout these chapters for both kinds of rescue.

So the chapter that began with a village refusing him because they knew him too well ends with strangers running across a plain with beds. Nazareth had every advantage and would not stretch out a hand. Gennesaret had almost no understanding and grabbed the hem of his coat.

Between those two lies the whole difference — and it is not intelligence, and it is not opportunity, and it was never information. One town thought it already knew him. The other only knew it needed him.

6.theology:
Could he not, or would he not? Verse 5 should not be softened — Mark wrote he could do no mighty work there, where Matthew writes did not do many (Matt. 13:58). But the exception clause settles the sense: he healed a few sick people that afternoon, so it was no failure of power. The impossibility is moral. In a village that had already decided what he was, mighty works would have been spectacle, and he does not do spectacle — he refuses a sign to the Pharisees (8:11–12) and stands silent before Herod, who wanted to watch one (Luke 23:8–9). Faith is not a mechanism that generates miracles, as though God were a machine and belief the coin. It is the setting in which he ordinarily works, because he deals with persons. Unbelief does not disable God; it makes his help unwelcome, and he does not force it.

He meant to pass by them (v. 48) is not a shortcut past a struggling boat. Passing by is the Old Testament's own vocabulary for God making himself visible: while my glory passes by (Ex. 33:22), behold, the LORD passed by (1 Kgs. 19:11). Most exactly, Job says of God that he alone stretched out the heavens and trampled the waves of the sea, and three verses later, behold, he passes by me, and I see him not (Job 9:8, 11). Trampling the sea and passing by, in one passage, about God. And when they scream he answers with egō eimi — it is I, the ordinary words for identifying yourself in the dark, and the words from the burning bush (Ex. 3:14).

And their hearts were hardened (v. 52) is said of the apostles, in the very word used of the men in the synagogue who watched a hand restored and left to plan a murder (3:5). Hardness is not a disease of unbelievers only. It is not disbelief — the Twelve believed a great deal. It is the slow loss of the capacity to be affected, the state in which a man can carry the bread and never taste it.
6.examples:
Herod is the most searching portrait in the chapter, because he is not a scoffer. He feared John, knew he was a righteous and holy man, protected him from a wife who wanted him dead, was greatly perplexed by his preaching — and heard him gladly. He sent for him. He came back for more. He is the rocky ground of chapter 4 given a name and a palace: real interest, real feeling, real pleasure, and no root.

Everything was there except the one thing John was actually asking for. Herodias stayed. And a man who will not repent must eventually silence the voice that keeps asking him to — it took only a party, a dance and an audience to finish what had been decided long before.

Then: a king who kept his oath and killed a prophet, because of his oaths and his guests. Not conscience — he had already lost that argument. He could not bear to look foolish in front of people whose opinion he had spent his life courting.

Now: almost nobody does the worst thing they ever do because they wanted to. They do it because backing out in front of the people watching was unthinkable — the joke laughed at, the thing gone along with once the room had turned, the stand not taken because of who would have seen. Peter is eight chapters from exactly this, in a courtyard, in front of a servant girl. The fear of man lays a snare (Prov. 29:25), and it walked a king with an army into a murder he did not want to commit.

So the test is not whether you enjoy good preaching. Herod did. It is whether you can name one thing it has actually cost you this year.

7.title: What Really Defiles a Man
7.text: <sup>1</sup>Now when the Pharisees gathered to him, with some of the scribes who had come from Jerusalem, <sup>2</sup>they saw that some of his disciples ate with hands that were defiled, that is, unwashed. <sup>3</sup>(For the Pharisees and all the Jews do not eat unless they wash their hands properly, holding to the tradition of the elders, <sup>4</sup>and when they come from the marketplace, they do not eat unless they wash. And there are many other traditions that they observe, such as the washing of cups and pots and copper vessels and dining couches.) <sup>5</sup>And the Pharisees and the scribes asked him, “Why do your disciples not walk according to the tradition of the elders, but eat with defiled hands?” <sup>6</sup>And he said to them, “Well did Isaiah prophesy of you hypocrites, as it is written, ‘This people honors me with their lips, but their heart is far from me; <sup>7</sup>in vain do they worship me, teaching as doctrines the commandments of men.’ <sup>8</sup>You leave the commandment of God and hold to the tradition of men.” <sup>9</sup>And he said to them, “You have a fine way of rejecting the commandment of God in order to establish your tradition! <sup>10</sup>For Moses said, ‘Honor your father and your mother’; and, ‘Whoever reviles father or mother must surely die.’ <sup>11</sup>But you say, ‘If a man tells his father or his mother, “Whatever you would have gained from me is Corban”’ (that is, given to God)— <sup>12</sup>then you no longer permit him to do anything for his father or mother, <sup>13</sup>thus making void the word of God by your tradition that you have handed down. And many such things you do.” <sup>14</sup>And he called the people to him again and said to them, “Hear me, all of you, and understand: <sup>15</sup>There is nothing outside a person that by going into him can defile him, but the things that come out of a person are what defile him.” <sup>17</sup>And when he had entered the house and left the people, his disciples asked him about the parable. <sup>18</sup>And he said to them, “Then are you also without understanding? Do you not see that whatever goes into a person from outside cannot defile him, <sup>19</sup>since it enters not his heart but his stomach, and is expelled?” (Thus he declared all foods clean.) <sup>20</sup>And he said, “What comes out of a person is what defiles him. <sup>21</sup>For from within, out of the heart of man, come evil thoughts, sexual immorality, theft, murder, adultery, <sup>22</sup>coveting, wickedness, deceit, sensuality, envy, slander, pride, foolishness. <sup>23</sup>All these evil things come from within, and they defile a person.” <sup>24</sup>And from there he arose and went away to the region of Tyre and Sidon. And he entered a house and did not want anyone to know, yet he could not be hidden. <sup>25</sup>But immediately a woman whose little daughter had an unclean spirit heard of him and came and fell down at his feet. <sup>26</sup>Now the woman was a Gentile, a Syrophoenician by birth. And she begged him to cast the demon out of her daughter. <sup>27</sup>And he said to her, “Let the children be fed first, for it is not right to take the children’s bread and throw it to the dogs.” <sup>28</sup>But she answered him, “Yes, Lord; yet even the dogs under the table eat the children’s crumbs.” <sup>29</sup>And he said to her, “For this statement you may go your way; the demon has left your daughter.” <sup>30</sup>And she went home and found the child lying in bed and the demon gone. <sup>31</sup>Then he returned from the region of Tyre and went through Sidon to the Sea of Galilee, in the region of the Decapolis. <sup>32</sup>And they brought to him a man who was deaf and had a speech impediment, and they begged him to lay his hand on him. <sup>33</sup>And taking him aside from the crowd privately, he put his fingers into his ears, and after spitting touched his tongue. <sup>34</sup>And looking up to heaven, he sighed and said to him, “Ephphatha,” that is, “Be opened.” <sup>35</sup>And his ears were opened, his tongue was released, and he spoke plainly. <sup>36</sup>And Jesus charged them to tell no one. But the more he charged them, the more zealously they proclaimed it. <sup>37</sup>And they were astonished beyond measure, saying, “He has done all things well. He even makes the deaf hear and the mute speak.”
7.overview:
Chapter 7 takes down a wall, and then walks through the gap.

It opens with a delegation from Jerusalem who have travelled ninety miles to raise the matter of unwashed hands. Jesus does not defend his disciples; he quotes Isaiah at the delegation, and then proves the charge with a single devastating example. Corban was a vow that could put a man's money beyond his parents' reach by declaring it dedicated to God — and the tradition would not merely permit it but forbid him to change his mind. A rule invented to honour God had become a device for robbing your father, with a straight face and in God's name.

Then he calls the crowd over and says the thing that changed everything: there is nothing outside a person that by going into him can defile him. Mark, writing down Peter's preaching years later, adds four words in a bracket — thus he declared all foods clean — and the boundary between clean and unclean peoples, kept for fifteen centuries, is gone.

And having dissolved it, he crosses it. The second half of the chapter is two healings on Gentile ground: a Phoenician mother who takes his own hard word and finds the door in it, and a deaf man in the Decapolis brought by friends, taken quietly aside, and given his hearing with one Aramaic word. The crowd's verdict is bigger than they know — he has done all things well is the sentence pronounced over the finished creation.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–23 — Tradition, the Word of God, and the Human Heart
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The complaint (vv. 1–5). A delegation arrives from Jerusalem — the second one in this Gospel — and what they have come ninety miles to raise is that the disciples do not wash their hands before eating. Mark stops to explain the custom, which tells you he is writing for people who have never heard of it.

The answer (vv. 6–8). Jesus does not defend his men. He quotes Isaiah at the delegation and calls them hypocrites: lips near, heart far, and human rules taught as though God had given them.

The example (vv. 9–13). Then he makes it concrete with a case anyone can follow. A man could put the money owed to his aged parents beyond their reach by pronouncing one word over it — and the tradition would back him. That is not a lapse in the system. That is the system working.

The principle (vv. 14–23). He calls the crowd over and says the most subversive thing in the chapter: nothing that goes into a man can defile him. Mark, writing years later with Peter's memory in his hand, adds a parenthesis that changed the church — thus he declared all foods clean — and then Jesus tells the disciples in private where defilement actually comes from, and lists twelve of them.
verseByVerse.theology:
Why does your Bible skip verse 16? Look down the page and the numbers run 15, 17. Nothing has been lost and nothing has been hidden.

The oldest and best manuscripts of Mark do not have a verse 16. Later copies add the familiar refrain if anyone has ears to hear, let him hear — a sentence Jesus certainly said, and which Mark records elsewhere (4:9, 4:23). What almost certainly happened is that a scribe, copying by hand, felt the sentence belonged after v. 15 and wrote it in the margin, and a later copyist took the margin note for part of the text.

The verse numbering itself is not ancient — it was added in the sixteenth century, long after the manuscripts. So when translators went back to the earliest copies and found the sentence absent, they could not renumber the whole New Testament; they simply left the number empty and put the words in a footnote.

That is worth a plain word of reassurance to any reader who finds a gap like this unsettling. Nothing has been taken out of your Bible. The opposite has happened: we now have older and better copies than were available in 1611, and where those copies show that a sentence crept in later, honest translators tell you so in the margin rather than quietly leaving it in. A faith that will not look at its own manuscripts has something to hide. This one publishes the workings.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Corban — a rule invented to honour God, turned into a device for robbing your parents, with a straight face and in God's name.

Now: the shape survives perfectly, and it is almost never dishonest. It is the man so committed at church that his mother has not had a visit in four months. It is the giving that goes to the building fund while a brother in the same congregation cannot pay his heating bill. It is any arrangement in which something genuinely religious has been placed in front of a plain duty God commanded, so that the duty can be quietly dropped without anybody feeling wicked.

So here is a test you can actually run, and it is the one this passage supplies. Take any tradition you hold — a practice, a standard, a way of doing things — and ask whether keeping it is currently costing somebody else something God told you to give them. Not whether it is in the Bible; a good many decent traditions are not, and need not be. Whether it has begun to displace a commandment.

Jesus does not attack tradition as such. He attacks tradition that has been promoted — set level with Scripture, and then used against it.

verseByVerse.quote: Now when the Pharisees gathered to him, with some of the scribes who had come from Jerusalem, they saw that some of his disciples ate with hands that were defiled, that is, unwashed.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now when the Pharisees gathered to him, with some of the scribes who had come from Jerusalem.

This is the second delegation from the capital in this Gospel. The first came in chapter 3 and concluded that he was possessed by the prince of demons (3:22). These men have made the same journey — ninety miles, four or five days on the road — and they are not here to learn.

Note the word gathered. They collect around him, the way a committee collects.

They saw that some of his disciples ate with hands that were defiled, that is, unwashed.

And this is what they came for.
