Sit with the disproportion for a moment, because it is the point of the whole passage. Trained theologians have travelled from Jerusalem to Galilee, at real expense, and what they have found and what they will raise is that some of the men in this group did not rinse their hands before a meal.

They are standing in front of a man who has cleansed a leper, raised a dead girl, fed a district on five loaves, and stilled a storm. They have taken notes on his catering.

Two things need saying so that we are fair to them, and then one thing that is not fair to them at all.

First, this is not about hygiene. Mark says defiled and then explains it means unwashed, and the word he uses is koinos — common, profane, the opposite of holy. Nobody is worried about germs. This is about ritual purity.

Second, their intention was honourable. The Law required priests to wash before handling holy things (Ex. 30:19–21). The Pharisees, wanting the whole nation to be what God had called it — a kingdom of priests and a holy nation (Ex. 19:6) — extended the priestly rule to every Jew and every meal. Every table becomes an altar. Every family becomes a priesthood. As an idea it is not contemptible; it is devout.

And here is what is not fair. God never asked for it. The washing of hands before ordinary food is nowhere in the Law of Moses. It was a good idea that men had, and by this point it had hardened into an obligation with the force of a commandment — and men were being judged by it.

Which is how this always happens, and it is worth naming carefully because it is not a first-century disease. Nobody sets out to replace Scripture. A wise practice is adopted for good reasons. In a generation it is the way we do things. In two it is the way serious Christians do things. In three, a man who does not do it is regarded as unsound, and nobody can any longer say which chapter and verse required it.

The Pharisees did not steal the Bible. They buried it under good ideas.

verseByVerse.quote: (For the Pharisees and all the Jews do not eat unless they wash their hands properly, holding to the tradition of the elders, and when they come from the marketplace, they do not eat unless they wash. And there are many other traditions that they observe, such as the washing of cups and pots and copper vessels and dining couches.) And the Pharisees and the scribes asked him, "Why do your disciples not walk according to the tradition of the elders, but eat with defiled hands?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
For the Pharisees and all the Jews do not eat unless they wash their hands properly, holding to the tradition of the elders.

Mark stops the narrative and explains the custom, in a bracket, for two whole verses.

That is worth noticing before anything else, because it tells you who this Gospel was written for. A Jewish reader would need none of this; it would be like explaining to an Englishman what a kettle is. Mark is writing for Gentiles — almost certainly for the church in Rome — and he keeps doing this: translating Aramaic phrases, converting money into Roman coinage, using Latin loan-words. The oldest Gospel we have was written for people outside the covenant, and that fact is quietly relevant to a chapter that ends with a Gentile woman and a Gentile deaf man.

The tradition of the elders. Here is the thing being defended, and it needs a proper introduction because everything in the passage turns on it.

Alongside the written Law, Israel had developed an enormous body of oral interpretation — rulings on what the commandments meant in practice, handed down from teacher to teacher over centuries. It was eventually written down around AD 200 as the Mishnah, and it runs to a substantial book. There is a whole tractate on hand-washing. It specifies the quantity of water, the position of the hands, the number of rinses.

And the Pharisees held — this is the crucial point — that this oral tradition had itself been given to Moses at Sinai alongside the written Law, and carried equal authority.

That is the claim Jesus is about to deny flatly.

Such as the washing of cups and pots and copper vessels and dining couches. Mark's list is faintly comic and probably meant to be. Cups. Pots. Bronze vessels. The furniture you eat on. There were rules for all of it, and men had spent their lives mastering them.

And the Pharisees and the scribes asked him, Why do your disciples not walk according to the tradition of the elders, but eat with defiled hands?

Now look hard at how they frame the question, because the framing gives the whole game away.

They do not ask why the disciples break the Law of God. They ask why they do not walk according to the tradition of the elders. They know exactly which authority is being contravened, and they name it accurately — and they are perfectly confident that it settles the matter.

That is the position of a man who has stopped being able to feel the difference between what God said and what his tradition says God meant. He would tell you, sincerely, that he holds Scripture supreme. And when a real question arises, the answer he reaches for is the tradition, because that is where the practical authority has quietly migrated.

It is worth asking, without cynicism, where the practical authority sits in your own convictions. When you are challenged about something you believe a Christian should or should not do, what do you reach for first — the text, or the settled instinct of the people you were formed by? The second is not always wrong. But a man who cannot tell which one he is using has already made the Pharisees' mistake.

verseByVerse.quote: And he said to them, "Well did Isaiah prophesy of you hypocrites, as it is written, 'This people honors me with their lips, but their heart is far from me; in vain do they worship me, teaching as doctrines the commandments of men.' You leave the commandment of God and hold to the tradition of men."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Well did Isaiah prophesy of you hypocrites.

He does not answer the question. He does not defend the disciples, explain the circumstances, or concede that the men might have washed. He goes straight past the complaint to the men making it, and he opens with a quotation from the prophet they revered.

Hypocrites. The word is from the Greek theatre and originally meant an actor — a man wearing a mask, speaking lines. It does not necessarily mean conscious pretence, and it is important to see that, because otherwise the charge slides off us. Jesus is not merely saying they are lying. He is saying there is a gap between the performance and the person, and that the performance has taken over.

This people honors me with their lips, but their heart is far from me.

The quotation is Isaiah 29:13, and it was spoken to a generation that was scrupulously religious. That is what makes it lethal. Isaiah was not addressing idolaters who had abandoned the temple; he was addressing men who were keeping it all up.

And the diagnosis is a measurement of distance. The lips are close. The heart is far. Both parts of that are true at once, and the first is what makes the second so hard to detect.

Because how would you know? That is the honest question, and it deserves a concrete answer rather than a shudder.

Here is one test. What happens to your religion when nobody is watching? The lips are, by definition, the public part. Prayer that only happens in company, a Bible opened only where somebody might see, generosity that is known about — none of these are wrong, and all of them can be maintained by a heart that has quietly gone somewhere else. Subtract the audience and see what is left standing.

Here is another. When did you last enjoy God? Not enjoy a service, or a sermon, or the company of Christians. Him. A heart that is far off can keep every observance and has usually stopped finding any pleasure in the Person the observances are about, and has stopped noticing that it stopped.

In vain do they worship me, teaching as doctrines the commandments of men.

In vain — emptily, to no purpose. This is worship that happens, and is offered to the right God, and achieves nothing. That should sober anyone who assumes that attendance is the same as acceptance.

And the reason given is precise: teaching as doctrines the commandments of men. Not having human customs — every church on earth has those, and must. Teaching them as though they came from God.

You leave the commandment of God and hold to the tradition of men.

And here is the summary, and the two verbs are worth setting side by side. They leave — abandon, let go of — one thing, and hold — grip, cling to — the other. It is a picture of a man with both hands full who has to drop something to pick up something else.

Nobody in that delegation thought of himself as abandoning the commandment of God. Every one of them would have said he was defending it. That is precisely why Jesus has to prove it, and in the next five verses he does, with a single devastating example.

verseByVerse.quote: And he said to them, "You have a fine way of rejecting the commandment of God in order to establish your tradition! For Moses said, 'Honor your father and your mother'; and, 'Whoever reviles father or mother must surely die.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
You have a fine way of rejecting the commandment of God in order to establish your tradition!

The sarcasm is unmistakable, and it is one of the few places in the Gospels where you can hear Jesus being witheringly ironic. You have a fine way — beautifully done, expertly managed. It is the tone of a man watching a skilled piece of work he despises.

And note the direction of the sentence. He is not saying they neglect the commandment while pursuing their tradition. He says they reject the commandment in order to establish the tradition. The setting aside is not a side effect. It is the mechanism.

Now he proves it, and he chooses his ground with great care.

For Moses said, Honor your father and your mother.

He goes to the Ten Commandments — not to an obscure regulation but to the fifth word of the Decalogue, written by the finger of God, the first commandment with a promise attached (Ex. 20:12; Deut. 5:16). Nobody in that delegation could plead ignorance or claim it was disputed.

And he takes the commandment in its plain, practical sense, which is worth pausing on because we have sentimentalised it. Honour your father and mother is not primarily about the manners of small children. In that world it was chiefly an economic obligation, and everyone understood it as such. There were no pensions and no state provision. Ageing parents were kept alive by their sons. To honour your father meant to feed him when he could no longer work.

And, Whoever reviles father or mother must surely die.

He adds a second text, from Exodus 21:17, and it raises the stakes considerably. Under the Law, treating your parents with contempt was a capital matter. That is how seriously God took this.

So Jesus has now put down two immovable stones. God commanded the care of parents. God attached the severest possible sanction to its contempt.

And in the next verse he will show the delegation from Jerusalem a legal device, taught by their own school, that let a man walk away from both — and feel devout while doing it.

Before that, one thing worth carrying. Jesus's chosen example of what real obedience to God looks like is not a spiritual exercise. It is a middle-aged man paying his mother's bills. When he wants a case that everybody can measure, he does not reach for prayer or fasting or the temple. He reaches for whether the old people in your family are being looked after — which is exactly where the New Testament keeps landing when it wants to test a religion. Religion that is pure and undefiled before God the Father is this: to visit orphans and widows in their affliction (Jas. 1:27). If anyone does not provide for his relatives, and especially for members of his household, he has denied the faith and is worse than an unbeliever (1 Tim. 5:8).

verseByVerse.quote: But you say, 'If a man tells his father or his mother, "Whatever you would have gained from me is Corban"' (that is, given to God)— then you no longer permit him to do anything for his father or mother, thus making void the word of God by your tradition that you have handed down. And many such things you do."
verseByVerse.commentary:
But you say. Two words, and they carry the whole indictment. God said one thing; you say another. Jesus sets the two speakers side by side and lets the room hear it.

If a man tells his father or his mother, Whatever you would have gained from me is Corban.

Mark leaves the word untranslated and then glosses it, which means it was a technical term his readers would not know. And the mechanism, once you see it, is breathtaking.

To pronounce something Corban was to declare it dedicated to God — set apart, as though laid on the altar, no longer available for ordinary use. The scribes taught that such a vow was binding and could not be revoked; a man's word to God outranked everything.

Now watch how it was worked.

A man has ageing parents. The fifth commandment obliges him to support them, and everyone knows it — the money he owes their care is a real, visible, calculable sum. He does not want to part with it, and he cannot simply refuse without disgrace.

So he looks at his parents and says the word. Whatever you would have gained from me is Corban. Dedicated to God.

And now his hands are tied by piety. The money is holy. He cannot spend it on his father, because it belongs to God, and a vow may not be broken. The tradition itself has fastened the handcuffs on him, and everyone will agree that his hands are tied.

Then you no longer permit him to do anything for his father or mother.

And here is the sting Jesus puts on it: the tradition does not merely allow this. It forbids him to change his mind. Having sworn, he is not permitted to go back and help them even if he wants to. The system has made repentance illegal.

And in practice — this is the part that turns a legal curiosity into a scandal — the money very often never reached the temple at all. The vow made it unavailable to his parents; it did not necessarily make it unavailable to him. He kept the use of it, shielded from his duty by a holy-sounding word.

So an old man goes hungry, and his son is regarded as a devout person, and the machinery of religion has been used to produce exactly the outcome that God's commandment existed to prevent.

Thus making void the word of God by your tradition that you have handed down.

Making void — cancelling, depriving of authority. The word is used of annulling a will.

And Jesus adds a sentence that should stop anyone who thinks this is a single embarrassing loophole: And many such things you do. Corban is not the disease. It is one symptom he happens to have picked up, because it was the clearest.

So take the test this passage actually supplies, and take it in its modern clothes, because the shape has survived perfectly and it is almost never dishonest.

It is the man so committed at church four nights a week that his mother has not had a visit since March. It is the money given to a fund while a brother in the same congregation cannot pay his heating bill. It is any arrangement in which something genuinely religious has been set in front of a plain duty God commanded, so that the duty can be quietly dropped without anybody feeling wicked.

Ask it of yourself in one sentence: is anything I do for God currently costing somebody else something God told me to give them? That is Corban, whatever it is called, and there is no version of it that God accepts.

verseByVerse.quote: And he called the people to him again and said to them, "Hear me, all of you, and understand: There is nothing outside a person that by going into him can defile him, but the things that come out of a person are what defile him."
verseByVerse.commentary:
And he called the people to him again.

Notice the change of audience. He has been talking to a delegation of scholars from Jerusalem. Now he turns away from them, raises his voice, and calls the crowd over — the ordinary people who have been standing at the edge of the argument.

He is about to say something the experts will not like, and he says it to everybody. This is deliberately public.

Hear me, all of you, and understand. Both verbs are commands, and the second one is doing real work. He is not asking for attention; he is asking them to think. What follows is compressed enough to need it.

There is nothing outside a person that by going into him can defile him, but the things that come out of a person are what defile him.

Read that slowly, and then read it as a Jew standing in that crowd would have heard it, because we are so far from the world it detonated in that we hardly feel the blast.

Their entire national life was organised around the distinction he has just erased. Leviticus 11 lists at length what may and may not be eaten. Pork, shellfish, rabbit, camel, birds of prey — unclean. Contact with a corpse, a leper, a discharge — unclean. It ran through every meal, every kitchen, every market transaction, every relationship with a Gentile neighbour. It was not a dietary preference; it was the boundary marker of the people of God, and men had died in the Maccabean persecution rather than eat pork.

And he says: nothing that goes into a man from outside can defile him.

That is either an outrage or it is the arrival of the thing the whole system was pointing to. There is no third option, which is presumably why he told them to understand.

Here is what makes it the second. The food laws had always been a picture — a daily, physical, unavoidable lesson in the difference between clean and unclean, drummed into a nation three times a day for fifteen centuries so that they would know in their bones that holiness matters and that not everything is acceptable to God. A picture is not abolished when the thing it pictured arrives. It is fulfilled, and put away.

What the picture was teaching, all along, is that there is such a thing as defilement — and he is about to tell them where it actually lives.

A word about the verse your Bible does not have. Look down the page and the numbers run 15, then 17. Nothing has gone missing, and it is worth a plain explanation.

The oldest and best manuscripts of Mark have no verse 16. Later copies add the familiar refrain if anyone has ears to hear, let him hear — a sentence Jesus certainly said, and which Mark records twice elsewhere (4:9, 4:23). What almost certainly happened is that a scribe felt it belonged here and wrote it in the margin, and a later copyist mistook the margin note for the text.

The verse numbers themselves are not ancient; they were added in the sixteenth century, long after the manuscripts. So when translators went back to the earliest copies and found the sentence absent, they could not renumber the entire New Testament — they left the number empty and put the words in a footnote.

So nothing has been removed from your Bible. The reverse has happened: we have older and better copies than were available four hundred years ago, and where those copies show that a sentence crept in later, honest translators tell you in the margin instead of quietly leaving it in. A faith that would not let you see its own manuscripts would have something to hide. This one prints the workings at the bottom of the page.

verseByVerse.quote: And when he had entered the house and left the people, his disciples asked him about the parable. And he said to them, "Then are you also without understanding? Do you not see that whatever goes into a person from outside cannot defile him, since it enters not his heart but his stomach, and is expelled?" (Thus he declared all foods clean.)
verseByVerse.commentary:
And when he had entered the house and left the people, his disciples asked him about the parable.

The pattern of chapter 4 again: public saying, private explanation, and the men who get the explanation are the ones who stayed and asked.

They call it a parable, which tells you they knew something large had been said and had no idea what.

Then are you also without understanding? There is a weariness in it. He has been at this a while, and these are the men who have watched everything.

But note that he answers. The rebuke and the explanation come in the same breath, as they did in chapter 4 (4:13). He does not withhold teaching from slow disciples; he sighs, and teaches them.

Do you not see that whatever goes into a person from outside cannot defile him, since it enters not his heart but his stomach, and is expelled?

The argument is almost crude, and deliberately so. Food does not travel to the soul. It goes to the stomach, does its work, and leaves the body. Whatever route moral corruption takes into a man, it is not that one.

He is drawing a distinction the whole system had blurred: between ceremonial uncleanness, which was about ritual standing, and moral defilement, which is about what a man actually is. The Pharisees had spent so long on the first that they had come to treat it as the second — and had ended up, as the last paragraph showed, ceremonially spotless and robbing their parents.

(Thus he declared all foods clean.)

And here is one of the most consequential parentheses in the Bible, and it is worth being clear about who is speaking.

That is not Jesus's sentence. It is Mark's, added as he wrote — an inspired comment drawing out what the saying meant. And Mark, by every early account, is writing down the preaching of Peter.

Which makes this a small, quiet confession, and once you see it you cannot unsee it.

Peter was in that house. He heard this explanation with his own ears, in a private room, from the Lord himself. And years later, on a rooftop in Joppa, God let down a sheet full of unclean animals and told him to kill and eat — and Peter said By no means, Lord; for I have never eaten anything that is common or unclean. It had to be done three times before he would take it in (Acts 10:9–16). Then he went to a Gentile's house, and was hauled before the Jerusalem church to explain himself, and years after that Paul had to rebuke him publicly at Antioch for pulling back from Gentile tables (Gal. 2:11–14).

So the parenthesis in verse 19 is the note of a man who has finally understood something he was told to his face a long time before.

Take the comfort in that, because you probably need it. It is entirely possible to be taught a truth clearly, by Christ himself, in Scripture, and to go on for years without it having landed — and then to have it land, at last, in a way that reorganises everything. That is not a sign that you were never taught. It is what learning actually looks like in creatures like us. Peter needed the sermon, a vision, a Gentile household, a church council and a public rebuke, and he got there.

And note what this verse cost him to write. He is the one who tells us, in his own Gospel, that he had been told all along.

verseByVerse.quote: And he said, "What comes out of a person is what defiles him. For from within, out of the heart of man, come evil thoughts, sexual immorality, theft, murder, adultery, coveting, wickedness, deceit, sensuality, envy, slander, pride, foolishness. All these evil things come from within, and they defile a person."
verseByVerse.commentary:
What comes out of a person is what defiles him. He states the positive side, and then does something he rarely does: he makes a list.

For from within, out of the heart of man.

Fix the location before the list, because the location is the doctrine. Not from his circumstances. Not from his upbringing, his company, his poverty, his culture, or the food on his plate. From within — and the heart, in the Bible, is not the seat of the emotions but the control room of the person: what you love, choose, decide and are.

Then twelve items, and it repays reading them one at a time rather than letting them blur.

Evil thoughts — first, and rightly, because everything after it starts here. Sexual immorality — porneia, the whole range. Theft. Murder. Adultery. Three commandments from the second table, named flatly. Coveting — literally the desire to have more, the engine under a great deal of the rest. Wickedness. Deceit — the word for a baited trap. Sensuality — a word meaning shamelessness, the loss of the capacity to be embarrassed. Envy — Mark's phrase is literally an evil eye, the look you give what belongs to someone else. Slander. Pride. Foolishness — moral senselessness, the state of a man who has stopped thinking straight about God.

Notice the mixture. Murder sits in a list with envy; adultery next to pride; theft beside foolishness. We would have graded them. Jesus does not, because he is not ranking behaviours by their social damage. He is naming what comes out of one source.

All these evil things come from within, and they defile a person.

Now put that against the way our own culture talks, because the collision is total and it is worth stating plainly.

The modern account of human trouble is almost entirely external. People go wrong because of what was done to them, because of what surrounds them, because of systems and pressures and pasts. Some of that is true and Scripture never denies it — the Bible is fierce about oppression and tender about wounds. But the modern remedy follows from the modern diagnosis: change the environment, remove the influences, and what is underneath will come right.

And the counsel that follows is the one you will hear anywhere: trust yourself. Follow your heart.

Jesus says the heart is where it comes from.

Which is either the most pessimistic sentence in the chapter or the most hopeful, depending entirely on what comes next — because a diagnosis is not a verdict, and this one is the reason the gospel exists.

Here is the test, and it is uncomfortable but it is honest. Look at the twelve and find the ones you would have quietly excluded from your own account of yourself. Most of us can manage the first three from a distance. Try coveting. Try envy — the evil eye, the small drop in your stomach when a colleague does well. Try slander, which does not require a lie, only a true thing said to lower someone. Try pride.

If those are in you — and they are — then they did not come in from outside, and no adjustment of your circumstances will remove them, and no washing of hands will touch them.

So what is the remedy? Not a better system, and not a stricter one. God promised the only one that reaches this far, and he promised it centuries before: I will give you a new heart, and a new spirit I will put within you; I will remove the heart of stone from your flesh and give you a heart of flesh (Ezek. 36:26).

That is what the man in front of them had come to do. He is not offering to clean the outside of the cup. He is offering to make the man new — and he will do it by being defiled himself, made sin for us who knew no sin (2 Cor. 5:21), so that what comes out of a human heart can finally be something other than this list.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 24–37 — Two Healings Beyond Israel’s Borders
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Tyre (vv. 24–30). Having just dismantled the boundary between clean and unclean, Jesus walks across it. He goes north into pagan Phoenicia, tries to stay hidden, and fails within hours — because a woman with a demonised daughter has heard he is there. What passes between them is the hardest exchange in the Gospel and one of the greatest lessons in prayer anywhere in Scripture.

The Decapolis (vv. 31–37). Then a long looping journey back down the eastern side of the lake — through Gentile country the whole way — and a man is brought to him who is deaf and can barely speak. Jesus takes him away from the crowd, uses touch instead of words because touch is the only language the man can receive, looks up, groans, and says one word.

The two halves belong together and the order is not accidental. The teaching cleared the ground: nothing outside a man defiles him. The healings show what that means in practice — a Phoenician mother and a Gentile deaf man, both of them outside every boundary Israel had, both of them served.

And the crowd's verdict at the end is bigger than they know: he has done all things well.
verseByVerse.theology:
Was Jesus being cruel to the Syrophoenician woman? It is the first question any honest reader asks, and it deserves a straight answer rather than an embarrassed one.

Three things take the sting out without softening the difficulty. The word first (v. 27) is the hinge: let the children be fed first. That is not a refusal; it is an order of service, and it implies a second course. Paul states the same order without apology — to the Jew first and also to the Greek (Rom. 1:16). The word for dogs is a diminutive, and the picture is domestic: not the scavengers of the street but the household pets under the table while the family eats. They are inside the house. And the outcome is the loudest commentary of all — he grants what she asks, immediately, at a distance, and Matthew records him saying O woman, great is your faith! (Matt. 15:28).

He was not insulting her. He was handing her a picture with a door in it, to see whether she would find the door. She did, in one sentence, and it is the only exchange in the Gospels where someone answers Jesus back and he says they are right.

And the deaf man's healing is the new creation beginning. The crowd's he has done all things well is Genesis 1:31 in Greek — God saw everything he had made, and it was very good. And he even makes the deaf hear and the mute speak is Isaiah's sign of the age of the Messiah: then the ears of the deaf shall be unstopped... and the tongue of the mute sing for joy (Isa. 35:5–6). They meant only that this healer was impressive. They were quoting the first page of the Bible and the promise of the last days in the same breath.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: a man who could not hear, brought by friends who could — because he could not hear the news, could not ask, and could not have explained what he needed.

Now: every person who is carried to Christ by somebody else. It is the four on the roof in chapter 2 all over again, and it is worth noticing how often in this Gospel the person healed did not get there under their own power.

And look at how he handles him. He takes him aside from the crowd privately. A deaf man in a jostling crowd is a man being stared at and unable to follow a word of it. Jesus removes him from the audience before he touches him — which is a rebuke to every way of helping people that requires the helped to be visible.

Then he uses touch, because touch is the only language the man has: fingers into the ears, saliva on the tongue, a look up to heaven to say where this is coming from. It is not a ritual; it is a conversation conducted in the only vocabulary available. He tells the man what is about to happen to him in signs he can read.

And he sighed. The word is a groan. Standing in front of one ruined pair of ears, the Creator groans — the same groan Paul says the whole creation is making, and we with it, waiting for redemption (Rom. 8:22–23). He is not indifferent to what has been done to his world. He feels it, in the body he took, over one man nobody has named.

verseByVerse.quote: And from there he arose and went away to the region of Tyre and Sidon. And he entered a house and did not want anyone to know, yet he could not be hidden. But immediately a woman whose little daughter had an unclean spirit heard of him and came and fell down at his feet. Now the woman was a Gentile, a Syrophoenician by birth. And she begged him to cast the demon out of her daughter.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And from there he arose and went away to the region of Tyre and Sidon.

He leaves Israel. Tyre is a Phoenician port on the Mediterranean coast, thirty-odd miles north-west of Galilee, and it is thoroughly pagan territory — the country of Jezebel's father (1 Kgs. 16:31), a city the prophets denounced (Isa. 23; Ezek. 26–28), a place a devout Jew would not go without a reason.

And the placing is deliberate. He has just said that nothing outside a man can defile him, and Mark has told us what that meant. Now he walks straight over the boundary he has dissolved.

And he entered a house and did not want anyone to know.

He is trying to disappear. That is what this trip is for — the rest that never happened in chapter 6, attempted again by leaving the country. He wants a house, a door, and nobody knowing where he is.

Yet he could not be hidden.

Four words, and they have a double bottom. On the surface: his reputation has crossed the border ahead of him, and even in Phoenicia people know. Underneath: it is simply not possible for this Person to be concealed. Whatever room he enters, he is what he is.

But immediately a woman whose little daughter had an unclean spirit heard of him and came and fell down at his feet.

Mark gives us the child first — little daughter, the same tender diminutive Jairus used (5:23) — and then the mother at his feet.

Consider what she has already had to overcome to be lying on that floor. She is a woman, approaching a male Jewish teacher, uninvited, in a private house, on behalf of a child who is not present. Every social convention in the region is against it. And she has a daughter at home with an unclean spirit, which means she has already tried everything Tyre had to offer.

Now the woman was a Gentile, a Syrophoenician by birth.

Mark makes sure we know exactly what she is, and it is three distances at once. A Gentile — literally a Greek, meaning Greek in language and culture. Syrophoenician — a Phoenician of the Syrian province, to distinguish her from the Phoenicians of North Africa. Matthew calls her a Canaanite (Matt. 15:22), reaching for the ancient word, the name of the peoples Israel was commanded to drive out of the land.

So: not Jewish by blood, not Jewish by religion, not Jewish by language, and descended from the nations under the ban. There is no category of outsider she does not occupy.

And she begged him to cast the demon out of her daughter. The tense is continuous — she kept on asking. Matthew records the disciples' reaction, which is entirely in character: send her away, for she is crying out after us (Matt. 15:23).

And into that scene — a foreign woman on the floor of a borrowed house, asking repeatedly for a child she has left at home — comes the hardest sentence Jesus speaks to anyone in this Gospel.

verseByVerse.quote: And he said to her, "Let the children be fed first, for it is not right to take the children's bread and throw it to the dogs."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Let the children be fed first, for it is not right to take the children's bread and throw it to the dogs.

There is no use pretending this is easy. It is the one saying of Jesus that makes readers wince, and a commentary that hurries past it is not worth reading. So take it apart properly.

First, understand the picture he has drawn. A family at a meal. Bread on the table. Children being fed. And dogs, which in this house are under the table rather than out in the yard.

The children are Israel — a standard image, and God's own word for the nation: Israel is my firstborn son (Ex. 4:22).

The bread is what he has come with, and Mark's readers have just watched five thousand people fed from five loaves.

The dogs are the Gentiles, and it was, bluntly, a term of contempt in Jewish speech. That has to be admitted rather than explained away.

Now the three things that change the sentence.

First: the word first. Let the children be fed first. That single word is a door, and it is standing open. A man who says first has a second course in mind. This is not a refusal; it is an order of service. And it is exactly the order the New Testament states without embarrassment: the gospel is the power of God for salvation to everyone who believes, to the Jew first and also to the Greek (Rom. 1:16). There is a sequence in the plan of God, and she is not being told there is no place for her — she is being told about the timing.

Second: the word for dogs is a diminutive. Not the pariah dogs of the street, the scavengers that ran in packs outside the town. The word is kynarion — the household dog, the one under the table. And that matters enormously, because it means the animal in his picture is inside the house. He has drawn a scene in which the outsider is already in the room.

Third: watch what he actually does. He grants her request, immediately, at a distance, and Matthew records what he said about her while doing it: O woman, great is your faith! (Matt. 15:28). That is the loudest commentary available on the tone of verse 27, and it is not the commentary of a man who has just insulted somebody.

So what was he doing?

He was handing her a picture with a door in it, to see whether she would find the door. Everything she needs is in his own sentence: first, and a dog that is under the table rather than in the street. He has not shut her out. He has given her the material to argue with, and then waited.

He does this. He tests faith to bring it out, not to break it — as he did with Jairus, kept standing in the street while a woman told her whole story and his daughter died. The testing is never the withholding.

And it is worth being honest about how it must have felt from the floor. She did not have Matthew's account or a commentary. She had a hard sentence and a sick child, and what she did with it in the next verse is the reason we still know who she was.

verseByVerse.quote: But she answered him, "Yes, Lord; yet even the dogs under the table eat the children's crumbs."
verseByVerse.commentary:
But she answered him, Yes, Lord; yet even the dogs under the table eat the children's crumbs.

Eighteen words, and it is the only place in the four Gospels where somebody answers Jesus back in an argument and he tells them they are right.

Take it apart, because every clause is doing something.

Yes, Lord. She does not fight the picture. She does not say the comparison is unfair, or that she has as much right as anybody, or that she is offended. She concedes the whole framework: yes, the children come first; yes, I am not one of them.

That is not weakness. It is the opposite. She has stopped arguing about her standing, which is the argument she could never win, and she is about to argue about his generosity, which is an argument nobody has ever lost.

Yet even the dogs under the table. And now she picks up his own word — the household dog, the one inside — and stands on it. He put the animal under the table. She is simply pointing out where he put it.

Eat the children's crumbs. And there is the door. Nothing is taken from the children. The crumbs are not the loaf; feeding a dog under the table does not deprive a single child of a mouthful. She is not asking for the meal to be reassigned. She is asking for the overflow — and she has understood, apparently by instinct, that there is always overflow where he is. Mark's readers have just counted twelve baskets of it (6:43).

So she has argued with Jesus from Jesus. Not from her rights, her need, or her daughter's suffering, though all three were real and she might have pleaded any of them. From his own words and his own character.

And that is the lesson in prayer, and it is worth having in plain terms because it is the difference between persevering faith and mere nagging.

She came with a desperate need and met what looked like a closed door. She did not take offence and walk away. She also did not stand outside the door pleading louder in the hope of wearing him down. She listened to the very word that sounded like a refusal, took hold of it, and pressed further in. Her confidence did not rest on her own persistence; it rested on his goodness — which is why she could hold on through an apparent no, because she had grasped something true about him underneath it.

So if you are praying into silence, or into an answer that so far looks like no, learn her method rather than merely admiring her. Do not read the delay as the final verdict. Take God at his revealed character and his promises and press into them. Plead the crumbs. Plead his own word back to him — you said, you promised, you are the God who. That is not impertinence; it is the way every great prayer in Scripture is built, from Abraham at Sodom to Moses on the mountain.

And hold it with the balance Scripture keeps everywhere. This is not a technique for bending God to your will. The Lord himself, praying in Gethsemane with perfect faith, added nevertheless, not what I will, but what you will (14:36), and the cup did not pass. Her persistence was answered because it was persistence within his purpose, not against it.

So pray like her, refusing to let go — and trust like him, that the Father's no, when it comes, is as wise and as loving as his yes.

verseByVerse.quote: And he said to her, "For this statement you may go your way; the demon has left your daughter." And she went home and found the child lying in bed and the demon gone.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For this statement you may go your way.

Literally: because of this word. He names the thing that moved him, and it was her sentence — the one she made out of his own.

Matthew gives what Mark leaves out: O woman, great is your faith! Be it done for you as you desire (Matt. 15:28). And it is worth noting where the two great commendations of faith in the Gospels land. This woman, and a Roman centurion (Luke 7:9). Neither of them Jewish. Neither of them raised on the Scriptures. Both of them, in the Lord's own judgement, ahead of anyone in Israel.

The demon has left your daughter.

Past tense. It is already done, and it was done at a distance, in a house she cannot see, to a child she has not been able to help for however long this has been going on.

He does not go with her. He does not lay a hand on the girl or speak to the spirit. In this Gospel, that is unusual — Mark's exorcisms are close-range, physical, noisy. Here there is a sentence in one house and a quiet room in another.

Which is worth having, because most of our praying is at a distance. The people we are most desperate about are usually not in the room: the child in another city, the friend in a hospital we cannot get to, the person who will not see us. Nothing in this account requires proximity. He said it where she was, and it was true where the child was.

And she went home.

Three words, and they are the last act of her faith and easy to miss.

She has been given a sentence and nothing else. No sign, no accompanying miracle, no proof. She turns round and walks back — thirty-odd miles, quite possibly — on nothing but what he said.

That is the whole of it, and it is what faith always finally looks like: going home on the word.

And found the child lying in bed and the demon gone.

Mark's detail is beautifully understated. Lying in bed. A child who had been thrown about by an unclean spirit — Mark has shown us in chapter 5 and will again in chapter 9 what that looked like — is lying down, quiet, resting.

Her mother came in and found her asleep.

And so a Phoenician woman, with no covenant, no Scriptures, no synagogue and no standing, got what she asked for from the God of Israel because she believed he was generous and would not stop saying so. The children were fed first. But the crumbs, it turns out, were enough to cast out a demon — and the second course, when it came, would be the nations of the earth sitting down at the table.

verseByVerse.quote: Then he returned from the region of Tyre and went through Sidon to the Sea of Galilee, in the region of the Decapolis. And they brought to him a man who was deaf and had a speech impediment, and they begged him to lay his hand on him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then he returned from the region of Tyre and went through Sidon to the Sea of Galilee, in the region of the Decapolis.

The route is strange enough that it has puzzled readers for centuries, and it is worth tracing on a map. Tyre is on the coast. Sidon is twenty-five miles further north, in the wrong direction entirely. From there he comes down to the Sea of Galilee and into the Decapolis, which is the eastern side.

It is a long, looping, inefficient journey — quite possibly months on the road — and its one consistent feature is that almost every mile of it is Gentile ground. He has left Israel and is taking the long way round through the nations.

And notice where it ends up. The Decapolis is where he met the man among the tombs, and where the townspeople begged him to leave, and where he left one restored madman with a story and no training (5:1–20). The man went out and proclaimed in the Decapolis how much Jesus had done for him, and everyone marvelled.

Now Jesus comes back — and instead of being asked to go, he is met by people bringing him their sick.

Mark does not connect the dots for you. He does not need to. One man told one district what had happened to him, and when the Lord returned, the ground was ready.

And they brought to him a man who was deaf and had a speech impediment.

The man does not come. He is brought.

And think about why, because it is not incidental. He is deaf — which in that world meant he had never heard the reports about Jesus, could not have overheard the conversation about where he was, and could not have asked. Whatever he knew, somebody had to get across to him without words.

His speech is affected too. Mark's word is a rare one, mogilalos, which occurs only once in the Greek Old Testament — in Isaiah 35:6, in the passage about what will happen when God comes to save. That is not likely to be an accident.

So the whole way this man came to Christ was other people. They heard, they went, they made him understand, and they carried the request for him.

And they begged him to lay his hand on him.

They ask on his behalf, because he cannot. It is the four on the roof again (2:3–5), and it is one of the most frequent patterns in this Gospel: a person who could not get to Jesus, and someone who would not let that be the end of it.

If you are carrying somebody like that — praying for a person who cannot or will not pray, who does not understand enough to ask, who has no idea you have been at it for years — this is the man in the Bible for you. Nobody records the names of the people who brought him. They are simply they, and without them he would have died deaf.

verseByVerse.quote: And taking him aside from the crowd privately, he put his fingers into his ears, and after spitting touched his tongue. And looking up to heaven, he sighed and said to him, "Ephphatha," that is, "Be opened."
verseByVerse.commentary:
And taking him aside from the crowd privately.

Before anything else, notice this, because it is the mark of the man.

There is a crowd. There always is. And Jesus takes hold of him and walks him out of it.

Think what a jostling crowd is like for a man who cannot hear. He can see faces turned toward him, mouths moving, people pointing, the whole apparatus of being discussed — and he cannot follow one word of it. He is the object of attention and shut out of it at the same time. Whatever is about to happen to him, it is not going to happen in front of an audience.

That is a rebuke to every way of helping people that requires the helped to be visible — the testimony extracted, the need described in public, the person made into an occasion. He took him aside.

He put his fingers into his ears, and after spitting touched his tongue.

This is the most elaborate thing Jesus does in any healing in Mark, and modern readers find it odd. It is not odd once you ask the obvious question: how do you tell a deaf man what you are about to do?

You cannot say it. So he says it in the only language available.

Fingers into the ears. This is what I am dealing with. Saliva on the tongue — and spittle was widely regarded as having healing properties, so the gesture would have read to that man as treatment being applied. This too. Looking up to heaven. And this is where it comes from.

It is not a ritual and there is no power in the technique. It is a conversation, conducted entirely in signs, with a man who has never heard a sentence. Before the miracle, Jesus takes the trouble to make sure he understands what is happening to him.

That is worth sitting with. He could have healed him from where he stood, as he had just healed a girl thirty miles away with a word. He goes to the trouble of being understood, by one man, in the man's own language.

And looking up to heaven, he sighed.

The word is stronger than a sigh. It means to groan — a sound forced out of the chest.

Why would he groan? He is not straining; the healing costs him no effort at all, and he will do it with one word. This is not exertion. It is grief.

He is standing in front of one ruined pair of ears and one tongue that cannot form words, and he is looking at what has been done to his own creation. He made ears to hear with. And Paul says the whole creation groans — the same root — and that we groan inwardly with it, waiting for the redemption of our bodies (Rom. 8:22–23).

So here is the Creator, in a body, groaning over the wreckage. He is not indifferent to your body or anyone else's. He does not regard the physical ruin of the world as a small matter to be tolerated until souls are saved. It draws a groan out of him, over a man whose name nobody bothered to write down.

And said to him, Ephphatha, that is, Be opened.

And Mark keeps the Aramaic — the second time in this Gospel, after Talitha cumi in the sick-room (5:41). Both times it is a word spoken to somebody helpless, in a private place, remembered exactly, because Peter was standing there and never forgot the sound of it.

One word. To a man who could not hear it — and heard it.

verseByVerse.quote: And his ears were opened, his tongue was released, and he spoke plainly. And Jesus charged them to tell no one. But the more he charged them, the more zealously they proclaimed it.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And his ears were opened, his tongue was released, and he spoke plainly.

Three clauses, and Mark reports them like a man ticking off what he saw.

His ears were opened. The word is the one Jesus used — be opened — and it happened. Try to imagine the first second of it: a man who has lived his whole life inside silence, and suddenly there is wind, and voices, and his own breathing, and the noise of a crowd fifty yards off.

His tongue was released. Mark's phrase is that the bond of his tongue was loosed, as though something had been tied and was now untied.

And he spoke plainly. Which is, medically speaking, the strangest part. A man who has never heard speech does not simply produce it; you learn to speak by hearing. This man opens his mouth and talks properly, at once, with no learning curve at all — which tells you that what happened here was not a repair. It was a creation.

And Jesus charged them to tell no one.

Again. And by now the reader is entitled to find it strange, because we are in Gentile territory, far from the Galilean crowds who wanted to crown him, and the political danger is much smaller here.

But the same logic holds wherever he is. He will not have a following built on what he can do to a body. A reputation as a healer is not the truth about him — it is a fragment of the truth that can be believed enthusiastically by people who have understood nothing, and it makes the road to the cross harder to walk. He is managing the story until it can be told properly, and it cannot be told properly until there is a cross in it.

But the more he charged them, the more zealously they proclaimed it.

And here Mark records the most cheerful piece of disobedience in the Gospel, and does not condemn it.

The construction in Greek is a see-saw: the more he told them to be quiet, the more they told everybody. Every additional instruction produced an equal and opposite quantity of talk.

It happened before. He told the cleansed leper to say nothing and the man went out and began to talk freely about it, so that Jesus could no longer openly enter a town (1:45). The pattern is consistent: the people commanded to speak are often slow, and the people commanded to be silent cannot be stopped.

There is something in that worth turning over. These were people with no theology, no covenant, no Scriptures, and no commission — the very opposite of the twelve trained men who had been explicitly sent out to preach. And they could not shut up.

It is a fair question why the news travels so much more easily among people who have just been astonished by Christ than among people who have known about him for thirty years. The difference is not information. Nobody has to be persuaded to talk about something that has just happened to them.

verseByVerse.quote: And they were astonished beyond measure, saying, "He has done all things well. He even makes the deaf hear and the mute speak."
verseByVerse.commentary:
And they were astonished beyond measure.

Mark's phrase is enormous and slightly ungrammatical — superabundantly, out of all proportion, they were knocked sideways. He has run out of ordinary words and piled two intensifiers on top of each other.

And then he gives us what the crowd actually said, and they said more than they knew. Both halves of their sentence are quotations they did not realise they were making.

He has done all things well.

That is Genesis 1:31, and in the Greek Old Testament the words are the same: God saw everything that he had made, and behold, it was very good.

The crowd means something quite modest. They mean: this healer is impressive, everything he touches turns out right. What they have in fact said is the sentence pronounced over the finished creation, on the last day of the week, when God looked at a world with nothing wrong in it.

Because that is what has just happened on that hillside. The one who made ears has repaired a pair of them. The one who gave the tongue its power of speech has given it back. This is not a rescue operation bolted on to a ruined world; it is the Creator returning to his own marred work and beginning, one man at a time, to make it good again.

He even makes the deaf hear and the mute speak.

And that is Isaiah, and it is even more specific. Then the eyes of the blind shall be opened, and the ears of the deaf unstopped; then shall the lame man leap like a deer, and the tongue of the mute sing for joy (Isa. 35:5–6).

Remember the odd word Mark used back in verse 32 for the man's speech impediment — mogilalos, which appears exactly once in the whole Greek Old Testament, and it is in that verse of Isaiah. Mark has been pointing at this since the man was first brought forward.

Isaiah 35 is not a general promise of better days. It is the description of what will happen when God himself comes to save his people: Behold, your God will come... He will come and save you, and then the blind, and the deaf, and the lame, and the mute (Isa. 35:4–6).

So the sign that God has come has just been given, in a Gentile district, to a man whose name we do not know, in front of a crowd that could not have quoted Isaiah if you had paid them.

And that is how he works, from one end of this Gospel to the other. The scholars came ninety miles from Jerusalem to raise the matter of unwashed hands, and went home unmoved. A pagan mother took hold of one word and got her daughter back. A deaf man was carried to him by friends and heard his own voice.

The chapter began with men measuring the cleanness of cups. It ends with the Creator of the world groaning over one broken body and then saying be opened — and one day he will say it over every grave that has ever been dug, and it will be very good.

7.theology:
Why does your Bible skip verse 16? The numbers run 15, then 17, and nothing has been lost. The oldest and best manuscripts of Mark have no verse 16; later copies add the familiar refrain if anyone has ears to hear, let him hear — a sentence Jesus certainly said and which Mark records elsewhere (4:9, 4:23) — almost certainly written first in a margin and then mistaken for text. The verse numbers themselves date only from the sixteenth century, so translators could not renumber the New Testament; they left the number empty and put the words in a footnote. Nothing has been removed from your Bible. We simply have older copies than were available in 1611, and honest translators tell you in the margin rather than quietly leaving something in.

Was Jesus cruel to the Syrophoenician woman? Three things settle it without softening the difficulty. The word first is a door standing open — let the children be fed first implies a second course, and Paul states the same order plainly (Rom. 1:16). The word for dogs is a diminutive: not the scavengers of the street but the household pets under the table, already inside the house. And the outcome is the loudest commentary of all — he grants her request at once, at a distance, and Matthew records him saying O woman, great is your faith! (Matt. 15:28). He handed her a picture with a door in it to see whether she would find the door, and she found it in one sentence.

And the crowd at the end quotes two texts without knowing it. He has done all things well is Genesis 1:31 in the Greek — God saw everything he had made, and it was very good. He even makes the deaf hear and the mute speak is Isaiah 35:5–6, the sign of the day when God himself comes to save. Mark had signalled it already: his rare word for the man's speech impediment (v. 32) occurs exactly once in the Greek Old Testament, in that verse of Isaiah.
7.examples:
Then: Corban — the money owed to an old man, put beyond his reach by a holy word, while his son kept the use of it and his reputation.

Now: the shape survives perfectly, and it is almost never dishonest. The man so committed at church four nights a week that his mother has not had a visit since March. The giving that goes to a fund while a brother in the same congregation cannot pay his heating bill. Any arrangement in which something genuinely religious has been set in front of a plain duty God commanded, so that the duty can be dropped without anybody feeling wicked.

So take the test the passage supplies, in one sentence: is anything I do for God currently costing somebody else something God told me to give them?

Note that Jesus does not attack tradition as such — every church has customs and must. He attacks tradition that has been promoted: set level with Scripture, and then used against it. And note what he reaches for when he wants a case anybody can measure. Not prayer, not fasting, not the temple. Whether the old people in your family are being looked after — which is exactly where the New Testament keeps landing (Jas. 1:27; 1 Tim. 5:8).

And one more, from the parenthesis in v. 19. Peter was in that house and heard the explanation with his own ears — and years later needed a sheet let down from heaven three times before he would eat with a Gentile (Acts 10:9–16), and a public rebuke from Paul after that (Gal. 2:11–14). It is possible to be taught a truth plainly by Christ himself and go years before it lands. That is not proof you were never taught. It is what learning looks like in creatures like us — and Peter is the one who tells us he had been told all along.

8.title: Who Do You Say That I Am?
8.text: <sup>1</sup>In those days, when again a great crowd had gathered, and they had nothing to eat, he called his disciples to him and said to them, <sup>2</sup>“I have compassion on the crowd, because they have been with me now three days and have nothing to eat. <sup>3</sup>And if I send them away hungry to their homes, they will faint on the way. And some of them have come from far away.” <sup>4</sup>And his disciples answered him, “How can one feed these people with bread here in this desolate place?” <sup>5</sup>And he asked them, “How many loaves do you have?” They said, “Seven.” <sup>6</sup>And he directed the crowd to sit down on the ground. And he took the seven loaves, and having given thanks, he broke them and gave them to his disciples to set before the people; and they set them before the crowd. <sup>7</sup>And they had a few small fish. And having blessed them, he said that these also should be set before them. <sup>8</sup>And they ate and were satisfied. And they took up the broken pieces left over, seven baskets full. <sup>9</sup>And there were about four thousand people. And he sent them away. <sup>10</sup>And immediately he got into the boat with his disciples and went to the district of Dalmanutha. <sup>11</sup>The Pharisees came and began to argue with him, seeking from him a sign from heaven to test him. <sup>12</sup>And he sighed deeply in his spirit and said, “Why does this generation seek a sign? Truly, I say to you, no sign will be given to this generation.” <sup>13</sup>And he left them, got into the boat again, and went to the other side. <sup>14</sup>Now they had forgotten to bring bread, and they had only one loaf with them in the boat. <sup>15</sup>And he cautioned them, saying, “Watch out; beware of the leaven of the Pharisees and the leaven of Herod.” <sup>16</sup>And they began discussing with one another the fact that they had no bread. <sup>17</sup>And Jesus, aware of this, said to them, “Why are you discussing the fact that you have no bread? Do you not yet perceive or understand? Are your hearts hardened? <sup>18</sup>Having eyes do you not see, and having ears do you not hear? And do you not remember? <sup>19</sup>When I broke the five loaves for the five thousand, how many baskets full of broken pieces did you take up?” They said to him, “Twelve.” <sup>20</sup>“And the seven for the four thousand, how many baskets full of broken pieces did you take up?” And they said to him, “Seven.” <sup>21</sup>And he said to them, “Do you not yet understand?” <sup>22</sup>And they came to Bethsaida. And some people brought to him a blind man and begged him to touch him. <sup>23</sup>And he took the blind man by the hand and led him out of the village, and when he had spit on his eyes and laid his hands on him, he asked him, “Do you see anything?” <sup>24</sup>And he looked up and said, “I see people, but they look like trees, walking.” <sup>25</sup>Then Jesus laid his hands on his eyes again; and he opened his eyes, his sight was restored, and he saw everything clearly. <sup>26</sup>And he sent him to his home, saying, “Do not even enter the village.” <sup>27</sup>And Jesus went on with his disciples to the villages of Caesarea Philippi. And on the way he asked his disciples, “Who do people say that I am?” <sup>28</sup>And they told him, “John the Baptist; and others say, Elijah; and others, one of the prophets.” <sup>29</sup>And he asked them, “But who do you say that I am?” Peter answered him, “You are the Christ.” <sup>30</sup>And he strictly charged them to tell no one about him. <sup>31</sup>And he began to teach them that the Son of Man must suffer many things and be rejected by the elders and the chief priests and the scribes and be killed, and after three days rise again. <sup>32</sup>And he said this plainly. And Peter took him aside and began to rebuke him. <sup>33</sup>But turning and seeing his disciples, he rebuked Peter and said, “Get behind me, Satan! For you are not setting your mind on the things of God, but on the things of man.” <sup>34</sup>And calling the crowd to him with his disciples, he said to them, “If anyone would come after me, let him deny himself and take up his cross and follow me. <sup>35</sup>For whoever would save his life will lose it, but whoever loses his life for my sake and the gospel’s will save it. <sup>36</sup>For what does it profit a man to gain the whole world and forfeit his soul? <sup>37</sup>For what can a man give in return for his soul? <sup>38</sup>For whoever is ashamed of me and of my words in this adulterous and sinful generation, of him will the Son of Man also be ashamed when he comes in the glory of his Father with the holy angels.”
8.overview:
Chapter 8 is the hinge of Mark, and everything in the book turns on it. The first half asks who Jesus is; the second half walks to Jerusalem to die.

It is built around sight. Four thousand Gentiles are fed on a hillside and the disciples learn nothing from it. The Pharisees, days after a district was fed from seven loaves, ask for a sign — and he groans, refuses flatly, and gets back in the boat. Then twelve men who have twice carried the surplus away in baskets sit worrying about having one loaf between them, and Jesus asks seven questions in five verses, ending with do you not yet understand?

So Mark puts a blind man next, and has him healed in two stages — the only such healing in the Gospels. I see people, but they look like trees, walking. Not blind. Genuinely seeing. Seeing wrong shapes. It is a picture of exactly what happens next.

At Caesarea Philippi — beneath a cliff of pagan shrines, in a city named for Caesar — Peter gets it right: You are the Christ. And immediately Jesus begins to teach that the Son of Man must suffer, be rejected, be killed, and rise, and Mark notes that he said it plainly, the first plain speech in the book. Peter takes him aside to correct him and is called Satan. Then the crowd is called over and told the terms: deny yourself, take up your cross, follow me.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–21 — Four Thousand Fed, a Sign Refused, and the Leaven
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The second hillside (vv. 1–10). A crowd of four thousand has been with him three days in an empty place, and some of them have a long walk home. Seven loaves, a few small fish, and seven hampers of scraps at the end. It is not a retelling of chapter 6 — Jesus himself will insist on the difference in verse 19.

The demand (vv. 11–13). The Pharisees arrive and ask for a sign from heaven, days after a hillside was fed from a basket. He groans, refuses flatly, gets back in the boat and leaves them.

The boat (vv. 14–21). A warning about leaven is heard as a comment about catering, and Jesus asks seven questions in four verses. The list of what they have seen is read back to them, with the numbers, and it changes nothing.

Everything in this half of the chapter is about seeing — a crowd fed and not understood, a sign demanded by men who have had a hundred, and twelve men in a boat with the bread-maker, worrying about bread. Which is exactly why the next thing Mark records is a man who could not see at all.
verseByVerse.theology:
Are the two feedings one story told twice? It is the standard suggestion, and Mark closes it off himself. In vv. 19–20 Jesus makes the disciples recite both, with the figures — five loaves and five thousand and twelve baskets; seven loaves and four thousand and seven baskets — as two separate events they were present at.

And Mark preserves a detail that no editor combining two versions of one story would have kept straight. In chapter 6 the baskets are kophinoi (6:43) — the small stiff wicker basket a Jew carried his own food in. Here they are spurides (v. 8) — a large hamper, the kind big enough to hold a man, and the very word used of the basket Paul was let down the Damascus wall in (Acts 9:25). In vv. 19–20 Jesus uses each word of its own occasion. Two words, two events, kept apart by a writer who was not trying to prove anything by it.

The settings differ too. The five thousand were Jews on the green grass of Galilee, seated in ranks of hundreds and fifties like Israel in the wilderness, with twelve baskets over. The four thousand are in the Decapolis, on Gentile ground, with seven — and some of them have come from far away, which is how the Old Testament speaks of the nations (Isa. 60:4; Josh. 9:6). Twelve is the number of the tribes. Seven is the number of fullness. He fed Israel and had a basket for every tribe; he fed the nations and there was more than enough.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: twelve men in a boat, worrying about having one loaf between them, having twice watched thousands fed out of nothing.

Now: exactly the same, and the comedy of it is uncomfortable rather than funny. We have documented evidence of God's provision — the job that came, the diagnosis that was not what we feared, the money that arrived, the marriage that held — and the next shortage finds us doing arithmetic as though none of it had happened.

Note where Jesus locates the failure. Not in their circumstances and not even in their fear. Do you not remember? The problem is memory. They had the facts; they had carried the baskets themselves; and the facts had not been converted into knowledge of the Person who supplied them.

So the practical remedy is unglamorous and it works. Keep a record. Write down what God has actually done, with dates, so that the next crisis meets a list rather than a mood. The disciples could still produce the numbers when they were asked — twelve, seven — and had drawn nothing from them. Israel was commanded to build cairns of stones in the Jordan so that children would ask what they meant (Josh. 4:6–7). We are people who forget, and God has never treated that as a small problem.

verseByVerse.quote: In those days, when again a great crowd had gathered, and they had nothing to eat, he called his disciples to him and said to them, "I have compassion on the crowd, because they have been with me now three days and have nothing to eat. And if I send them away hungry to their homes, they will faint on the way. And some of them have come from far away."
verseByVerse.commentary:
In those days, when again a great crowd had gathered. The word again is Mark's own signal that we have been somewhere like this before, and he expects the reader to remember it.

But we are not in Galilee. Chapter 7 has taken Jesus on a long loop through pagan country and left him in the Decapolis (7:31), and there is nothing in this account to bring him home. This is a Gentile crowd on Gentile ground, and everything that follows should be read in that light.

I have compassion on the crowd.

He speaks first, before anybody asks. In chapter 6 the disciples raised the problem and he handed it back; here nobody has raised anything. He is looking at the crowd and doing the arithmetic himself.

And the word is the same deep one as before — moved in the gut, the strongest verb for pity in the language. This is not a policy. It is what happens inside him when he looks at people.

Because they have been with me now three days and have nothing to eat.

Three days. Take that in, because it changes the picture entirely.

These people have not come out for an afternoon. They have stayed in a desolate place for three days, sleeping rough, listening to a Jewish teacher whose language and religion were not their own — and whatever they brought with them ran out a long time ago.

And he has noticed. That is the thing to hold. In the middle of teaching thousands of people, he has been keeping track of how long they have been there and what they have had to eat.

And if I send them away hungry to their homes, they will faint on the way.

Now watch what he is actually thinking about. Not the sermon. Not the crowd's response. He is thinking about the walk home — about people going light-headed on a hot road with miles still to go, and children, and the old.

The word is used of collapsing from exhaustion. He is picturing it.

And some of them have come from far away.

And here is a clause almost everybody reads past, and it is doing two things at once.

At the plain level it is pure pastoral care: some of these people have the furthest to travel, and he has factored that in. He is not calculating an average. He is thinking about the ones at the back of the queue with the longest road.

And underneath it, for a reader with the Old Testament open, from far away is how Scripture speaks of the nations coming in. Lift up your eyes all around, and see; they all gather together, they come to you; your sons shall come from afar (Isa. 60:4). Paul uses the same language of Gentile converts: you who once were far off have been brought near by the blood of Christ (Eph. 2:13).

So the sentence works in both directions. He is worried about their legs, and Mark is telling you who they are.

Which is worth taking personally if you are a Gentile reading this — and most of us are. The first thing recorded of him on the day the nations were fed is that he had noticed how far they had come, and did not want them to collapse on the way home.

verseByVerse.quote: And his disciples answered him, "How can one feed these people with bread here in this desolate place?" And he asked them, "How many loaves do you have?" They said, "Seven."
verseByVerse.commentary:
And his disciples answered him, How can one feed these people with bread here in this desolate place?

It is the same objection as chapter 6, and it is worse this time, because last time they had not seen it done.

Do not rush to enjoy their failure. Look first at the exact shape of the sentence, because it is remarkably familiar.

How can one feed these people? — the question is impersonal, and that is its trouble. Not how can you feed them, which would at least have put the problem where it belonged. They are surveying a situation and reporting that the resources are inadequate, and they are entirely right, and the Person standing beside them does not appear in the calculation at all.

And it is a very old sentence. When Israel wanted meat in the wilderness, Moses said to the LORD: Where am I to get meat to give to all this people? (Num. 11:13) — and God answered him with a question that could be printed over this whole chapter: Is the LORD's hand shortened? Now you shall see whether my word will come true for you or not (Num. 11:23).

So the disciples are standing in a wilderness, in front of a hungry multitude, saying what Moses said. Mark's readers were meant to hear it.

And he asked them, How many loaves do you have?

The same question as before, and the same method. He does not argue with their arithmetic and he does not lecture them about faith. He asks what is actually in their hands.

That is worth taking as a habit, because it is the practical antidote to being overwhelmed. The mind, faced with something too big, produces a paralysing survey of the gap. He turns it round: never mind the gap, what have you got? Count it. Bring it.

They said, Seven.

One word. And the second thing to notice about this exchange is what is missing from it.

Nobody says: Lord, last time you did this with five. Nobody looks up. They produce the number the way a man produces a stock figure, and wait.

They are not being obstructive; they are being ordinary. And that is precisely what Mark wants you to see, because the whole first half of this chapter is about people who have all the evidence and none of the sight — and it is about to end with a man who cannot see at all being led out of a village by the hand.

verseByVerse.quote: And he directed the crowd to sit down on the ground. And he took the seven loaves, and having given thanks, he broke them and gave them to his disciples to set before the people; and they set them before the crowd. And they had a few small fish. And having blessed them, he said that these also should be set before them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And he directed the crowd to sit down on the ground.

A small difference from chapter 6, and Mark, who was there in Peter's memory, keeps it. Last time it was the green grass, in a Galilean spring (6:39). Here it is simply the ground. Different place, different season, different crowd.

And there is no seating in ranks of hundreds and fifties this time. That arrangement was Israel in the wilderness, drawn up as Moses drew them up. These are Gentiles, and Mark does not impose the pattern on them.

And he took the seven loaves, and having given thanks, he broke them and gave them to his disciples.

The four verbs again — took, gave thanks, broke, gave — and by now the reader of this Gospel should be feeling the shape of them. They will be done once more in an upstairs room in Jerusalem, over bread that he will call his body (14:22).

One word is different from chapter 6, and it is worth having. There it was he blessed; here it is having given thanks — eucharistēsas, the word from which the church took the name Eucharist. Mark uses both, of the same action, which is its own small lesson: the thing being described is not a formula but a man thanking his Father for food that is plainly not enough.

To set before the people; and they set them before the crowd.

And there is the mechanism again, and Mark is emphatic about it — he says it twice in one verse. He gives it to the disciples; the disciples give it to the crowd.

The multiplication happens in their hands, out among the rows, exactly as it did before. These are the men who have just said it could not be done, and they are the ones who will find out that it can, by carrying it.

That is how he has always worked with his church. He does not usually rain provision directly onto the people who need it; he gives it to ordinary and unconvinced servants to distribute, and the sufficiency is discovered in the distributing. You will never settle the question of whether there is enough by standing at the front doing sums. You settle it on the fourth row.

And they had a few small fish. And having blessed them, he said that these also should be set before them.

Mark handles the fish as an afterthought, almost apologetically — a few small fish, and they are dealt with in a separate sentence and a separate blessing.

It is a very human detail: somebody remembered, halfway through, that there were also some fish. Nobody composing a legend includes that.

And it says something quietly about him. He blesses the few small fish too. The scraps are not beneath his notice, and nothing brought to him is handled carelessly — which is the same care that will send men out afterwards to pick up the broken pieces so that nothing is lost.

verseByVerse.quote: And they ate and were satisfied. And they took up the broken pieces left over, seven baskets full. And there were about four thousand people. And he sent them away. And immediately he got into the boat with his disciples and went to the district of Dalmanutha.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And they ate and were satisfied. The same emphatic word as chapter 6 — filled, fed to the point of stopping. Not a token, not a taste. Four thousand people ate until they had had enough.

And they took up the broken pieces left over, seven baskets full.

Now the detail that settles a long-running question, and it is a single word.

The basket here is a spuris — a large hamper, the sort of thing you would carry provisions in, big enough to hold a person. It is the very word Luke uses for the basket Paul was let down the Damascus city wall in (Acts 9:25).

In chapter 6 the baskets were kophinoi — the small stiff wicker basket a Jew carried his own food in, so distinctively Jewish that Roman satirists joked about it.

Two different words, for two different occasions. And when Jesus makes the disciples recite both events in verse 19 and 20, he uses each word of its own event.

That is not the behaviour of a story told twice and mistakenly recorded as two. Nobody duplicating a narrative keeps the crockery straight. Mark has two events because there were two.

Seven baskets. Twelve last time, seven now, and the numbers are doing work.
