Twelve is the number of the tribes: he fed Israel and there was a basket for every tribe. Seven is the Bible's number for fullness and completion — the days of the week, the finished creation. He has fed the nations, and there was more than enough.

And there were about four thousand people. Given last, as before, almost as a footnote.

And immediately he got into the boat with his disciples and went to the district of Dalmanutha.

Nobody knows where Dalmanutha was. The name appears nowhere else in ancient literature, and copyists were already substituting more familiar places for it. Which is, in its own way, a small argument for the account: an inventor puts his story somewhere the reader has heard of.

What matters is the direction. He is crossing back to the Jewish side of the lake, having fed the Gentiles on the far shore — and the first thing waiting for him at home is a delegation asking him to prove himself.

verseByVerse.quote: The Pharisees came and began to argue with him, seeking from him a sign from heaven to test him. And he sighed deeply in his spirit and said, "Why does this generation seek a sign? Truly, I say to you, no sign will be given to this generation." And he left them, got into the boat again, and went to the other side.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Pharisees came and began to argue with him, seeking from him a sign from heaven to test him.

The boat has barely touched the shore. He has been away in Gentile country for weeks, and this is the reception committee.

A sign from heaven. Note the phrase, because it is a specific request. They are not asking whether he can heal — that has been settled for chapters. They want something in the sky. Something meteorological or astronomical, on demand, of the kind Elijah called down on Carmel or Samuel produced in the wheat harvest. Healing a man could always be explained away; a fire from heaven, they thought, could not.

To test him. Mark tells us the motive and does not leave it for us to infer. The verb is peirazō — the same word used of Satan in the wilderness (1:13). This is not enquiry. It is an examination set by men who have already marked the paper.

And consider the timing. Somewhere behind him on the eastern shore, four thousand people are walking home fed. Before that, five thousand. Before that, a leper, a paralytic, a withered hand, a legion, a dead girl, a hurricane.

They want a sign.

And he sighed deeply in his spirit.

The word is a groan, intensified — it occurs nowhere else in the New Testament. Mark has used the simpler form once already, in chapter 7, when Jesus stood in front of a deaf man and groaned over what had been done to his creation (7:34).

So the same sound is drawn out of him twice, and the two occasions are worth putting side by side. He groans over a body that cannot hear. And he groans over men who will not see. The second one is deeper.

This is not irritation. It is grief, and it comes up from somewhere.

Why does this generation seek a sign? Truly, I say to you, no sign will be given to this generation.

The Greek is a Hebrew oath-form, blunter than the English: if a sign shall be given to this generation — with the curse left unspoken, the way a man says may I be damned if. It is the most emphatic refusal he ever makes.

And it needs saying clearly what he is refusing, because it is not evidence.

He has given evidence continuously and will give more. What he refuses is a miracle produced on demand as a condition of belief — because faith manufactured that way is not faith at all but a calculated response to a demonstration, and because the men asking have already shown what they do with the evidence they have.

That is the settled principle, and Jesus states it elsewhere with total clarity: if they do not hear Moses and the Prophets, neither will they be convinced if someone should rise from the dead (Luke 16:31). Which turned out to be exactly right. Somebody did rise from the dead, and the men who had the report first paid soldiers to say the body was stolen (Matt. 28:12–13).

So if you have ever wished God would do something undeniable — settle it once and for all, in the sky, where nobody could argue — this passage is a kindness, though it does not feel like one. The problem was never the quantity of evidence. Every one of the men in this conversation had watched things that could not be explained, and it moved them not an inch, because the trouble was never in their eyes.

And he left them, got into the boat again, and went to the other side.

He does not argue. He does not stay to win. He gets back in the boat and goes.

It is the third time in this Gospel he has walked away from people who did not want him — the Nazareth synagogue (6:6), the Gerasene town that asked him to leave (5:17), and now the Pharisees at Dalmanutha. He never forces himself on anybody, and there is no more frightening fact about him than that.

verseByVerse.quote: Now they had forgotten to bring bread, and they had only one loaf with them in the boat. And he cautioned them, saying, "Watch out; beware of the leaven of the Pharisees and the leaven of Herod." And they began discussing with one another the fact that they had no bread.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now they had forgotten to bring bread, and they had only one loaf with them in the boat.

Mark's detail is precise and slightly comic, and he sets it up deliberately. They pushed off in a hurry and nobody did the shopping. There is one loaf on board and thirteen men.

Hold on to that phrase — only one loaf — because Mark has placed it with great care. There is one loaf in that boat, and the disciples are worried about it. There is also one Person in that boat who has twice this month fed a district out of a basket.

And he cautioned them, saying, Watch out; beware of the leaven of the Pharisees and the leaven of Herod.

Two commands, both about vigilance. And then a metaphor which they are about to get spectacularly wrong.

Leaven in that world was not a sachet of yeast. It was a lump of last week's dough, kept back and going sour, worked into the new batch — and the point of the image everywhere in Scripture is that a very small quantity changes the whole mass, silently, from inside. A little leaven leavens the whole lump (Gal. 5:9; 1 Cor. 5:6).

So the warning is about something that gets in unnoticed and works.

The leaven of the Pharisees. He has just walked away from them, and their disease is fresh in the mind: the demand for evidence from men who have all the evidence they will ever get. It is unbelief dressed as rigour — the settled habit of a mind that keeps asking for one more proof because it has no intention of yielding to any.

And the leaven of Herod. Mark has given us thirteen verses on Herod in chapter 6 so that we will know exactly what this means. Herod feared John, knew he was righteous, protected him, heard him gladly — and killed him because of his oaths and his guests. That leaven is the accommodation of power: religion kept as an interest, and conscience overruled every time it collides with what the room expects.

Set the two side by side and they cover most of the ways a person is lost. One is too clever to believe. The other believes well enough and will not pay. And Jesus warns his own disciples about both, which means neither is a danger only to outsiders.

And they began discussing with one another the fact that they had no bread.

And there it is, and Mark reports it deadpan.

He has warned them about a spiritual infection that destroys men from the inside — and they conclude he is making a pointed remark about the catering. You can imagine the muttering: he is talking about bread because somebody was supposed to bring bread. Perhaps they thought he meant not to buy bread from Pharisees or Herodians.

They have taken the deepest warning of the chapter and turned it into a domestic grievance.

Before that is laughed at, notice how easily it is done. It is entirely possible to sit under a sermon that names the thing quietly killing you, and to spend the drive home discussing the length of the service, the temperature of the building, or whether that illustration was quite fair. The mind will reach for the manageable subject every time — and the smaller subject is always the more comfortable one.

verseByVerse.quote: And Jesus, aware of this, said to them, "Why are you discussing the fact that you have no bread? Do you not yet perceive or understand? Are your hearts hardened? Having eyes do you not see, and having ears do you not hear? And do you not remember?
verseByVerse.commentary:
And Jesus, aware of this. He is not told. Mark keeps quietly noting that he knows what is going on inside people (2:8), and this time it is his own men.

What follows is the sharpest thing he ever says to the Twelve — seven questions in the space of five verses, one after another, with no pause for answers until the very end.

Why are you discussing the fact that you have no bread? The first question simply holds the absurdity up. You are in a boat, with me, discussing a shortage of bread.

Do you not yet perceive or understand? The word yet is the painful one. It has been eight chapters. There has been a leper, a paralytic, a hurricane, a legion, a dead girl raised, five thousand fed, a man walking on water, four thousand fed. Yet.

Are your hearts hardened?

And here is the sentence that should stop any Christian reading comfortably.

It is the third time Mark has used this word. In chapter 3 it described the men in the synagogue who watched a withered hand restored and went out to arrange a murder (3:5). In chapter 6 it was said of the disciples after the walking on water (6:52). And now Jesus says it to their faces, as a question.

The word is the one for a callus — soft tissue that thickens at the point of injury until it can no longer feel. It is not disbelief; these men believed a great deal, had left everything, and had just been out casting out demons in his name. It is the loss of the capacity to be affected. A hardened heart can carry the bread and never taste it.

And it is put as a question rather than a verdict, which is the mercy in it. He is asking them to check.

Having eyes do you not see, and having ears do you not hear?

Now he quotes Scripture at them, and it is worth knowing which Scripture, because it lands like a slap.

These are the words of Jeremiah to a rebellious nation — who have eyes, but see not, who have ears, but hear not (Jer. 5:21) — and behind that, Isaiah 6:9–10, the passage Jesus quoted in chapter 4 about those outside who see and do not perceive (4:12).

He is applying the outsiders' text to the inner circle. The men who were given the secret of the kingdom are being described in the language of those who were not.

That is the warning of this passage, and it is not for the world. It is for people who have been near Christ a long time. Proximity is not immunity. It is entirely possible to hold the correct doctrine, attend the right church, do genuine work in his name, and be steadily losing the ability to be moved by him — and the loss is undetectable from inside, which is why he has to ask.

And do you not remember?

And with the last question he turns the corner, because this one has an answer, and the answer is going to be their own.

He does not tell them what they have forgotten. He is about to make them say it.

verseByVerse.quote: When I broke the five loaves for the five thousand, how many baskets full of broken pieces did you take up?" They said to him, "Twelve." "And the seven for the four thousand, how many baskets full of broken pieces did you take up?" And they said to him, "Seven." And he said to them, "Do you not yet understand?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
When I broke the five loaves for the five thousand, how many baskets full of broken pieces did you take up?

He does not preach at them. He examines them, and the examination consists of making them state facts they already know.

They said to him, Twelve.

Straight away. No hesitation. They have the number at their fingertips, because each of them carried one.

And the seven for the four thousand, how many baskets full of broken pieces did you take up? And they said to him, Seven.

Again, instantly. The data is intact. The filing system is perfect.

And note in passing what this exchange does to the old suggestion that the two feedings are one event told twice. Jesus makes them recite both, with different loaves, different crowds, different baskets — and Mark preserves the two different words for basket, using each of its own occasion. The men in that boat were at both.

And he said to them, Do you not yet understand?

The seventh question, and it hangs there. Mark records no answer.

Now see exactly what he has proved, because it is not what we would expect and it is the most useful thing in the chapter.

He has just demonstrated that they remembered everything and had understood nothing. The facts were not missing. They could produce the figures on demand. What had never happened was the step from the figures to the Person — from twelve baskets to therefore the man in this boat will not be defeated by a bread shortage.

That is the disease, and it is extremely common among people who have been Christians for years. We are not usually short of information. Most of us could give an account of God's dealings with us — the provision that came, the door that opened, the illness that turned, the year we could not have got through and did. And the next difficulty arrives and finds us exactly where the disciples were, doing sums in a boat.

So take the remedy, which is plain and practical and is more or less what he does here. Make yourself recite it. Not vaguely — with numbers and dates, the way they answered him. Write down what God has actually done for you, and keep the list where you will see it when the next thing comes.

That is not sentiment; it is a command running right through Scripture. Israel was told to pile twelve stones out of the Jordan so that when the children asked what they meant, the fathers would have to tell the story (Josh. 4:6–7). Bless the LORD, O my soul, and forget not all his benefits (Ps. 103:2) is a man giving orders to his own memory, because he knows it will not do it by itself.

And notice what Jesus does not do at the end of this. He does not put them out of the boat. He asks the question, gets no answer, and takes them to Bethsaida — where the very next thing that happens is a blind man being led out of a village by the hand and given his sight in two stages.

Mark has put that story exactly there on purpose.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 22–38 — Two-Stage Sight and the Great Confession
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The blind man (vv. 22–26). The only healing in the Gospels that happens in two stages, and it is placed here on purpose. A man is led out of the village by the hand, sees people like walking trees, is touched again, and sees clearly. It is a picture of what is about to happen to the men in the boat.

The question (vv. 27–30). At Caesarea Philippi — at the foot of a mountain, beside a cave sacred to Pan, in a city named for Caesar — Jesus asks the question the whole Gospel has been building to, and Peter answers it: You are the Christ.

The correction (vv. 31–33). And immediately Jesus starts teaching them something they cannot bear: that the Son of Man must suffer, be rejected, be killed, and rise. Mark says he said it plainly — the first plain speech in the book. Peter takes him aside to put him right, and gets the hardest sentence any disciple ever heard.

The terms (vv. 34–38). Then he calls the crowd over, so that nobody can say the terms were for professionals only, and states them: deny yourself, take up your cross, follow me.

This is the hinge of the Gospel. Everything before it asks who he is. Everything after it walks to Jerusalem.
verseByVerse.theology:
Why two touches? Not because the first failed. Mark places this healing between the disciples who have eyes and do not see (v. 18) and Peter's half-sighted confession, and it is an enacted parable of exactly that. I see people, but they look like trees, walking is a precise description of where the Twelve now stand: no longer blind, genuinely seeing, and seeing wrong shapes. Peter will name him Christ in seven verses and rebuke him in eleven.

And why "after three days"? Mark writes after three days (v. 31; also 9:31; 10:34) where Matthew and Luke have on the third day, and honest readers have wondered whether that requires a fourth day and breaks the Friday-to-Sunday timeline. It does not; it is simply the Jewish way of counting, in which any part of a day counted as a whole day. Scripture proves it on the spot: the chief priests remember this very prediction as After three days I will rise, and in the same breath ask Pilate for a guard until the third day (Matt. 27:63–64) — both phrases, of one morning, without a flicker of contradiction.

And why "Get behind me, Satan"? Not because Peter was demonic. Because the content of his objection was the wilderness temptation returning through the mouth of a friend: a kingdom without a cross. Jesus had heard it before (1:13), and he will hear it again from passers-by at the foot of the cross itself — save yourself, and come down (15:30). Peter meant it lovingly, which is precisely what made it dangerous.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: a crowd in Galilee hearing the words take up his cross, in a country where Varus had crucified two thousand men within living memory. Nobody in that crowd thought of a metaphor. They had seen men carrying the crossbeam through the streets, stripped, jeered at, on a walk with one destination.

Now: we have worn the phrase smooth. A cross has become a difficulty — a hard marriage, an illness, a colleague. That is not what it meant. A man carrying a cross was not a man with a burden; he was a man already condemned, publicly, walking away from everything he had.

And note who is being addressed. Mark says he called the crowd — not just the Twelve. This is not a higher path for the heroic few. It is the entry requirement, stated to the general public, by a man who knew exactly what he was asking because he was going to do it first.

So make it concrete rather than admiring it in the abstract. Deny himself is not going without sugar; it is the removal of the self from the throne — the decision, in a specific matter this week, that what you want is no longer the deciding vote. Name the matter. If you cannot name one, the denial is theoretical.

verseByVerse.quote: And they came to Bethsaida. And some people brought to him a blind man and begged him to touch him. And he took the blind man by the hand and led him out of the village, and when he had spit on his eyes and laid his hands on him, he asked him, "Do you see anything?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
And they came to Bethsaida. The town Philip, Andrew and Peter came from (John 1:44), on the north-east shore. It is also one of the towns Jesus will later pronounce woe over for its unbelief (Matt. 11:21), which gives the last verse of this little account its edge.

And some people brought to him a blind man and begged him to touch him.

Again the pattern: the man is brought. He did not find his way here; somebody led him. It is the fourth time in this Gospel that a person who could not get to Christ was carried by people who could — the paralytic through the roof, the deaf man in the Decapolis, the little girl's father, and now this.

And he took the blind man by the hand and led him out of the village.

Stop on that, because it is one of the tenderest sentences in Mark.

The Lord of glory takes a blind man's hand and walks him out of town. Not a word is recorded. Just a man in the dark, holding on, going somewhere he cannot see, led by somebody he has never met.

It takes as long as it takes. Nobody is hurrying a blind man over rough ground. And Mark keeps this detail because it is the whole disposition of the Christ toward people who cannot see: he does not shout instructions from a distance. He comes and takes the hand.

Why out of the village? Partly what he did with the deaf man in chapter 7 — away from a crowd that stares. Partly, in this town, because of what he says in verse 26. Whatever else, the privacy is deliberate: at the hinge of the Gospel, the two great healings are done quietly, off to one side, for one man at a time.

And when he had spit on his eyes and laid his hands on him.

The saliva again, as in chapter 7. It was widely regarded as having healing properties, which means the gesture would have registered with the man as treatment. It is also, once more, a way of communicating with somebody who cannot follow what is going on: this is what I am dealing with.

And note that there is nothing fastidious about it. He touches the man's eyes with his own hands and his own saliva. This is a very physical Saviour.

He asked him, Do you see anything?

Which is the strangest sentence in the account, and it is the reason people have always found this healing difficult. Jesus asks a question — as though the outcome were not certain, as though he were checking.

He was not checking. Nothing in this Gospel suggests he ever needed a second attempt at anything; he had just fed four thousand people and silenced a hurricane with two words.

He is doing something deliberate, and the next verse shows what.

verseByVerse.quote: And he looked up and said, "I see people, but they look like trees, walking." Then Jesus laid his hands on his eyes again; and he opened his eyes, his sight was restored, and he saw everything clearly. And he sent him to his home, saying, "Do not even enter the village."
verseByVerse.commentary:
And he looked up and said, I see people, but they look like trees, walking.

It is one of the most vivid sentences in the New Testament, and it can only have come from the man himself. Shapes, upright, tall, moving. He can tell they are people because they are moving; without the movement they would be a wood.

Two things follow from that. He is genuinely seeing — this is not blindness. And he is genuinely not seeing properly — he could not have crossed a street.

Then Jesus laid his hands on his eyes again; and he opened his eyes, his sight was restored, and he saw everything clearly.

Mark piles up three phrases where one would do — opened, restored, saw everything clearly — as though determined that nobody should be left wondering whether the job was finished.

Now, why in two stages? Not because the first touch failed. Look where Mark has put this story.

Four verses ago Jesus said to the Twelve: having eyes do you not see? Five verses later Peter will say you are the Christ — and six verses after that he will take Jesus aside and try to correct him about the cross.

That is a man seeing people like trees walking. Not blind. Genuinely seeing. Seeing wrong shapes.

The whole hinge of this Gospel is bracketed by a healing that took two touches, and it is the picture of what the disciples are going through: first sight at Caesarea Philippi, full sight only after a cross and an empty tomb.

But take it first as it stands, because a great many honest believers are the man in this story.

He was not blind any longer; he genuinely saw. But he did not yet see clearly, and if the account had stopped there he would have gone home able to make out shapes and nothing more.

A great many Christians live at exactly that stage. They see enough to know that Jesus is real, that the gospel is true, that they belong to him — and so much is still blurred. Prayers that feel like talking to a ceiling. Promises believed and not felt. A grasp of who he is that is more outline than face.

If that is you, hear what this healing says before it says anything about the Twelve. The same hand that gave the first touch gave the second. Jesus did not lead him out of the village, open his eyes halfway, and walk off satisfied. He stayed, and laid his hands on him again, and did not stop until the man saw everything clearly.

So do not despise a dim sight of Christ, and do not conclude from its dimness that you do not truly see him. Partial sight is real sight; the man who saw walking trees was no longer blind. But do not settle there either, as though blurred vision were all this life allows. Keep coming for the second touch — in the word, at the Table, on your knees, among his people — and know that the clearing of your sight is finally his work and not yours. He who began a good work in you will bring it to completion at the day of Jesus Christ (Phil. 1:6).

The full sight the disciples lacked came to them at last, after the cross and the empty tomb. And the day is coming when everyone who now sees through a glass darkly will see him face to face (1 Cor. 13:12). He has never yet left a work of his half-finished.

And he sent him to his home, saying, Do not even enter the village.

He is sent home rather than back into Bethsaida. Given what Jesus says elsewhere about that town's unbelief (Matt. 11:21), the instruction reads like mercy: a man with new eyes is not to be turned into a spectacle for people who will not be changed by him anyway.

verseByVerse.quote: And Jesus went on with his disciples to the villages of Caesarea Philippi. And on the way he asked his disciples, "Who do people say that I am?" And they told him, "John the Baptist; and others say, Elijah; and others, one of the prophets."
verseByVerse.commentary:
And Jesus went on with his disciples to the villages of Caesarea Philippi.

The location is chosen, and it is worth knowing what kind of place it was, because the setting is part of the sermon.

Caesarea Philippi sat twenty-five miles north of the Sea of Galilee at the foot of Mount Hermon, where one of the sources of the Jordan comes out of the rock. Beside that spring was a great cave sacred to Pan, the goat-god — the place was called Paneas — with niches cut into the cliff face for idols. Herod the Great had built a temple of white marble there to the divinity of Augustus. His son Philip had enlarged the town and renamed it after Caesar and himself.

So: a cliff full of pagan shrines, a temple to a man who called himself a god, and a city named for the emperor of the world.

That is where Jesus stops and asks who he is.

And on the way he asked his disciples. It happens on the road, walking. Mark keeps saying on the way from here on, and the way leads to Jerusalem.

Who do people say that I am?

He starts with the safe question. It is the one anybody can answer, because it requires nothing of the person answering. Report the opinions.

And they told him, John the Baptist; and others say, Elijah; and others, one of the prophets.

The same three answers Mark gave us in chapter 6, when the news reached Herod's palace (6:14–15). Nothing has moved. Months of ministry, thousands fed, a district full of healings, and the public verdict is exactly where it was.

And look at the quality of the answers, because they are not insults. Every one is a compliment.

John the Baptist — the greatest man born of women, come back. Elijah — the prophet Malachi said would come before the day of the LORD (Mal. 4:5). One of the prophets — a man who speaks for God.

These are the largest categories available, and every one of them is far too small. The crowd is doing what crowds always do: reaching for the biggest box it already owns, rather than admitting that a new one is required.

And the modern versions are the same shape at a lower altitude. A great moral teacher. A revolutionary. A mystic. A good man. All respectful, all inadequate, and all of them costing nothing — which is precisely their appeal. You can admire a prophet from a distance. You cannot admire the Son of God; you either fall down or walk away.

verseByVerse.quote: And he asked them, "But who do you say that I am?" Peter answered him, "You are the Christ." And he strictly charged them to tell no one about him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And he asked them, But who do you say that I am?

The but is a hinge, and the pronoun is emphatic in the Greek: you — what about you?

This is the question the whole Gospel has been walking toward, and it is put to them personally after they have safely reported what everyone else thinks. That order is deliberate, and it is worth applying.

It is perfectly possible to spend years discussing what people say about Jesus — what the church teaches, what your parents believed, what the current arguments are, what the objections come to. All of it can be conducted at a comfortable distance, and none of it commits you to anything.

Then a moment comes when the question is asked in the second person, and nobody can answer it on your behalf. Not a godly mother. Not a good church. Not a tradition you were raised in and still respect. Who do you say that I am?

If you have never answered that in your own words, you have not yet been asked anything by Christianity. You have only been informed.

Peter answered him, You are the Christ.

Four words in English, three in Greek. Peter, as always, gets there first and speaks for all of them.

The Christ — Christos, the Greek for the Hebrew Messiah, the Anointed One. It is not a surname. It is a title, and it carried the whole freight of Israel's hope: the promised son of David who would come and reign, restore the kingdom, and put the world right.

And it is correct. Jesus does not qualify it, does not correct it, and does not deny it.

Notice, though, what Mark leaves out. In Matthew's account of this same moment, Jesus answers Peter with a blessing — Blessed are you, Simon Bar-Jonah! For flesh and blood has not revealed this to you, but my Father who is in heaven, and the promise about the rock and the keys (Matt. 16:17–19).

Mark has none of it. This Gospel gives Peter's finest hour in four words and then gives his worst moment in full.

And this Gospel is Peter's own preaching. That is not an accident. The man remembered the rebuke and let the commendation go.

And he strictly charged them to tell no one about him.

The right answer, and immediately silenced.

Why? Because Christ was a word with a national programme attached, and the programme was wrong. A Messiah, in Galilee in that decade, meant a king who would raise an army and clear out Rome. Peter has said the true word with a false picture behind it — and the next verse is going to show just how false.

Jesus will let the title be shouted eventually. He accepts it under oath in front of the high priest, on the night it kills him (14:61–62), when there is no possibility of misunderstanding what kind of king he is.

verseByVerse.quote: And he began to teach them that the Son of Man must suffer many things and be rejected by the elders and the chief priests and the scribes and be killed, and after three days rise again. And he said this plainly. And Peter took him aside and began to rebuke him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And he began to teach them. Mark's word began marks a turn. Something starts here that had not been said before, and from now on it is the burden of everything.

That the Son of Man must suffer many things.

The little word must is one of the great words of the New Testament. It is dei — it is necessary, it is bound to be — and it is not the language of resignation. It is the language of a plan.

This is the point to be clear about, because everything about the cross depends on it. What is coming is not a defeat, an accident, a miscalculation, or a good movement overtaken by its enemies. It is a necessity — delivered up according to the definite plan and foreknowledge of God (Acts 2:23). The Lamb was slain from the foundation of the world.

And notice the four items, in order, because he gives them as a list.

Suffer many things. Be rejected by the elders and the chief priests and the scribes — that is the full Sanhedrin, all three constituencies of it named separately. Not rejected by the mob or the Romans, but by the official leadership of the people of God. And be killed. Flat, unadorned, no euphemism. And after three days rise again.

He told them the resurrection at the same time as the death, in the same sentence, the first time he ever mentioned either. They will not hear the second half at all — nobody in this Gospel ever refers to it again until the women come to the tomb — but he said it, from the very first telling.

A word about that phrase, after three days. Mark writes after three days here and twice more (9:31; 10:34), where Matthew and Luke say on the third day, and honest readers have wondered whether that demands a fourth day and breaks the Friday-to-Sunday timeline.

It does not. It is simply the Jewish way of counting, in which any part of a day counted as a whole day — so Friday, Saturday and Sunday are three days. And Scripture settles it on the spot: the chief priests, remembering this very prediction, tell Pilate that Jesus said After three days I will rise, and in the same breath ask for a guard until the third day (Matt. 27:63–64). Both phrases, of one and the same morning, from men who had every motive to be exact. There is no discrepancy — only two idioms for one promise.

And he said this plainly.

Four words, and they are a landmark in this Gospel.

Until now everything has been managed. Demons silenced. Healed men told to say nothing. Crowds taught in parables, with private explanations for those who stayed. Mark's Jesus has spent eight chapters keeping the lid on.

And the moment they get the title right, the lid comes off — and the first plain, unveiled, unparabolic thing he says to them is that he is going to be killed.

Which tells you what the secret was protecting. It was never that he was the Christ. It was what kind.

And Peter took him aside and began to rebuke him.

Read that slowly. Took him aside — a private word, man to man, kindly meant, out of earshot of the others. And then the verb: rebuke. It is the word used of Jesus rebuking demons and rebuking the wind.

Six verses after confessing him as the Christ, Peter takes the Christ to one side to correct him.

And he is doing it out of love. That is the thing to hold on to. He has just seen who this is, and he cannot bear what he has heard, and everything decent in him wants to stop it. Matthew records what he actually said: Far be it from you, Lord! This shall never happen to you (Matt. 16:22).

It is the most affectionate sentence in the chapter, and it gets the hardest answer in the book.

verseByVerse.quote: But turning and seeing his disciples, he rebuked Peter and said, "Get behind me, Satan! For you are not setting your mind on the things of God, but on the things of man."
verseByVerse.commentary:
But turning and seeing his disciples, he rebuked Peter.

Mark gives the choreography before the words, and it matters. Peter has taken him aside for a private conversation. Jesus turns round — away from Peter, toward the others — and looks at them, and only then speaks.

He makes it public, deliberately. Peter said it quietly; the answer is given in front of everybody, because every man there is thinking it and the correction is for all of them.

Get behind me, Satan!

The hardest sentence any disciple ever heard, spoken to the man who six verses earlier had given the best answer in the Gospel.

Two things keep it from being what it first appears.

First, it is not a verdict on Peter's soul. Jesus is not saying that Peter is demonic or damned; he goes on walking with him, takes him up the mountain in the very next chapter, and after the resurrection restores him on a beach. What is being identified is the source of the objection, not the state of the man.

Second, look at the content of what Peter said, and it is instantly recognisable. This shall never happen to you. A Messiah without a cross. A crown without a death. Glory by a shorter road.

He has heard that before. Mark told us in two verses that after the baptism the Spirit drove him into the wilderness and he was tempted by Satan for forty days (1:13), and Matthew and Luke record what the offer was: all the kingdoms of the world, without Calvary.

And he will hear it again, at the end. Passers-by at the foot of the cross, wagging their heads: save yourself, and come down from the cross (15:30). Same voice, same offer, three times — in a wilderness, from a friend, and from a crowd at an execution.

Get behind me is worth hearing precisely. It is not get away from me. It is the language of position: get back where a disciple stands, which is behind. Peter has got in front and started giving directions. He is being told to resume following.

For you are not setting your mind on the things of God, but on the things of man.

And there is the diagnosis, and it is the most useful sentence here for ordinary people, because it names a category rather than a sin.

Peter was not being wicked. He was thinking like a man. Every human instinct says that suffering is to be avoided, that a good plan does not end in a grave, that if you love somebody you get them out of danger. All of that is decent, and all of it is the things of man — and when it is set against the declared purpose of God it becomes, whatever the intention, the devil's argument.

Which is the warning to take away, and it is not what we expect from a passage with Satan in it. The most dangerous opposition to the will of God in your life will not come from your enemies. It will come from people who love you, meaning it kindly, taking you aside for a quiet word — and from the reasonable, protective, entirely natural voice in your own head that says: surely not this. Surely there is another way.

Peter's motives were good. Peter was wrong. And the two facts sat together in one man, in one sentence, six verses after the best confession in the Gospel.

verseByVerse.quote: And calling the crowd to him with his disciples, he said to them, "If anyone would come after me, let him deny himself and take up his cross and follow me.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And calling the crowd to him with his disciples.

Before a word of it, notice the audience. There is a crowd around, and he calls them over.

He could have said this to the Twelve. What follows is the most demanding thing in the Gospel, and every instinct of religious management would keep it for the committed. Instead he gathers the general public and states the terms out loud.

That settles a question permanently. Cross-bearing is not an advanced course for the heroic few, a special vocation for missionaries and martyrs while ordinary believers get an easier arrangement. It is the entry requirement, published, to anyone considering him.

If anyone would come after me. Anyone. And the phrase is the ordinary one for discipleship — to come after somebody is to walk behind them, which is exactly where Peter has just been told to get back to.

Then three things, in an order that cannot be rearranged.

Let him deny himself.

The verb is the one used of Peter in the courtyard: he denied Jesus, three times — I do not know the man, I have no connection with him, he is nothing to do with me (14:68–71).

That is the force of it, and it is much stronger than we usually allow. To deny yourself is to say about yourself what Peter said about Christ: I do not know this man; his claims have no authority over me; he does not get a vote.

So it is not self-improvement, and it is not asceticism. Giving up sugar for a season is not this. Nor is it self-hatred — the Bible never asks you to despise a creature God made and Christ died for. It is the removal of the self from the throne. The question what do I want? stops being the question that decides.

And that will not stay abstract if you make it concrete. Name the matter this week where what you want and what he wants are pulling in different directions — the money, the relationship, the grudge, the ambition, the hour of the day. If you cannot name one, the denial is theoretical, and theoretical self-denial has never cost anybody anything.

And take up his cross.

We have worn this phrase completely smooth, and it needs its edge back.

Nobody in that crowd heard a metaphor. Crucifixion was not a distant Roman practice; it was local and recent. When the revolt broke out after Herod the Great died, the governor Varus crucified two thousand Jews — and that was within living memory of the older people standing there.

They had all seen it: a condemned man carrying the crossbeam out to the execution site, stripped, jeered at along the road, walking in one direction only.

So take up your cross does not mean put up with a difficulty. We say it of a hard marriage, an illness, a tiresome colleague — and none of those is what the word meant to the people it was spoken to. A man carrying a cross was not a man with a burden. He was a man already condemned, publicly, on his way out of his own life.

Which means the call is to accept that the old self is under sentence, that the sentence is public, and that the walk goes one way. I have been crucified with Christ (Gal. 2:20) is not poetry; it is Paul saying he stood in that crowd, heard this, and agreed to it.

And follow me.

And the third is what turns the first two from grim heroism into something else entirely.

You are not asked to carry a cross into the dark by yourself. You are asked to walk behind someone — and he is going first, and he is not asking anything he has not already accepted. Within the week he will be in Gethsemane; within months he will carry the actual beam up an actual road.

The whole difference between Christian self-denial and mere religious severity is in that last word. It is not a discipline. It is a Person, walking ahead, whose back you can see.

verseByVerse.quote: For whoever would save his life will lose it, but whoever loses his life for my sake and the gospel's will save it. For what does it profit a man to gain the whole world and forfeit his soul? For what can a man give in return for his soul?
verseByVerse.commentary:
For whoever would save his life will lose it, but whoever loses his life for my sake and the gospel's will save it.

This is the reason for the demand, and it is worth noticing that it is an argument. He does not say because I say so. He gives a for — three of them in a row — and every one is an appeal to self-interest properly understood.

The word for life here is psychē, and it is the same word rendered soul in the next two verses. English has to use two words; Mark uses one, and the pun is the whole point. Your life, your self, your soul — the thing that is you.

So the sentence runs: whoever wants to hold on to himself will lose himself. Whoever hands himself over — for Christ, and for the gospel — gets himself back.

And this is not a religious paradox invented to sound deep. It is the most easily verified thing in the passage.

Look at the people you know. The ones who have organised their lives around protecting themselves — their comfort, their reputation, their options, their feelings — have they become larger or smaller? A life curved in on itself gets steadily narrower; the range of what can be enjoyed shrinks, the tolerance for inconvenience drops, and the person ends up with very little that is not about them. Everyone has watched this happen to somebody.

And the people you know who have genuinely spent themselves — on their children, on the sick, on a church, on the work of God in some obscure place — are almost always the ones with the most life in them. They are not depleted. They are the ones you go to when you are in trouble.

Jesus is not asking for a sacrifice that leaves you poorer. He is telling you where the arithmetic actually comes out.

For what does it profit a man to gain the whole world and forfeit his soul?

The most quoted sentence in this Gospel, and worn as smooth as the cross was. Give it back its teeth by taking the two halves seriously.

Gain the whole world. Not a good career. Not a comfortable house. The whole thing — everything there is to have, all of it, with nothing left over for anyone else. He is being deliberately extravagant, because he wants the best possible case for the other side. Suppose you won completely.

And forfeit his soul. The word is commercial, like the rest of the sentence — to be fined, to be charged, to suffer the loss of. He is doing a transaction: assets acquired, price paid.

And the sum does not work even at the maximum. Even if you got everything, you would have paid too much, because the thing paid over is the thing that would have enjoyed it.

Which is what makes this verse useful rather than merely solemn, because almost nobody is actually offered the whole world. What people trade their souls for is invariably smaller. A promotion. A house in the right street. A relationship that could not survive their being a Christian. The good opinion of a particular set of people. Twenty more years of being left alone.

If the whole world is a bad price, what is the price you are quietly considering?

For what can a man give in return for his soul?

The last question closes the door, and it is about redemption — the price of a life. What could you produce, if you had lost it, to get it back?

The psalmist asks the same thing and answers it: no man can ransom his brother or give to God the price of his life, for the ransom of their life is costly, and can never suffice (Ps. 49:7–8).

Never suffice. There is nothing in the world large enough, which means that a soul, once traded, cannot be bought back by any means available to the man who traded it.

And that is precisely why the next thing this Gospel says about the Son of Man is the sentence it has been walking toward: he came to give his life as a ransom for many (10:45). The price no man could pay was paid. Not by the world, which was never worth it — by him.

verseByVerse.quote: For whoever is ashamed of me and of my words in this adulterous and sinful generation, of him will the Son of Man also be ashamed when he comes in the glory of his Father with the holy angels."
verseByVerse.commentary:
For whoever is ashamed of me and of my words.

The last for, and it moves from the sums to something far more ordinary and far more likely.

Notice that he does not say whoever denies me, though Peter will do that within months, or whoever renounces me. He says ashamed — which is not a decision, not a denial, and not usually a moment at all. It is a temperature.

And it covers two things: me, and my words. A man can be quite content to be associated with Jesus in general and thoroughly embarrassed by particular things he said. Most of us find some of his words easy to quote and others we would rather were not there.

In this adulterous and sinful generation.

Adulterous is not primarily about sexual sin. It is the prophets' word for a people unfaithful to God, married to him and gone after other lovers (Hos. 1–3; Jer. 3). He is describing the pressure of the surrounding culture — the atmosphere in which being ashamed of him feels like good manners.

And that is exactly how it operates. Very few Christians in a comfortable country ever face a moment of denial. What we face is a thousand small pressures toward silence, and every one of them can be given a respectable name.

It is the conversation at work that turns, and the sentence you do not say. It is the qualifying phrase — I mean, I'm not one of those Christians — offered up to buy a little distance. It is the dinner party where you let it be assumed you agree, and tell yourself it was not the moment. It is the grace not said in a restaurant, the belief not mentioned to the new colleague after four years, the Bible turned face down when somebody comes in.

None of it feels like betrayal. All of it is what this verse is about.

Of him will the Son of Man also be ashamed when he comes in the glory of his Father with the holy angels.

And here is the answer, and it is a straight reciprocity: shame now, shame then.

Do not soften it, but do understand what it is measuring. He is not threatening people for a failure of nerve in a hard moment — the man who wrote down this sentence had failed exactly that, in a courtyard, three times, with oaths, and was forgiven on a beach and made the leader of the church. Settled shame is not the same as a moment of cowardice, and the difference is what you do afterwards.

What he is describing is a life in which he was quietly kept out of sight because the cost of being known with him was judged too high.

And now look at the picture in the last clause, because everything turns on it.

Consider who is speaking. A Galilean carpenter, standing on a road near a pagan shrine, in an occupied province, with a few dozen people around him, twelve of whom have just proved they do not understand a word. He has told them he is going to be arrested by the leadership of his own nation and executed.

And he says: when I come in the glory of my Father, with the holy angels.

That is Daniel's vision, and he has already told them he is that figure — one like a son of man coming with the clouds of heaven, given dominion and glory and a kingdom, and all peoples serving him (Dan. 7:13–14).

So the whole question of shame is finally a question of timing. There is a case for being embarrassed by him now: he is a provincial nobody with a crucifixion in front of him, and the world's opinion of him has not improved much since. And there is a day coming when the sky opens and the Son of Man arrives in his Father's glory with the armies of heaven, and every one of the people you were afraid of is looking at him.

Nobody will be ashamed of him then. The only question is whether you were ashamed of him now, when it cost something — and whether, on that day, the one thing you want is to hear him say your name in front of the holy angels and not look away.

8.theology:
Two feedings, not one story told twice. Jesus makes the disciples recite both with the figures (vv. 19–20), and Mark preserves a detail no editor combining two versions would keep straight: in chapter 6 the baskets are kophinoi, the small stiff wicker basket a Jew carried his own food in; here they are spurides, large hampers — the word used of the basket Paul was let down the Damascus wall in (Acts 9:25). Jesus uses each word of its own occasion. Twelve baskets for Israel, one for each tribe; seven for the nations, the number of fullness. And some of them have come from far away is how Scripture speaks of the Gentiles coming in (Isa. 60:4; Eph. 2:13).

Why no sign? Not because evidence is illegitimate — he had given a great deal and would give more. What he refuses is a miracle produced on demand as the price of belief, from men who have already shown what they do with the evidence they have. If they do not hear Moses and the Prophets, neither will they be convinced if someone should rise from the dead (Luke 16:31) — which proved exactly right, since somebody did, and the men who got the report first paid soldiers to say the body was stolen (Matt. 28:12–13).

After three days. Mark's phrase (v. 31; 9:31; 10:34) against Matthew's and Luke's on the third day is not a discrepancy but the Jewish reckoning, in which any part of a day counts as a day. Scripture settles it: the chief priests recall this prediction as After three days I will rise and in the same breath ask Pilate for a guard until the third day (Matt. 27:63–64).

Get behind me, Satan. Not a verdict on Peter — Jesus takes him up the mountain in the next chapter and restores him on a beach at the end. It names the source of the objection. This shall never happen to you (Matt. 16:22) is a kingdom without a cross, which is the wilderness offer (1:13) returning through the mouth of a friend, and it will come a third time from passers-by at the foot of the cross — save yourself, and come down (15:30).
8.examples:
Then: a crowd in Galilee hearing take up his cross in a country where the governor Varus had crucified two thousand men within living memory. Nobody heard a metaphor. They had watched condemned men carry the crossbeam out through the streets, stripped and jeered at, walking in one direction only.

Now: we have worn the phrase smooth and made a cross into a difficulty — a hard marriage, an illness, a colleague. That is not what it meant. A man carrying a cross was not a man with a burden; he was a man already condemned, publicly, on his way out of his own life.

And deny himself is the verb used of Peter in the courtyard: I do not know the man, he is nothing to do with me. That is what you are asked to say about yourself — not self-hatred, and not going without sugar, but the removal of the self from the throne, so that what do I want? stops being the question that decides. Name the specific matter this week where that is in play. If you cannot name one, the denial is theoretical.

And the third word is what keeps this from being grim heroism: follow me. You are not asked to carry a cross into the dark alone. You are asked to walk behind somebody whose back you can see, who is going first, and who within months will carry an actual beam up an actual road.

One more, from v. 38. He does not say whoever denies me — he says ashamed, which is not a decision or a moment but a temperature. Very few Christians in a comfortable country face a moment of denial. What we face is a thousand small pressures toward silence, each with a respectable name: the sentence not said when the conversation turned, the qualifying phrase offered up to buy distance (I'm not one of those Christians), the belief not mentioned to a colleague in four years. None of it feels like betrayal. All of it is what the verse is about.

9.title: Transfiguration, Unbelief, and Greatness Redefined
9.text: "Immediately the father of the child cried out and said, 'I believe; help my unbelief!'" (Mark 9:24 ESV)
9.overview:
Chapter 9 moves from the heights of the Transfiguration to the depths of the disciples' failure in the valley, and then settles into a series of teachings on discipleship that are among the most demanding in the gospels. The Transfiguration (vv. 1–13) is the second touch on the disciples' eyes — the fuller sight that the first touch (the confession) was preparing them for. On the mountain, the full identity of Jesus is disclosed: his clothes become dazzling white, Moses and Elijah appear, and the Father's voice speaks again as at the baptism — 'This is my beloved Son; listen to him.' The command is directed at the disciples: whatever else you listen to, listen to him.

The immediate descent from the mountain into the crisis of the epileptic boy (vv. 14–29) is one of the most vivid transitions in the gospels, and one of the most theologically rich. The disciples who could not cast out the demon represent every generation of Christians who have attempted ministry in their own strength and found it inadequate. Jesus's identification of the problem — 'This kind cannot be driven out by anything but prayer' — is the gospel's clearest statement that spiritual power is not a possession to be deployed but a dependence to be maintained. The father's cry — 'I believe; help my unbelief!' — is the most honest prayer in the chapter and one of the most honest in all of Scripture.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–29 — The Transfiguration and the Failed Exorcism
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The six days that separate the Transfiguration from the confession (v. 2) recall Exodus 24:16, where Moses waited six days on Sinai before the glory of the Lord appeared. The Transfiguration is a Sinai-event: a mountain, a cloud, a voice from the cloud, Moses present. But where the glory of Sinai was external to Moses — he reflected it — here the glory is intrinsic to Jesus. His garments become dazzling white, beyond any laundry. He is not reflecting glory; he is radiating it from within. For a moment, the veil of flesh is transparent, and the disciples see what is always true of the one they follow.

The descent from the mountain and the encounter with the epileptic boy (vv. 14–29) is framed by the disciples' failure. They could not cast out the demon; they had done it before (6:7–13) and now they cannot. The scribes are arguing with them — presumably about the failure. Jesus arrives and takes control. His frustration — 'O faithless generation, how long am I to be with you? How long am I to bear with you?' — is addressed not just to the disciples but to the whole generation. The healing is dramatic, violent, public. Afterward, privately, the disciples ask why they could not cast it out. The answer is prayer.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Transfiguration confirms what Peter confessed in chapter 8 and opens to view what the cross has temporarily veiled. The voice from the cloud ('This is my beloved Son; listen to him') adds to the baptismal declaration ('You are my beloved Son') a command directed at the disciples: listen to him. Specifically listen to him about what he has just told them — the suffering, rejection, death, and resurrection of the Son of Man. The Transfiguration does not revoke the passion prediction; it confirms that the one heading toward the cross is the one whose face shines like the sun. The glory is going into the darkness voluntarily. That is what makes the cross an act of love rather than a defeat.

Moses and Elijah appearing with Jesus represent the Law and the Prophets — the entire Old Testament witness — coming to do homage to the one they were always pointing toward. The conversation, Luke tells us, was about his 'departure' (exodus) which he was about to accomplish in Jerusalem. The OT witnesses are discussing the cross. The entire canonical tradition converges on this moment and this destination.
verseByVerse.examples: The father of the epileptic boy has brought his son to the disciples in Jesus's absence and found them powerless. When Jesus arrives, the man's plea is tinged with disappointment: 'If you can do anything, have compassion on us and help us.' 'If you can' — the doubt has crept in from the disciples' failure. Jesus's response redirects the condition: 'If you can! All things are possible for one who believes.' The father's answer is the most honest thing anyone says to Jesus in the gospels: 'I believe; help my unbelief!' He does not pretend to have more faith than he has; he does not manufacture a confidence he doesn't feel. He brings his faith — real but mixed with doubt — and asks Jesus to supply what is lacking. This is the prayer that God always answers, because it comes from a person who is genuinely honest rather than performing spiritual adequacy.

verseByVerse.quote: And after six days Jesus took with him Peter and James and John, and led them up a high mountain by themselves. And he was transfigured before them, and his garments became radiant, intensely white, as no one on earth could bleach them. And there appeared to them Elijah with Moses, and they were talking with Jesus.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Verse 1 — 'There are some standing here who will not taste death until they see the kingdom of God after it has come with power' — is one of the most debated verses in Mark. The most natural interpretation within Mark's narrative is that the Transfiguration is the event referred to: some of the disciples (Peter, James, John) will see it six days later. The Transfiguration is a proleptic vision of the kingdom of God in power — a temporary lifting of the veil on what is always and finally true. The interpretation that refers this to the resurrection (more likely given the 'after it has come' and 'in power') or to Pentecost or to the fall of Jerusalem all find their adherents; the Transfiguration remains the most immediate and textually connected referent.

The dazzling white of Jesus's garments — beyond the whitening capacity of any launderer — is Mark's equivalent of Matthew's 'his face shone like the sun.' The glory is not borrowed or reflected; it is his own, released from within. Peter's suggestion to build three shelters (one for Jesus, one for Moses, one for Elijah) is well-intentioned and theologically confused: he is proposing to domesticate the vision, to make the temporary permanent, to treat the three figures as equals. The cloud and the voice correct him: 'This is my beloved Son; listen to him.' One authority. One voice. One obedience.

Ask why these two men in particular. Moses is the Law; Elijah is the Prophets — between them they are the whole Old Testament standing on that mountain, and they have not come to be admired alongside Jesus but to attend upon him. And Luke, telling the same scene, lets us hear what they were talking about: they spoke of his departure, which he was about to accomplish at Jerusalem (Luke 9:31). The word Luke uses is exodus. Moses, who led the first one out of Egypt, is discussing the greater one with the man who will lead it — and the road out runs through a cross. So the Law and the Prophets, given six days after Jesus first told his disciples he must suffer and be killed, appear in glory and talk about exactly that. The whole canonical witness converges here, on this man, and points at the same destination he has just been rebuked by Peter for naming. Then Moses and Elijah are gone and Jesus is left alone, which is Mark's way of saying what the voice has already said: they have done their work; now listen to him.

verseByVerse.quote: And as they were coming down the mountain, he charged them to tell no one what they had seen, until the Son of Man had risen from the dead. So they kept the matter to themselves, questioning what this rising from the dead meant.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The instruction to maintain silence 'until the Son of Man had risen from the dead' acknowledges the disciples' bewilderment — they do not understand what resurrection from the dead means, apparently imagining some kind of private experience rather than a bodily event. The silence is maintained until the appropriate time; the Transfiguration's disclosure will make full sense only in light of the resurrection. The sequence is important: you cannot understand the mountain without the empty tomb.

The disciples' question about Elijah (vv. 11–13) arises from the scribal teaching that Elijah must come before the Messiah (Mal. 4:5). Jesus confirms: Elijah does come first, to restore all things. And then identifies John the Baptist as the Elijah who came — and who was treated 'as they wished' (that is, beheaded). The implication is explicit: 'as it is written of him' — the Son of Man will also suffer many things and be treated with contempt. The pattern of the forerunner is the pattern of the one he announced.

verseByVerse.quote: And when they came to the disciples, they saw a great crowd around them, and scribes arguing with them. And immediately all the crowd, when they saw him, were greatly amazed and ran to him and greeted him. And he asked them, 'What are you arguing about with them?' And someone from the crowd answered him, 'Teacher, I brought my son to you, for he has a spirit that makes him mute… and I asked your disciples to cast it out, and they were not able.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
The transition from the mountain of the Transfiguration to the valley of the failed exorcism is one of Mark's most deliberate contrasts. On the mountain: the Son of God blazing with uncreated light, Moses and Elijah attending, the Father's voice certifying his identity. In the valley: a convulsing child, a desperate father, scribes pressing their advantage over embarrassed disciples. The glory was real; the failure is also real; and both are part of the same story.

The scribes are arguing with the disciples — presumably about their failure. They have found the crack in the apostolic armour and are pressing it. Jesus's question ('What are you arguing about?') draws the whole situation into his hands before a single word of healing is spoken. The crowd runs to him and greets him — the word (aspazomenoi) suggests something like astonished reverence. His arrival changes everything.

The disciples who could not cast out the demon had been given authority over unclean spirits (3:15) and had exercised it successfully (6:13). They are not beginners. Their failure is not for lack of experience but for lack of dependence — they have begun to treat spiritual authority as a possession rather than a delegated gift maintained through ongoing relationship with the one who gave it. The gap between the mountain and the valley is exactly the gap between the disciples who stayed behind and the three who saw the glory. But Jesus's frustration — 'O faithless generation, how long am I to be with you? How long am I to bear with you?' (v. 19) — is not directed only at the nine. It is the voice of the eternal Son, momentarily unveiled in the Transfiguration, now confronting the unbelief of a whole generation, including his own disciples.

verseByVerse.quote: And they brought the boy to him. And when the spirit saw him, immediately it convulsed the boy, and he fell on the ground and rolled about, foaming at the mouth… Jesus said to him, 'How long has this been happening to him?' And he said, 'From childhood. And it has often cast him into fire and into water, to destroy him. But if you can do anything, have compassion on us and help us.' And Jesus said to him, 'If you can! All things are possible for one who believes.' Immediately the father of the child cried out and said, 'I believe; help my unbelief!'
verseByVerse.commentary:
The father has watched his son suffer from childhood. Every fire, every body of water has been a potential grave. He has lived with the weight of it for years. And now the disciples have failed him. His words to Jesus are tinged with that failure: 'If you can do anything' — the condition that has crept in from the disciples' powerlessness. The faith that brought him here is real but wounded.

Jesus's response is astonishing in its rhetorical force. He does not answer the condition; he reverses it: 'If you can! All things are possible for one who believes.' The 'if you can' is bounced back. The question is not about Jesus's capacity — that is not in doubt. The question is about the father's faith. And here Mark gives us one of the most honest and beautiful moments in all the gospels.

“I believe; help my unbelief!” (v. 24)

This is the prayer of a man who refuses to pretend. He does not claim more faith than he has. He does not perform confidence he does not feel. He does not stay silent because his faith is impure. He brings both things to Jesus at once: the faith that is there, however small, and the unbelief that is also there, however unwelcome. And he asks Jesus to do something with both. I believe — the faith is real. Help my unbelief — so is the doubt. Both are laid at the feet of Christ.

This is perhaps the most theologically honest prayer in Scripture, and the answer Jesus gives to it is the most important thing about it: he heals the boy. He does not say, come back when your faith is complete. He does not require pure, unmingled trust before he acts. He meets the faith that is there, however trembling, however mixed with doubt, and he does what the man's doubt said he couldn't. The healing is the answer to both halves of the prayer — to the faith and to the unbelief. The father believed; and his unbelief was helped, not by an improved feeling, but by the sight of his son standing on his feet.

The exorcism itself is violent: the spirit throws the boy into terrible convulsions and comes out with a shriek. The boy lies like a corpse. 'He is dead,' say many in the crowd. Jesus takes him by the hand — the same gesture used for Jairus's daughter (5:41) and Peter's mother-in-law (1:31) — and lifts him up. The Son of Man who on the mountain was shown to be Lord over death demonstrates it again in the valley, quietly, with a hand extended to a broken child.

verseByVerse.quote: And when he had entered the house, his disciples asked him privately, 'Why could we not cast it out?' And he said to them, 'This kind cannot be driven out by anything but prayer.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
The disciples' question is asked privately — they are not embarrassed publicly, but they are genuinely confused. They have done this before. They have the authority. Why did it fail? Jesus's answer does not identify a defect in technique, a wrong formula, an insufficient intensity of command. The problem is not the word spoken but the life lived. 'This kind cannot be driven out by anything but prayer.'

Prayer here is not a method added to the exorcism — it is the posture of the whole life. The disciples who could not cast out the demon had apparently been operating out of a kind of spiritual capital accumulated from their earlier successes. Authority was something they possessed. Prayer is the constant, conscious, moment-by-moment acknowledgment that you possess nothing — that every act of spiritual power is the extension of his authority through your dependence, not the exercise of your own. The disciples' failure was a failure of prayer in this deeper sense: they had stopped living in the place of radical dependence where spiritual authority actually operates.

Alistair Begg notes that the disciples' failure is not unique to the first century. Every generation of the church faces the same temptation: to deploy the forms of spiritual ministry without the reality of ongoing communion with the one who gives it its power. Technique without prayer is the disciples in the valley. Prayer without ceasing — the maintained, humble, daily dependence — is the life that keeps the authority fresh. cf. John 15:5; Luke 18:1

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 30–50 — Second Passion Prediction and Discipleship Teaching
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The second passion prediction (vv. 30–32) is delivered quietly, on the road through Galilee, and the disciples 'did not understand the saying, and were afraid to ask him.' The fear of asking is almost worse than the failure to understand: they know something important is being said, and they do not want to face what it means. Into the silence of their non-question they substitute a discussion about which of them is the greatest. The juxtaposition is Mark at his most pointed: Jesus is describing his death, and the disciples are arguing about pre-eminence.

The teaching that follows (vv. 33–50) is a sustained engagement with the question of greatness and the nature of the kingdom. Greatness in the kingdom is measured by servanthood; the child placed in the centre is the model of kingdom receptivity; the outsider casting out demons in Jesus's name is to be welcomed; and the alternative to the radical amputation of sin is the consuming fire of judgment. The teaching is demanding, concrete, and urgent.
verseByVerse.theology: The child placed in the disciples' midst (vv. 36–37) is a powerful kingdom symbol. In the ancient world, children had no social standing — they were economically dependent, legally invisible, socially marginal. To receive a child 'in my name' is to receive the one who has no claim, who brings nothing, who can contribute nothing. And Jesus says: whoever receives such a one receives me, and whoever receives me receives the one who sent me. The economy of the kingdom inverts the economy of the world: status is assigned not by what you produce or contribute but by who you are — a beloved child of the Father. The child in the middle is not an object lesson in innocence; it is an object lesson in dependence and receptivity, the qualities that characterize kingdom membership.
verseByVerse.examples: The three sayings about hell (vv. 43–48) use the image of Gehenna — the Valley of Hinnom south of Jerusalem, which had been the site of child sacrifice under Ahaz and Manasseh (2 Chr. 28:3; 33:6) and became in Jewish thought the image of final judgment and destruction. The threefold repetition — 'where their worm does not die and the fire is not quenched' (quoting Isa. 66:24) — is designed to penetrate. Jesus is speaking about the permanent consequences of a life of sin, and he is serious. The radical surgery he recommends — cutting off the hand, plucking out the eye — is hyperbole designed to convey the seriousness of the stakes, not literal self-mutilation. The point: sin is serious enough to require radical measures. What you allow to remain in your life will take you where you do not want to go. Better to arrive at the kingdom impoverished than to go to destruction intact.

verseByVerse.quote: And they came to Capernaum. And when he was in the house he asked them, 'What were you discussing on the way?' But they kept silent, for on the way they had argued with one another about who was the greatest. And he sat down and called the twelve. And he said to them, 'If anyone would be first, he must be last of all and servant of all.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
The second passion prediction (vv. 31–32) — 'The Son of Man is going to be delivered into the hands of men, and they will kill him. And when he is killed, after three days he will rise' — is the most compressed of the three. The disciples do not understand and are afraid to ask. Their subsequent argument about greatness is not merely a lapse of attention; it is the revelation of where their minds are when Jesus talks about the cross. They are pursuing a future in which they are great; he is walking toward one in which he is killed. The kingdom they imagine and the kingdom he is bringing are not the same kingdom.

Jesus's definition of greatness — 'last of all and servant of all' — is followed by a physical demonstration: he takes a child, places it in the midst, and says whoever receives one such child in his name receives him. The child is the embodied sermon. Greatness is not measured by the significance of the people you serve — it is measured by the willingness to serve those who have nothing to offer in return. The child gives the disciple nothing. That is precisely the point.

verseByVerse.quote: John said to him, 'Teacher, we saw someone casting out demons in your name, and we tried to stop him, because he was not following us.' But Jesus said, 'Do not stop him, for no one who does a mighty work in my name will be able soon afterward to speak evil of me. For the one who is not against us is for us.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
The disciples' attempt to stop the unnamed exorcist is an expression of the same concern for institutional boundaries that produced the argument about greatness. If you're not part of our group, you're not authorized. Jesus's response is generous and practical: if someone is successfully doing what you're doing, in my name, they're not your opponent. The criterion of kingdom membership is not association with the Twelve but relationship with the name of Jesus. The boundaries of the kingdom are wider than the boundaries of the official movement, and attempts to police those wider boundaries are not God's work.

But 'the one who is not against us is for us' (v. 40) seems to collide head-on with something Jesus says elsewhere — 'whoever is not with me is against me' (Matt 12:30; Luke 11:23) — and a reader who notices it deserves an answer. Set side by side the two look like opposites: here neutrality counts in a man's favour, there it counts against him. But they are not answering the same question, and that is the whole key. Here the subject is a fellow worker — a man casting out demons in Jesus' name, plainly on Christ's side, who simply does not belong to the disciples' circle; and the lesson is generosity: do not treat an ally as an enemy merely because he is not one of your party. There the subject is Christ himself, and the men in view are the Pharisees who had just called his works the devil's — open opponents; and the lesson is that toward Jesus there is no neutral ground, no fence to sit on. So the two sayings guard two different errors. Toward other Christians who serve under a different banner than ours, we are far too quick to say 'against us,' and Jesus says: not so — if he is for me, he is for you. Toward the Lord himself, we would love to imagine a comfortable middle ground of the undecided, and Jesus says: there is none — a heart not with him is already against him. Read together they are not a contradiction but a pair of fences: be generous about the boundaries of the movement, and be uncompromising about the claims of the King.

verseByVerse.quote: 'And if your hand causes you to sin, cut it off. It is better for you to enter life crippled than with two hands to go to hell, to the unquenchable fire. And if your foot causes you to sin, cut it off… And if your eye causes you to sin, tear it out.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
The 'little ones who believe' (v. 42) are not children but the newly believing, the vulnerable, the easily discouraged — anyone whose faith is still fragile. To cause one of them to stumble — to sin, to fall away — is the worst possible action; better to be thrown into the sea with a millstone around your neck. The severity is not rhetorical excess; it reflects the value Jesus places on those who belong to him, however small their faith.

The three-fold radical surgery (hand, foot, eye) uses the rabbinic technique of progressive examples to make a single point: no attachment, however important to your life, is worth more than your eternal wellbeing. The examples are hyperbolic — Jesus is not commending literal self-mutilation, which could not in any case remove the sin that originates in the heart. The point is the seriousness of sin and the ruthlessness that genuine holiness requires toward it.

The word rendered 'hell' three times over is Gehenna — the Valley of Hinnom, a ravine just outside Jerusalem. There, in the darkest days of the kingdom, apostate Israel had burned its own children alive in sacrifice to Molech (2 Kgs 23:10; Jer 7:31), and ever after the place was accursed, a smouldering rubbish-heap where the city's refuse and the corpses of criminals were thrown to burn. Jesus takes that real, stinking, fire-lit valley and makes it his picture of final judgment: the place fit only for what is utterly rejected. And his words 'where their worm does not die and the fire is not quenched' (v. 48) are not his own invention but a quotation of the last verse of Isaiah (Isa 66:24), which pictures the endless corpses of those who rebelled against God — the undying worm and unquenchable fire together saying one terrible thing: this ruin does not end. (A reader with a King James Bible will find this refrain also at verses 44 and 46; those repetitions are a copyist's echo of verse 48 and are not in the earliest manuscripts, which is why modern Bibles drop them to a footnote. Nothing is lost — the sentence stands, once, in full force, at verse 48.)

Then the strangest line of all: 'everyone will be salted with fire' (v. 49). It is deliberately double-edged. Fire in this passage has just meant judgment — and everyone will meet it. But salt, in the Old Testament, was rubbed into every sacrifice offered to God (Lev 2:13, 'the salt of the covenant'). So the saying holds two destinies in one breath: the unrepentant will be salted with the fire that consumes, but the disciple — who has just been told to cut off hand and foot rather than perish — is salted with the fire that purifies, the costly, cleansing fire of a life laid on the altar. The same fire destroys the one and refines the other. Which is why Jesus can turn at once to the gentler word: 'Salt is good' (v. 50) — salt preserves and flavours and creates peace; have it in yourselves and be at peace with one another. The connection to the preceding teaching: radical inward holiness (not outward self-harm) is the salt that preserves the community.
